 (2005-2006) of the Department of  Scientific and Industrial Research which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 25
th

P.G,NARAYANAN

REPORT
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research
 on the Recommendations contained in the One Hundred Forty Second Report of the Department-related Parliamentary
 Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2005-2006) of the
 Department of Scientific & Industrial Research, presented to both Houses of Parliament on 25 th April, 2005.  There
 were eighteen Recommendations contained in the Report. Action Taken note on those Recommendations was received

 from the Department on 3rd August, 2005.  The Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report in its meeting held
 on 18 th November, 2005 and decided to seek clarification/additional information on certain points  contained in paras 
 21, 29, 37, 40, 44, 48, 58 and 68.  The Department’s clarification/additional information on the points was received on
 1st December, 2005.
The Committee’s Recommendations, Action Taken thereon by the Department of Scientific & Industrial Research,
 points raised by the Committee (wherever necessary), clarifications by the Department and comments of the Committee
 thereon are set out in the succeeding paragraphs:-
 BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendation  
        The Committee finds that pace of expenditure for the fourth quarter of 2004-2005 is not uniform and there is a lot
 of variation in them. The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Department in this regard and is of the
 considered view that the Department needs to evolve a mechanism to maintain uniform pace of expenditure, to the
 extent possible, throughout the year.                                                                      (Para 11)                    
Action Taken by the Department
     During the financial year 2004-05, the vote on account was passed by the Parliament twice. On the first occasion it
 was for four months before dissolution of the Lok Sabha and thereafter for two months after formation of new Lok
 Sabha. Due to this, the Grant-in-aid to CSIR which constitutes a major portion of the total grant of the Department was
 released twice in the 1
st and 3 rd quarter of the financial year. No grant-in-aid could be released to CSIR in the 2 nd
 quarter of the year resulting in an un-even booking of the expenditure during the financial year. However, in the 4 th
 quarter an amount of Rs. 342.28 crore was released on the basis of approved Revised Estimates of the Department Thus
 except for 2 nd quarter, the pace of expenditure was uniform. However, considering the observations of the Committee
 various measures have been taken by the Department. to book the expenditure proportionately throughout the current
 financial year. These include phasing of the project activities in a manner that expenditure is booked evenly without
 affecting their progress. The progress of expenditure is monitored on monthly basis to maintain uniformity in each
 quarter of the financial year. Secondly, the expenditure details under each scheme/project are put on the website for
 quick decision making. Quarterly monitoring meetings of the progress of projects will further help in utilizing the
 budget resources in a uniform manner.
Comments
       The Committee notes the reply. 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR)
Recommendation
            The Committee appreciates that the CSIR is striving towards undertaking a wide gamut of research and
 developmental activities in the area of high technology, which would help in projecting India as a forerunner amongst
 scientifically advanced nations. The Committee, however, feels that emphasis of CSIR should be dissemination of new
 technologies from the laboratories for the benefit of the common man.                (Para 21)                              
                                                   
Action Taken by the Department
CSIR’s research outputs of new knowledge, products/technologies are placed in the public domain through

Thus information about various R&D programs, new technologies and other activities of CSIR laboratories is
 disseminated through CSIR Samachar (Hindi, monthly) and CSIR News (English, fortnightly). CSIR News and
 CSIR Samachar not only provide information on R&D programmes but also help in forming useful links between
 various CSIR constituents and users, other R&D organizations, university departments and industry.
·            Research-based scientific information, covering all the major disciplines of Science & Technology, is
 disseminated through 17 scholarly research journals and two secondary scientific journals brought out by
 NISCAIR.  All journals are peer-reviewed and covered by major indexing and abstracting services.
·            CSIR is also committed to inculcating scientific temper among common people and achieve this through three
 well-circulated popular science magazines brought out by NISCAIR – Vigyan Pragati, Science Reporter and
 Science ki Duniya.  These magazines apart from publishing informative popular science articles on
 contemporary science topics, science news from around the world, inventions and discoveries, science projects,
 biographies of scientists, etc. also disseminate information on new technologies/developments in CSIR
 laboratories.
·
            CSIR is bringing out a journal of Rural Technology, (English) aimed at disseminating information on
 emerging rural technologies and their outreach to rural communities, Is this Hindi and English or  bilingual
 specify.
    Besides specially the dissemination through print media, CSIR laboratories establish interactions with common
 man and other stake holders through measures such as participation in Exhibitions; business development and
 marketing through IPR acquisition/ exploitation; establishing direct interaction/linkages/joint ventures with
 industry.
          Following is the illustrative list of specific initiatives by some of the labs:
·
        CIMAP disseminates its technology for the entrepreneurs, industry personnel, researchers and farmers by
 organizing the “National Interactive Meet (NIM)” every two years and “Kisan Melas-Farmers Fairs” on yearly
 basis where the newly developed agrotechnologies (plant varieties), process technologies and processes for
 herbal product formulations are displayed for their commercial exploitation. CIMAP gets a high positive
 response and most of the newly developed agrotechnologies get transferred to the farmers/growers for the
 benefits of the common man.
·
         CMERI disseminates information on the new technologies for the common man through different channels (i)
 Newspaper (ii) Exhibition (iii) Trade fair (iv) Industrial Get together (v) Leaflet (vi) Technical film (vi) CMERI
 updated website (www.cmeri.res.in) and (vii) Training in new technologies.
·        IIP disseminates the information about the developed technologies through means such as participating in
 exhibitions, seminar/workshops, special publications such as “Compendium of technologies/techniques
 developed” and “ An Insight-IIP” IIP- Industry Meets etc.
·        NBRI disseminates its technologies by way of training demonstrations to      various sections of society
Point raised by the Committee
How is the effectiveness of Programmes like NIM and Kisan Melas are measured?  How many agro technologies
 have been developed so far and transferred to the farmers? 
Clarification by the Department
 (i)        The National Interactive Meets (NIM) organised by Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants (CIMAP)
 provide effective platform for close interaction among participating industry leaders, growers of medicinal and
 aromatic plants and the scientists. These are the business like meets wherein technologies developed are

Comments
        The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction. It would at the same time observe that our country with a
 substantial population of small and marginal farmers having small land holdings require technology suited to them at
 affordable prices. If the technology does not suit their requirement or beyond their affording capacity, our efforts, in that
 case, may not have the desired result. Involving Industry for commercial production of such technology and creating
 market among farmers for such indigenous technologies is the need of the hour. Interactive programmes like “National
 Interactive Meet (NIM)” and Kisan Melas should be organized frequently throughout the country in order to
 disseminate the developed technologies and also to get the necessary feedback from the users.
NATIONAL LABORATORIES
Recommendation
The Committee commends the efforts of the Department to keep pace with the new technologies and to project
 the country as a technologically developed nation. The Committee feels that keeping in view the fact that the CSIR
 infrastructure was built or acquired more than thirty years ago, building of new infrastructure and renovation of the
 existing ones are of utmost importance and should be taken up in right
 earnest.                                                                                                     
(Para 25)
Action Taken by the Department

           A scheme on Infrastructure Renovation and Refurbishing has been taken up in the X Plan for upgrading the
 ageing infrastructures at CSIR laboratories. Under this, 33% of the budgetary resources provided by the government
 have been allocated to renovation/refurbishing and the rest of the resources would be met from the internal resources of
 CSIR.
Comments
      The decision of the Department to mobilize two- third of the resources required for renovation of its labs on its own
 from the internal resources is a welcome step and indicative of future scheme of things. In all likelihood self-financing
 of projects under the aegis of the State will be the trend of the future. The Committee appreciates the scheme as a step in
 right direction.
RESEARCH SCHEMES, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS
Recommendation
      The Committee notes that most of the scholarships/fellowships are provided to students at the higher level i.e. Ph.D /
 Research levels. The Committee recommends that scholarships/fellowships may be provided at the entry level i.e.
 graduation level and may be increased for students in Post-graduate level to stimulate interest among the new generation
 towards basic sciences. The Committee also recommends that the number and amount of fellowships/scholarships
 should be increased over a period of time. The Committee feels that for the development of science, there is a need to
 improve the opportunities for well-trained scientists and young talents to pursue innovative research, to educate the next
 generation to apply science in areas of importance for the health, prosperity and security of the nation .                           
 (Para 29)
Action Taken by the Department
CSIR Fellowships/Scholarships are provided for doing doctoral & post-doctoral research.  CSIR has, however,
 initiated two programmes during the recent years, which cater to graduate & post graduate students: -
CSIR has initiated a unique ‘hand holding scheme’ “CSIR programme on Youth for Leadership in Science
 (CPYLS)” during the X Plan to attract the best young school students towards science. Every year top 100
 students at the Secondary School Examination (X Class) from CBSE, ICSE & State Boards are invited at CSIR
 expense to visit the nearest CSIR Laboratory for two open days along with one of their parents/guardian/teacher.
 The objective of this scheme is to expose the young students to the exciting world of science so as to build
 scientific temper at an early age. Amongst these students, who secure over 90% marks in natural science subjects
 (Physics, Chemistry, Biology & Mathematics) in the Senior Secondary Examination and continue to pursue
 science subjects, at graduation level are supported financially for 14 weeks in a year for another three years till
 graduation to do project work in a CSIR laboratory of their interest.
CSIR is also supporting “Integrated Ph.D. programme in specialized areas” on an experimental basis under the
 theme ‘catch them young’. Under this programme, fellowships are given to M.Sc. students for two years. After
 two years on getting M.Sc. degree, Junior Research Fellowships are provided to those students who qualify NET
 (National Eligibility Test for Junior Research Fellowship & Eligibility for Lecturership).
Point raised by the Committee
            In a competitive world where business studies and information technology disciplines promise faster and higher
 growth, incentives offered in the area of Basic Science Research seem meagre. What has been done by the Department
 to bring back talented students to basic science courses keeping in mind lucrative careers offered in other fields?

Clarification by the Department
             CSIR reiterates that it has initiated a unique ‘hand holding scheme’ “CSIR Programme on Youth for Leadership
 in Science (CPYLS)” to attract the best young school students towards science. Every year top 100 students at the
 Secondary School Examination (X Class) from CBSE, ICSE & States Boards are invited at CSIR expenses to the
 nearest CSIR laboratory for two open days along with one of their parents/guardian/teacher. The objective of this
 scheme is to expose the young students to the exciting world of science so as to build scientific temper at an early age
 and attract them towards science education.
In furtherance to the objective encouraging budding young scientific talent and to nourish the scientific research
 in basic sciences, CSIR has a special fellowship scheme, named Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Fellowship (SPMF), for
 selected top 20% of NET qualified scholars and top 100 GATE qualified scholars with percentile 99.
The SPM Fellowship carries an amount of Rs. 12,000/- p.m. for the first two years followed by Rs. 15,000/- p.m.
 for the remaining tenure plus other benefits like HRA and medical allowances, as applicable to CSIR’ NET JRFs and a
 contingent grant of Rs. 50,000/- per annum.
Comments
       The Committee notes that a number of incentive schemes have been introduced by the Department to attract young
 talent towards basic science and research.  The Department should, however, periodically  evaluate and monitor these
 schemes to ensure their effectiveness and suitably amend them, if necessary.   
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT
Recommendation   
        The Committee commends the CSIR for achieving number one position in securing Patents in India and abroad and
 hopes that the CSIR would strive towards safeguarding the country's interests, specially keeping in view the efforts
 made by foreign organizations to encroach upon our traditional base.                                                (Para 37)
Action Taken by the Department
     To safeguard our traditional knowledge base, CSIR through its NISCAIR is jointly working with the Department of
 Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha and Homeopathy (AYUSH), Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Govt. of India on
 Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL). The information available from this library will be useful to the
 examiners in the patent offices worldwide in several languages to prevent the grant of patents based on such knowledge
 available & used/practised for thousands of years in our country.
Point raised by the Committee
       When is the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) likely to be completed?
Clarification by the Department
 i)         TKDL has been created for 56,900 formulations in Ayurveda out of the target of 59,000 formulations.
(ii)        With respect to TKDL Unani out of 77,000 formulations, transcription has been completed for 48,000
 formulations.
(iii)       TKDL for Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha systems of medicine is likely to be completed by December 2006.
(iv)   TKDL presently contains information on 10 million pages in five international languages, which would protect
 1,07,000 formulations in Ayurveda and Unani. India has also received request for access to TKDL from European
 Patent Office (EPO) in July 2005 itself.  However, clearance for giving access to EPO is presently pending with

 World Intellectual Property Organization.
Comments
            The Committee hopes that the TKDL for Ayurveda, Unani and siddha will be completed by December, 2006, as

 our traditional knowledge. 
NEW MILLENIUM INDIAN TECHNOLOGY LEADERSHIP INITIATIVE (NMITLI)        
Recommendation
           The Committee recommends that a special cell may be set up to coordinate and pool the knowledge gained in the
 CSIR laboratories and the private sector companies and disseminate it through direct interactions with the industry or
 through the print and electronic media. Efforts may also be made to ensure that there is no duplication in the research
 work carried out in the CSIR laboratories and the private sector companies so that country's scarce resource is not
 wasted.                                                               (Para 40)
 Action Taken by the Department    
         CSIR has put in place the scheme New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) to provide
 leadership role to India through CSIR-Industry active participation. CSIR has placed dedicated manpower for
 implementation and monitoring of the NMITLI projects. CSIR, as a part of the process, interacts with industry at every
 stage in development of the project.  For each defined area, an expert group is specially constituted to formulate the
 project and invariably, industry expert is associated with the expert group.  Besides helping in pooling the expertise and
 establishing synergistic relationship, it helps in avoiding duplication of R&D effort in industry and research institutes.
Point raised by the Committee
       How many such expert groups have been constituted? What are the details of industry participation over the last
 couple of years?
Clarification by the Department
       Under the NMITLI scheme, all the projects are developed with the help of eminent experts transcending the interests
 as well as expertise of the wide spectrum of constituencies. So far, 37 projects are under implementation. Each project
 has been developed as per the guidance of expert groups specifically constituted for it. Thus, 37 individual expert
 groups were constituted to develop all the projects.
In the last couple of years following industries were enrolled into NMITLI Scheme.
Lensel Optics Pvt. Ltd., Pune; Intra Ocular Care Pvt. Ltd., Baroda; Xcyton, Bangalore; TVS Motor, Chennai; Godavari
 Sugar Mills Ltd., Mumbai; Reliance Group of Ind., Mumbai; Avestha Gen, Bangalore;  Strand Genomics, Bangalore;
 TCS, Hyderabad, USV, Mumbai; Rallis Res. Centre, Bangalore; JK Paper Ltd., Ballarpur Ind. Ltd.; ITC Ltd.; Biocon,
 Bangalore; Shantha Biotechnics Pvt. Ltd, Hyderabad; TTK Healthcare; Universal Orthosystems, Vadodara; Genova
 Biotech, Hyderabad; Bharat Biotech International Limited (BBIL), Hyderabad; Phytotron, Bangalore Excel Industries,
 Mumbai; JK Agrti, Kolkata, DiviNet, Pune.
Comments
   The Committee notes the reply.

INFRASTRUCTURE RENOVATION AND REFURBISHMENT
Recommendation
       The Committee feels that India needs the most advanced infrastructure and laboratories for carrying out cutting edge
 research in various fields. The infrastructure should be seen as a strategic national resource and funding should be given
 on a long-term basis so that the modernization becomes a continued process for effectiveness and improvement in our
 scientific growth. The Committee is also of the view that the laboratories at the graduate/post-graduate level should be
 upgraded so that interest can be generated among the young students for further research.                                  (Para 44)
Action Taken by the Department
·
        A scheme on ICT Infrastructure Renovation and Refurbishing is being pursued at an estimated cost of Rs. 97.50
 crores. The salient features of this project are:
·        Modernisation and Upgradation of the ICT Infrastructure of all the 38 laboratories of CSIR.
·        Video Conferencing facilities are proposed to be set-up among laboratories, CSIR HQs. etc. so that project reviews
 could get facilitated.
·        Integrate the entire ICT Infrastructure of CSIR and its laboratories over E-GRID to enforce common technical
 standards and office procedures.
·        Through this project, common standards software/solutions in the area of e-governance shall also get implemented.
 For establishing grid enabled system and implementing e-governance systems a Data Centre with state of art
 computing facilities is to be created at New Delhi (CRRI Complex) with mirror site at CSE, NCL, Pune.
·        For providing development of science in the country funding through Research Scheme is being provided to well
 trained scientists in regular jobs in the universities/R&D Institutions.   To do innovative research infrastructure is
 being continually improved in the universities / R&D Institutions through small equipment grant component under
 the Research Schemes. Efforts are being made to upgrade laboratories at the school/college level to generate interest
 among the young students for future research through “Adoption of school & colleges by CSIR labs”, a scheme
 instituted by CSIR during the X plan.
·
        UGC has created UGC Information Network connecting all colleges & universities.  The Universities are connected
 through 100 MBPS backbone and they enjoy both the Intra as well as Internet connectivity.
·        Access to around 2500-research journals on-line manner was provided to the researchers as well as the teaching
 faculty.
Point raised by the Committee
       It has been observed that in India interaction between Universities and R&D Institutions is weak. What has been
 done by the Department to improve it?
Clarification by the Department
       Many of the CSIR laboratories have been working in collaboration with Universities on many research and teaching
 programmes. A Task Force constituted by the Government of India, Ministry of HRD for leveraging synergies between
 Premier Academic Institutions (PAIs) and CSIR system for promoting a symbolic partnership has recently made several
 recommendations. The recommendations interalia include partnership in research activities for work of mutual interests,
 setting up of joint high class R&D facility, joint offering of skill up gradations/training programmes for R&D personnel,

 offering academic programmes  jointly in emerging transdisciplinery subjects etc. The Task Force has also suggested
 implementation mechanism, which include setting up a CSIR-PAI Steering Committee as an overarching policy,

Comments
            The Committee hopes that expeditious follow-up action will be taken by the Department on the recommendations
 of the Task Force constituted for promoting symbolic partnership between Premier Academic Institutions (PAIs) and

TECHNOLOGY PROMOTION, DEVELOPMENT AND UTILIZATION PROGRAMMES
Recommendation
         The Committee feels that the Department should initiate action to coordinate the research work undertaken by the
 CSIR laboratories and the industrial houses and an atmosphere of co-operation should be generated so that both stand to
 benefit from each other's expertise.                                                                                                               (Para 48)
Action Taken by the Department
DSIR has taken proactive steps through its Technology Development and Demonstration Programme (TDDP)
 under Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization (TPDU) Scheme to interact with industries and
 National laboratories in technology development and demonstration projects. The Scheme supports lab
 scale/bench scale technologies developed by CSIR, National Laboratories /institutions and Universities for scale
 up and commercialization by Indian industries. In addition to this, DSIR also considers consortium projects for
 development of technologies of common interests for group of industries/associations to be undertaken by
 industrial units jointly with National Laboratories in important focused areas.
·
              The TDDP also provides support to projects for development of technologies at     National
 Laboratories/institutions for use of cluster of industries.  DSIR has supported few such projects for cluster of
 industries at National Laboratories/institutions during X Plan period.
·              As suggested by the Committee, the Department would further enhance its             interaction with CSIR
 laboratories and industrial units to formulate joint         technology development and demonstration projects to
 benefit from each others         expertise.
Point raised by the Committee
        How many lab scale/bench scale technologies developed by CSIR have actually been commercialized and
 successfully entered the market? How many consortium projects for development of technologies have been undertaken
 by the Department?
Clarification by the Department

 Development & Utilization Scheme has been supporting projects of industries for development of technologies for new

Action Taken by the Department
            As per the recommendations of the Committee, NGRI has taken action and conducted feasibility study with
 regard to the points raised by the Hon’ble Members. NGRI’s observations are as follows:
    Earth Dynamo action: It is believed that radiogenic potassium, if present in the earth's core in substantial
 quantities, has the potential to generate heat adequate enough to power earth's geodynamo action. Recent studies
 indicate the possibility of the compatibility of radioactivity in producing earth's early magnetic field, which helps
 in dynamo action. To verify this hypothesis experiments are being conducted at few places in USA and some
 other countries.
    Geo-neutrinos imaging of earth's interior: Geo-neutrinos are produced by beta-decay of radioactive elements
 present inside the earth, in particular, the long-lived isotopes of U238, Th232, Rb87 and K40. It is believed that
 measuring these geo-neutrinos directly will provide information on the magnetic field of the earth and the
 geodynamo. The only attempt to directly detect geo-neutrinos is being attempted using sophisticated low energy
 Kam LAND (Kamioka Liquid Scintillator Anti-Neutrino Detector) facility being built at Honshu in Japan.
 Indirect methods to estimate geo-neutrino flux theoretically are quite ambiguous.
      Both the points raised by the Hon’ble Members are linked, viz., earth’s dynamo action is believed to be
 caused by the magnetic field inside the earth, partly due to heat flow from radiogenic isotopes including
 potassium which produces geo-neutrinos by beta-decay. The concern of the Members is valid and well taken as
 they feel that these studies could be linked to the generation of earthquakes, which are of prime concern to the
 mankind, especially, in view of the recent damaging earthquakes including generation of tsunamis.
    NGRI is already in the forefront of studying the phenomenon of earthquakes and the assessment of hazard
 associated with it so that mankind can be saved from this natural disaster. Several seismological observatories in
 the country are being operated and maintained by NGRI. The preparation of the Seismic Hazard Map covering
 Himalayan and other seismically active regions in India under a Global Seismic Hazard Assessment Programme
 is one such action in this direction. It is now well known that earthquakes occur only up to depths of about 700
 km beneath the earth.  For an earthquake to occur the material has to be brittle.  This is probably the reason that
 earthquakes do not occur at great depths due to increase in temperature and pressure, which makes the material
 more plastic, or fluid in nature.   This molten material inside the earth drives the tectonic plates, which collides,
 and cause damaging earthquakes along collision boundaries and other parts of the earth.  The movement of these
 tectonic plates can be measured using Global Positioning System (GPS), which can provide information about the
 estimates of the rate of movements.  NGRI has already a major program on GPS studies with permanent and
 mobile observation stations.  In the last 5 years, a permanent GPS station has also been installed at the Indian
 Maitri Station in Antarctica. Several  other studies related to seismic structure of the earth are also being carried
 out at NGRI. All these studies directly address the earthquake phenomenon and also lead to the understanding of
 the geodynamics of the earth in terms of the convection in the earth’s interior.
    The concern of the Honorable Members in suggesting these studies seems to address the problem of earthquake
 generation, which is playing havoc with the lives of the people and causing great economic losses. NGRI is
 already addressing this concern by taking up appropriate and detailed studies as per the International
 understanding of the earthquake phenomenon. The studies recommended by the Honorable Members of
 Parliament are very important to understand the dynamics of the planet earth but do not directly address the
 problem of earthquake generation. However the recommendations of the Committee are well taken and in
 response, NGRI has setup a core group of scientists to explore the possibility of initiating the suggested studies in

NATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH INSTITUTE (NBRI), GURGAON
Recommendations
            The Committee understands that although the Brain Research Institute is doing state-of-the-art investigation in the field of various neuro-degenerative disorders and pathological mechanism of
 various ailments relating to human brain, there are still some important areas left where the institute needs to concentrate for giving brain research a holistic
 dimension.                                                                                              (Para 17)                                                                                        
            In the opinion of the Committee, such areas involve detailed investigations into the causes of the fatally life threatening brain cancers like oligodendro glioma, glioblastomas and other forms of
 complicated cancerous brain disorders.           (Para 18)                                                    
             Although the institute is pursuing a research project about the mechanisms of L-BOAA mediated neurotoxicity, the Committee would also like to advocate that research should be initiated by
 the institute regarding secretion of common brain hormones from substantia nigra and artificial development of L-DOPA to deal with basic mechanisms of neuro
 toxicity.                                                                                                        (Para 19)                      The Committee would further like to suggest that researches on endogenous opiates like enkephalin
 and endorphin should also be initiated for understanding the chemistry of pain for designing a comprehensive pain management strategy in case of certain killer disease like cancer etc.             
                                                         (Para 20)                                                                                                     
            The Committee has also noticed that no substantial research has been initiated on PRIONS (Proteinaceous Infectious Particles) by the institute, a Stanley Pruisner concept, which is the main
 cause of BSE (Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy).  The Committee has been given to understand that due to lack of P-2 containment facility available with the institute, no research is being carried
 on PRIONS and PRIONS related disease.   The Committee urges that since such type of disease may take alarming form in future, primary investigation of the causes of such diseases is the need of the
 hour through development of P-2 and even P-3 containment facility with the institute which at present the institute is lacking.                                                                                           (Para 21)
The Committee also understands that problem of Alzheimer, which is a common form of brain disease, particularly at senile age requires more research  as it is gradually on the rise among civil
 population. Latest research reports in the advanced countries show that real culprit in Alzheimer’s ailment is a copper and zinc build-up in the brain. It is believed by the scientists that accumulated
 metals mix abnormally with a protein called beta amyloid in the brain, oxidizes, literally rust and destroy nerve cells.  Amyloid protein plays a helpful role in the brain: absorbing metals like a sponge. 
 But in Alzheimer’s victims, the metals overwhelm the protein.  Copper mixes abnormally with amyloid, releasing hydrogen peroxide and other toxic chemicals and damage the nearby cells.  Some of
 that protein breaks free, becomes “rogue” amyloid, and mixes with zinc to form clumps that leak more hydrogen peroxide - metals as the real culprits. The scientists are of the opinion that excess
 copper and zinc built up in the brain dissolves the protein clumps in the brains, which has already been experimented in animal model.  Since the disease may assume alarming proportion in future due
 to increased stress owing to phenomenal rise in urban conglomerates and modernization, this aspect of the disease requires deep research so that a target drug for controlling the ailment could be
 designed for future medication. The Committee, therefore, recommends that researches in the following fields need to be given greater attention by the Institute:                             (Para
 22)                                                                
Cure for Alzheimer’s;
i)
                    Researches in the field of PRIONS related diseases;
ii)                   Investigation in the field of pain hormone related issues being secreted from Substantia Nigra by brain like enkephalin and endorphin;
iii)                 Cure for  fatal brain cancers like oligodndrogliomas etc. and
iv)                 Investigation into the causes and cure of Multiple Sclerosis (MS).
Action taken by the Department
            National Brain Research Center (NBRC) has already started work in the area of Alzheimer’s disease and currently evaluating and exploring ways of enhancing the efficacy of traditional Indian
 medicines for potential cure of Alzheimer related symptoms.  The center is also taking steps to initiate research in the area of glioma.  Recruitment of a scientist, who is an expert in this area, is under
 process.  Regarding the other areas of research that the Committee has suggested-pain management, prion related diseases, multiple sclerosis and further research into the area of neurotoxicity, NBRC
 is planning to expand and work on these important brain related diseases as and when the current constraints of resources, including manpower resources, faculty positions and other resource
 constraints, such as availability of P3 research facility are overcome.
Points raised by the Committee
            What has been the progress in enhancing the efficacy of traditional Indian Medicines for potential cure of Alzheimer related symptoms?
Clarification by the Department
Several Indian medicinal plants have been extracted and their efficacy for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease is being evaluated using cell culture and animal models of Alzheimer’s disease. 
 These animals contain some of the defective genes that cause Alzheimer’s disease and they develop the behavioural (loss of memory) and pathological symptoms (formation of plaques) in the brain as
 seen in Alzheimer’s disease.  Using these models, it is noted that some of the plant extracts have the capability to reduce the toxic effect of amyloid βpeptide, which is a key factor in the cause of
 Alzheimer’s disease.
Point raised by the Committee
Is there any blue print made by NBRC to expand and work on important brain related diseases? What has been done to overcome the above mentioned constraints?

NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF IMMUNOLOGY (NII), NEW DELHI
Recommendation
The Committee has noted that although this premier research Institute in the field of immunology has not undertaken any work relating to the production of interferons, it has, however, designed
 an appreciative investigation in the field.   The Committee has noticed that interferons have been implicated as signals controlling the way in which the immune system detects and recognises antigenic
 proteins of viruses, including those viruses associated with certain cancers.  Recent studies have shown that interferon-alpha therapy is beneficial in the prevention of liver cancer in patients with viral
 Hepatitis caused by Hepatitis B and C viruses.  Recently, NII has developed and patented a genetically manipulated mouse model of liver cancer to facilitate in-depth studies of preventive as well as
 curative effects of molecules such as interferons and other drugs.   The Committee feels that once these findings from the interferons research proves successful, it could be shared with other premier
 Oncoligical Research Centres in the country.                                                                                                                  (Para 24)
            The Committee has noted that the Institute has not been conducting any research relating to the treatment of some life threatening autoimmune diseases like Wegener’s Granulomatosis,
 myasthenia gravis and pemphigus vulgaris.  Although the Committee knows that these are rare type of auto-immune diseases among human population, the Committee is, however, apprehensive that
 they may become severely life threatening in distant future due to rapid increase in stress related syndrome owing to unabated urbanization and
 modernization.                                                                     (Para 25)                                                                                                                                                  
            Keeping this in view, the Committee feels that such type of auto-immune diseases also require deep investigation for establishing their causes and cure through promising research projects so
 that some concrete answer to these ailments could   be   designed   by medical science before they assume   any    life   threatening proportion. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Institute
 should consider   primary   investigation in the field of the following auto-immune diseases through the production of ‘interferons’: -
           
i)
                    Wegener’s Granulomatosis
ii)                   Myasthenia Gravis
iii)         Pemphigus Vulgaris                                                                           (Para 26)
 
Action taken by the Department
            Interferon-related investigations, addressing both their production and signaling characteristics, have been initiated.  NII scientists have initiated investigations in the way that interferons,
 particularly interferon-gamma, signals to phagocytic cells of the immune system so as to enable them to overcome the resistance of pathogenic bacteria, such as mycobacteria which cause tuberculosis,
 and protozoa such as Leishmania that cause kala azar.  Researchers at NII are also examining the cascade of signals that allow the immune system to determine whether to make interferon-gamma in
 the course of a T cell response.  This decision is crucial for generating a protective immune response against major diseases, such as typhoid fever, tuberculosis and kala azar.  The pathogenesis of
 autoantibody-dependent auto-immune syndromes such as the ones noted by the Committee depends critically on the formation of autoantibodies, and on their effect on cells such as neutrophil
 leucocytes (in Wegener’s granulomatosis).   Investigations to study some of these issues have been initiated at NII.  The genesis of autoantibodies in humans is being investigated by a genetic
 approach, using hybridomas generated from patients suffering from another, somewhat more common, autoimmune disorder, systemic lupus erythematosus.  The target specificities and the genetic
 structures of these autoantibodies are issues being dissected.  As clinical material becomes available, these studies will be extended to other autoimmune disorders mentioned above.  The molecular
 pathways by which neutrophil leucocytes undergo death in response to a number of stimuli are under active investigation in NII.  As insights are gained, these studies will be extended to autoantibody-
mediated death pathways.

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR PLANT GENOME RESEARCH (NCPGR), NEW DELHI
Recommendation
            The Committee believes that agriculture can be made sustainable only through the use of biotechnology.  Since agriculture is the main source of livelihood for a substantial portion of population
 of this country, improving the techniques used in agriculture will lead to the general upliftment of the quality of life of the rural people. This can only be achieved by developing better varieties of
 plants which are better yielding, having higher nutritional value and are resistant to various diseases and pests, through genetic modification. The Department should ensure that the results of the
 achievements in the laboratories are disseminated to the farmers at the earliest.                                         (Para 37)                                                                                                                                 
Action taken by the Department
            The Department has identified Agricultural Biotechnology as one of its priority areas and has been funding various research and other programmes to promote this area in the country.  The main
 objective of the programme is on improving productivity of crops, reducing their yield losses due to various biotic and abiotic stresses, improving their nutritional quality, etc.  The programme makes
 use of various biotechnological interventions like genetic transformation, engineering male sterility for hybrid seed production, molecular marker aided selection and molecular breeding.  In addition,
 programmes are also supported on Plant Genomics and on cloning and characterization of novel and useful genes.  The priority crops identified for the programme are rice, wheat, cotton, mustard,
 chickpea, pigeon pea, maize, potato, tomato, sorghum, pearl millet, groundnut, etc.

       Action taken by the Department
            The progress of the on going infrastructure projects is regularly scrutinized by the Task Force and during the current financial year the Department plans to conduct two meeting of the Task
 Force to monitor the progress of the on-going projects and decide on the funding for new project proposals in the identified thrust areas.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the opinion that there is an urgent need to streamline guidelines and procedures for approving genetically engineered pharmaceutical products, as this is a complex process
 involving multiple ministries and regulators that lack systematic coordination. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should set-up an autonomous body like “National
 Biotechnology Regulatory Authority” to approve biotechnology products — and dispense with similar tasks being handled by the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee of the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests.  The proposed authority should also incorporate separate divisions in areas like agricultural products and transgenic crops; pharmaceuticals and industrial products; and
 transgenic food, feed and animal aquaculture.                                                   (Para 42)
Action taken by the Department
            For approving genetically engineered products in the country, the department has already proposed an independent National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority (NBRA) during the
 deliberations of the Mashelkar Committee Report preparation, which has been set up for DNA pharma products.  For agriculture products, Dr. Swaminathan Committee has also recommended the
 same structure.  Once these reports are accepted by the appropriate authorities, the department would make efforts to set-up an independent National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority.  As far as
 dispensing with GEAC of  MoEF is concerned, it is not within the purview of the department as this committee has been formed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.  Once the independent
 NBRA is in place after the acceptance of the two reports as stated earlier, the role of approval of all biotech products would rest with the Authority and not the GEAC, as desired in the report of the
 Committee.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply. It believes that an independent National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority (NBRA) will soon be put in place so that regulatory bottlenecks can be removed
 and single window clearance could be made in case of genetically engineered pharmaceutical products
 Recommendation
            The Committee also recommends that besides clarifying regulatory mechanisms, there should be adequate focus on developing human resources — students specializing in biotechnology,
 researchers, teachers of biotechnologycourses and technicians. The Department should also plan setting up new Centers of excellence in food biotechnology, herbal medicine, molecular medicine,
 biomaterials and devices, and bioinformatics.                                                                                                                                         (Para 43)           
Action taken by the Department
            The areas referred to in the para have already been included as thrust areas in the draft National Biotechnology Development Strategy document.  Accordingly, while considering the new project
 proposals, the Department would encourage setting up of new Centers of Excellence in these specific areas.  Efforts would also be made to generate viable project proposals in consulatation with the
 experts available in these fields.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
Recommendation
The Committee notes that most of the funds allocated for Human Resource Development have been utilized for Graduate/Post Graduate/fellowships. The Committee feels that priority has still
 not been accorded to developing Human Resource at the under graduate level. The Committee recommends that proper resource allocation should be made at the under graduate level in consultation
 with the University Grants Commission and various Central/State Boards of Higher Secondary Education.                      (Para 46)
Action taken by the Department
            In the year 2001, DBT had convened a meeting of the agencies involved in biotechnology education, namely, UGC, AICTE and universities, to discuss the issue of appropriate level for
 biotechnology teaching.  The meeting was chaired by Secretary, DBT and attended by Vice Chairman, UGC; Chairman, AICTE and other eminent educationists.  The general consensus in the meeting

 was that biotechnology teaching at under-graduate level should not be encouraged.  It was felt that the basic knowledge of Life Sciences / Biological Sciences (Zoology, Botany, Microbiology,
 Biochemistry etc) is essentially required to study the multidisciplinary area of Biotechnology at post graduate level.  The recommendation of the meeting not to encourage / support Biotechnology
 courses at undergraduate level was circulated to all the agencies like UGC, AICTE etc.  In addition, it was also recommended that AICTE may consider the Biotechnology courses in engineering
 colleges / technical institutions having strength in Chemical Engineering, Biochemical Engineering, Bioprocess Engineering.  During the discussion on the National Biotechnology Development
 Strategy, the dominant view also has been that at the B.Sc. level there should be general exposure in life science subjects and specialization in biotechnology be considered only at the M.Sc. level. 
 Therefore, DBT does not consider it necessary to support teaching programmes at the B.Sc. level.
Comments
            The Committee decides not to pursue in view of the Department’s reply.    
Recommendation
            The Department of Biotechnology should also devise such a programme so that bright scientists working overseas are attracted back to Indian universities. The Committee is of the view that
 today much of the basic research in India is done in national laboratories, away from universities and this means that the teaching Centres and research Centres are disassociated, a situation that needs
 to be addressed seriously. Attracting young Scientists from abroad and involving them in coordinating the research in India would also tackle the problem of Brain Drain.                                        
 (Para 47)
          Action taken by the Department
            Department of Biotechnology is in the process of developing a programme for attracting bright Indian scientists working overseas to Indian universities.  This issue has also been widely
 discussed while preparing National Biotechnology Development Strategy.  The Strategy provides for the following specific measures in paras 2.1 (v) and (viii).  These paras provide as follows.
●          Para 2.1 (v) : Strengthening of teaching and R&D in life sciences and biotechnology in the university system.
●          Strengthening of R&D in life sciences and biotechnology in the university system will be accorded high priority.  This is considered important for improving the quality of education and
 providing exposure to new technologies for students at various levels.  Specific mechanisms to achieve the goal will include:
 
●          Creation of inter-disciplinary centers of excellence with world class infrastructure in key areas
●          Programme support to encourage inter-departmental networking
●          Visiting Professorship and creation of industry sponsored chairs in partnership with the Department of Biotechnology.
            Para 2.1 (viii): Arresting and reversing brain drain
●          The number of post-doctoral fellowships offered by the Department of Biotechnology will be increased to 200 per annum in order to attract talent.
●          Outstanding young investigator grants in biotechnology will be introduced. This will provide a package including salary support, research grant, equipment and opportunities to attend national
 and international conferences.  The salary support under the scheme will be at par with that of entry-level faculty positions.
●          Information on availability of positions in education/research establishments and industries will be provided on a website to facilitate employment of scientists with specific skills at appropriate
 positions.
●          A data base of scientists working in different areas of biotechnology within and outside the country will be created to utilize the expertise appropriately.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.  It hopes that the above measures will be implemented at the earliest.
 STEM CELL RESEARCH
Recommendation
            The Committee feels that extensive research needs to be carried out in the field of stem cell research specially keeping in view the fact that it can treat many diseases for which there seems to be
 either no cure or the alternate therapies are very expensive.  However, the Committee is of the opinion that as the research in this field is at nascent stage, publicity by various research institutions
 should be avoided.  The Committee is also of the view that research work on stem cell should be undertaken in coordination with all the concerned research
 institutions.                                                          (Para 52)                                                                     
 Action taken by the Department
            In order to initiate coordinated work in the area of stem cell research, city cluster programme on stem cells have been supported at Vellore and Pune by involving a number of basic researchers
 and clinicians.  More city cluster programmes on stem cells are being considered at Hyderabad, Bangalore and Delhi.
 
            Focused, targeted network programmes are also being initiated on human stem cell research with the clinicians after ascertaining their requirements for stem cell therapy by organising disease
 specific meetings.

       P.G.NARAYANAN

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Environment and Forests on the
 recommendations contained in the One Hundred Forty-sixth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2005-06) of the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests, presented to both Houses of Parliament on 25
th April, 2005. There were forty-five
 recommendations contained in the report.  Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received
 from the Ministry on 1
st September, 2005. The Committee considered the draft Action Taken Report in its meeting held on
 18th November, 2005 and decided to seek clarification/additional information on certain points contained in paras 18, 20,

 23, 52, 55, 59, 63, 70.1, 98 and 101. The Ministry’s clarification/additional information on the points raised by the
 Committee was received on ­­­­­­­­­­­­­­­19th December, 2005.
            The Committee’s recommendations, Action Taken thereon by the Ministry of Environment and Forests, points raised
 by the Committee (wherever necessary), clarifications by the Ministry and comments of the Committee thereon are set out
 in the succeeding paragraphs: -
OUTLAY FOR NORTH-EAST & SIKKIM
Recommendation
            The Committee recommends that as there has been greater emphasis on North-East region, the Ministry should make
 a lump sum budgetary support under one head equal to 10% of Plan funds for the North-Eastern Sector including Sikkim
 and not under separate heads as has been made in this financial year.(Para 5.2)
Action Taken by the Ministry
Ministry of Environment & Forests has been earmarking 10 percent of Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) for development of
 North East Region under Major Head 2552.  A provision of Rs. 123.50 crores out of total outlay of Rs. 1234.91 has been
 made under this Head during the current financial year.  Inadvertently, an amount of Rs. 35 crores, for the scheme
 Gregarious flowering of muli bamboos (melocanna baccifera) has been shown separately under Major Head 2552. It is
 clarified that this scheme has been drawn to meet emergent situation in North East Region. To ensure smooth passage of
 occurrence of gregarious flowering of muli bamboos in the north eastern states, without resulting into social, economic and
 ecological problems, is one of the major objectives of this scheme. It is also to ensure appropriate utilization of raw material
 that will be available on account of gregarious flowering by supplying to industrial concerns. Therefore, this programme is
 exclusively committed for North East Region and the allocation of Rs. 123.50 crores has been shown only under one Major
 Head 2552.
It will be ensured in the future that a lump sum provision for projects / schemes for North East Region and Sikkim will be
 shown only at one place under Major Head 2552. 
Comments
             The Committee notes the reply.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FOR 2005-2006
Recommendation
            The Committee is of the view that expenditure should be evenly spread over all the four quarters of the financial
 year.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that any variation in the expenditure is mainly due to inherent lacunae in
 the budgetary mechanism of the Ministry, which requires urgent attention and a well-planned action plan to ensure full
 utilization of allocated budget in a uniform manner spreading over all the four quarters of the financial year. The
 Committee, therefore, suggests that the Ministry may examine the existing procedure and see whether it can be further
 streamlined to make the expenditure uniform in all quarters.                                 (Para 10)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The system of monitoring of expenditure exists in this Ministry. Secretary (E&F) regularly chairs a Senior Officer meeting
 every fortnight to review the expenditure of the Ministry nearing even in all the quarters as the Ministry could spend only
 Rs. 1003.1 crores (approx.) in the last year. The quarter-wise expenditure is:
1
st Quarter         2nd Quarter              3rd Quarter                 4th Quarter
  19.1%                30.07%                   21.98%                      28.85%
The major constraints in the utilization of the plan outlay are:
Before releasing the first installment to the implementing agencies, the utilization certificate for the previous year is
 mandatory.
Annual Plan of the operations is received in the first quarter, cause slow progress. Inadequate schemes for North East States.
Inadequate provision of State’s share as per norms for CSS (Centrally Sponsored Schemes).
Comments
The Committee is not at all convinced with the Ministry’s reply and reiterates its recommendation that the entire procedure
 needs to  be reviewed and streamlined so as to  maintain to the extent possible, uniform pace of expenditure throughout the
 entire year.
            The Committee also urges upon the Ministry to make effective coordinative efforts in the direction of motivating
 states and other implementing agencies for utilizing their funds in a time-bound manner and timely furnishing of utilization
 certificates to the Ministry.
POLLUTON FROM COAL BASED METHANE AND CLEAN COAL TECHNOLOGIES
Recommendation
            The Committee is of  the opinion that although the coal constitutes a major source catering to the country's energy
 needs,  possibly with  proper technologies and new initiatives for better management, it is possible to reduce the hazards of
 coal production which is being otherwise caused due to extraction of this mineral without proper  planning. Through
 scientific mining practices followed by land reclamation, beneficiation for ash reduction at source, improvement in

 combustion methods, use of efficient electrostatic precipitators, bag filters for trapping of fly ash emission and effective
 management of ash including its utilization for bricks, cement and such other purpose, many of the problems can be
 prevented and controlled.                                        (Para 13)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The recommendations made in this para are essentially in the nature of observations only, however, it may be clarified that
 while appraising projects relating to mining and thermal power projects, the issues mentioned in this para such as land
 reclamation in case of mining projects and use of beneficiated coal, use of high efficiency electrostatic precipitators (ESPs),
 ash utilization etc. in case of thermal power plants are duly considered and stipulated as conditions while according
 environmental clearance to these projects. 
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation 
            The Committee feels that Central Pollution Control Board should lay down the environmental guidelines for coal
 mining activities prescribing the use of beneficiated coal with lower ash content in power plants and lay down specific
 norms for emission and effluents from coal combustion system.                                                           (Para 14)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) develops industry-specific standards for effluent and emissions. These
 standards are based on techno-economic feasibility and prevailing process technologies in India and abroad, cleaner
 production options, waste minimization/reuse/recycle/practices, pollution control technologies, retrofitment of
 upgraded/advanced process and pollution control technologies, economics of scale etc. The proposed standards are
 discussed in Peer & Core Committee of CPCB, which includes members from industries, Industrial Associations, experts in
 the field and representatives of concerned Ministries & SPCBs. The standards recommended by Peer & Core Committee are
 again reviewed by an Expert Committee in the Ministry of Environment & Forests and subsequently notified under the
 Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
The Environmental Standards  for the Pollution Prevention and Control for coal mines developed by CPCB had already been
 notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Notifications on use of beneficiated/ blended coal with lower ash
 content in power plants and norms for emission and effluent for power plants have also been promulgated by Govt. of India
 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The Code of Practice for the Pollution Prevention and Control for coal mines
 has also been evolved by CPCB.
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply and is of the view that though different measures exist to control the coal mining
 activities, the Ministry should ensure their proper implementation. 
Recommendation 
            The Committee feels that maximum land degradation in coal mining is caused by open-cast mining. Since the
 productivity is higher in open cast sector, this pace of growth cannot be sustained for long since the stripping ratios will
 increase the mining operations which may consequently run into land access and other environmental problems.
(Para 15)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The mining methodology i.e. opencast or underground has its own environmental impacts.  The choice of mining
 methodology depends on the geological formations and other mining considerations like conservation of reserves etc. 
 Based on the proposal submitted to this ministry, the project is appraised from environmental angle and necessary safeguard
 measures are stipulated as conditions to be complied with by the proponent during implementation of the project which
 inter-alia include rehabilitation of mines out areas, stability of over burden dumps and their reclamation, protection for
 subsidence, inundation of mine etc.  Mine plan approval by the competent authority is an essential requirement for granting
 environmental clearance for ensuring sustainability of the mine by restricting selective mining. 
Comments
            The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation 
            The mining operations like drilling, blasting, movement of the heavy earth moving machinery on haul roads,
 collection, transportation and handling of coal, screening, sizing and segregation units are the major sources of such
 emissions.  Underground mine fire is also a major source of air pollution in some of the coalfields.
(Para 16)
Action Taken by the Ministry
To control fugitive emissions of particulate matter in coal mines, the Emission Standards for Coal Mines have already been
 notified. State Pollution Control Boards are the implementing Authority for these standards. The level of methane, which is
 an inflammable gas, is periodically checked in underground coalmines for safety reasons. The level of SO2 and NOx
 emission levels have already been notified. Underground mine fire problem is complex in nature and coal companies are

Recommendation
            The proper management of methane emission should be one of the important factors which should be handled by the
 miners and mining authorities to reduce its emission into the atmosphere.                                                                       
          (Para 18)
Action Taken by the Ministry
Methane emissions cause safety hazards; therefore, the level of methane is periodically checked and the Director General,
 Mines & Safety (DGMS) has programmes for its control to prevent hazards.
Point raised by the Committee
The Committee would like to know about the details of the programmes to control and manage methane emission. What role
 does the Ministry of Environment and Forests   have in this? How it is ensured that the programmes/norms in this respect
 are strictly adhered to?
Clarification by the Ministry
The Ministry of Environment and Forests through its representative in Clean Development Mechanism  (CDM) Executive
 Board of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCC) has played an active role in approving
 the Methodology on Coal Based Methane and Coal Mine Methane in December, 2005.  Ministry of Coal & Mines as well
 as coal companies and Consultants are being advised of the new methodology for development of relevant CDM projects
 for approval.  Similarly, for methane emanating from Municipal wastes, local authorities have taken up waste and energy
 projects/waste management projects recovering methane by taking advantage of CDM.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
            Waste water from coal preparation plant and mine water are other sources of water pollution which requires
 immediate control.                                                     (Para 19)
Action Taken by the Ministry
Standards for effluent discharge from coal mines have already been notified under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The
 coal mines adopt appropriate water pollution control technology and install effluent treatment plants to ensure that the
 effluent discharge are within the stipulated standards.
Coalmines generally adopt the following water pollution control measures:
Maximum utilization of mine discharge
Appropriate water treatment system
Reuse of the waste water from the workshop in the workshop itself
Sewage treatment for the domestic waste
Garland drains to be provided around the toe of the OB dumps and coal stock yards to arrest the storm run-off from these
 areas.
The storm run-off from the OB dumps, coal stockyard etc. are to be settled in a suitable settling pond. The over flow of this
 settling pond may be discharged into the natural flowing stream. De-coaled pits may be utilized as settling pond.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation 
            The main sources of noise pollution, are blasting, movement of heavy earth moving machine and drilling and coal
 handling plants and the effective monitoring of all these issues are necessary for reducing noise pollution.                        
                      (Para 20)
Action Taken by the Ministry
The Standards for maximum permissible noise level have already been notified under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
 Code of practice for noise pollution control has also been evolved by CPCB. The coal mines adopt various noise pollution
 control techniques to ensure that noise level is within the stipulated standards.
Point raised by the Committee
The Committee would like to know the details of measures and techniques, being adopted by coal mines to keep the noise
 level within the stipulated standards.
Clarification by the Ministry
The main sources of noise pollution in  coal  mining activity can be attributed to blasting, drilling, movement of heavy earth
 moving machinery  and movement of trucks for transportation of mined coal. For controlling noise from various sources,
 the abatement measures initiated include the following :
Vide GSR No. 742(E) dated 25
th September, 2000, Ministry has issued standards for coal mine.  In clause IV of the

 Notification, noise level standards to be achieved by coal mines has been detailed and is as under :

 current and potential, that can influence forests and related social, economic, and environmental outcomes.  More focused
 interventions are required that address issues relating to opportunity, empowerment, and livelihood security of the poor
 people who depend on forests in different ways.  A broader livelihood approach, covering productive capacity, institutional
 and legal structures, market access and tenure must be adopted that puts forests into the broader context of rural
 development.  The focus should be on improving governance (especially correcting major distortions in incentives and
 markets that are reducing the value of the forest resources), and the development of efficient markets and encouraging
 competitive private sectors participating in the sector.  More focused interventions are required for maintaining natural
 forests for eco system protection and sustaining the global and local forest values.
(Para 60)
Action Taken by the Ministry
Forest Policy and Planning in India is a concurrent responsibility of the central government and state governments. Policy
 and Planning are linked to prescriptions contained in basic national legislation, including forestry legislations. In turn,
 policy shapes legislations in as much as legislations provide the structure and grounds for implementation of policies,
 strategies and priorities. Further, forestry is directly linked to overall land use. Hence forest policy and legislations flow
 from, and constitute a part of the national land use and legislative framework for natural resource management. The
 National Forest Policy, 1988 embodies the principles of sustainable forest management and treats forests primarily as
 environmental and social resources.    Recognizing the role of forests in rural livelihoods and in securing environmental
 security for future generations, the Government of India have formulated the National Forestry Action Plan (NFAP) which
 is a comprehensive work plan for the next twenty years to achieve the goal of sustainable development of forests and also to
 increase the forest/tree cover in the country to 33 percent of the land area as mandated in the National Forest Policy, 1988. 
 The National Forest Policy, 1988 contains essential elements to achieve sustainability of all types of forests, which are
 mainly (i) Increase in the extent of forest and tree cover; (ii) Maintenance, conservation and enhancement of bio-diversity;
 (iii) Maintenance and enhancement of ecosystem functions and vitality; (iv) Conservation and maintenance of soil and
 water resources; (v) Maintenance and enhancement of forest resource productivity; (vi) Optimization of forest resource
 utilization; (vii) Maintenance and enhancement of social cultural and spiritual benefits. The Government of India have
 adopted several schemes under National Forestry Programmes  to achieve Sustainable Forest Management and the national
 goal of one third of land area under forest/tree cover, and also simultaneously forging  linkages with livelihood and poverty
 alleviation issues of forest dependent communities.
2.         The sustainable management of forests and trees can make a meaningful contribution towards achieving livelihood
 opportunities to the people living in and around forests.  In particular : (i) the management, harvesting, processing and
 marketing of wood and non wood forest products can provide opportunities for employment and income generation (ii) The
 adoption of agro forestry practices can increase food production and food security in conjunction with provision of  wood
 products for sale or consumption, provide a source of household energy, and improve soil composition (iii) watershed
 management practices can provide multiple goods and services especially enhanced and sustained water production that is
 important to health and sanitation.
3.         MoEF has prepared comprehensive National Forestry Action Plan (NFAP) for 20 years to achieve sustainable
 development of forests and to increase forest and tree cover upto 33% of geographical area with a cost of Rs.133902 Crore.
 The forest and wild life sector is getting around 30%  financial resources of the required need including the budget at the
 national level and funding from external sources. It is a major constraint in achieving sustainability and thus providing
 required level of livelihood opportunities and incentives to the rural people dependent on forests. If adequate investment is
 made, forest and wild life sector is capable of providing livlihood opportunities to the poorest of the poor who live in and
 around forests.           
4.         As regards attracting investment from private sector, the MoEF is working on developing a multi-stakeholder
 partnership (MSP) for afforestation of degraded forest lands. MSP involves local community, State Forest Department  and
 private industry as partners.

 Education etc. to ensure that environmental components are adequately covered at the school level.
In 1999, MOEF commissioned Bharati Vidyapeeth Institute of Environment Education & Research (BVIEER) to conduct a
 nation wide survey to assess the extent of infusion of environmental concepts in the school curriculum and the effectiveness
 of its delivery in the classroom. Simultaneously, a National Consultation on EE was also organized in January 2000. The
 participants at this Consultation, which included officers from MHRD, MOEF, NCERT, State Government Departments of
 Education, SCERTs, etc. and representatives from NGOs besides educationists, were of the view that instead of teaching
 Environment as a separate subject, a separate space/forum should be created within the School System for integrating the
 various environmental concepts infused/introduced in other subjects. The Study revealed that the extent of infusion of
 environmental concepts into the school curriculum varied from State to State- while it was reasonably satisfactory in some
 States, it was very poor in some other states. It was also observed that appropriate training of teachers was necessary to
 ensure effective transaction of the environmental concepts in the class room. The study also recommended strengthening the
 infusion approach. Based on these recommendations, MOEF launched a pilot project on “Environment Education in School
 System” under the World Bank assisted Environmental Management Capacity Building Project with the basic objective of
 strengthening environmental education in the formal school system. The EESS project was implemented in 15 States in
 collaboration with the State Education Departments and the respective SCERTs for greening of the middle school level
 textbooks and their introduction in 100 schools in each state on experimental basis. The introduction of greened books in
 the project schools was preceded by the training of teachers in these schools.
The EESS project also stresses on hands-on activities. A hands-on Environmental learning program Global Learning and
 Observations to Benefit the Environment (GLOBE) was therefore, launched as a component of the EESS project.  India
 joined this program in August 2000 and has so far trained about 1800 GLOBE teachers from about 1700 schools in the
 country. Teachers of the 100 pilot schools were trained in various protocols for conducting the experiments in four broad
 environmental parameters-Hydrology, Soil, Land Cover and Atmospheric temperature / rainfall.  GLOBE provides a unique
 opportunity to its students to carry out various measurements so that they can learn about scientific protocols and perform
 environmental learning activities, which have already been introduced as theory in the greened textbooks developed for
 EESS project.  
The Ministry had also been interacting with the UGC to ensure coverage of environmental components at the college level
 education. A course module has been worked out through UGC for teaching EE as a separate paper at entry level in all
 streams of undergraduate education.
The MOEF has also launched an initiative to integrate environmental concepts and issues in the Management Education
 Syllabi of various professional Management courses in consultation with AICTE in 2002.  The courses content has been
 examined. Workshops have also been conducted to sensitize the faculty of more than 250 management colleges towards
 environmental issues. A Curriculum Development Workshop was also conducted to develop new curriculum and also to
 develop a resource base for teaching material.  An inventory of the courses offered in India and abroad has been prepared
 along with an inventory of resource material.
Besides the above initiatives, the Working Group constituted by the MOEF in April 2004 for the preparation of a
 Comprehensive plan for Environment Education in school; with members drawn from MHRD, NCERT, MOEF, a few State
 Education Departments and representative of organizations (namely CEE, CPREEC and IES) working in the field of
 Environment Education; has recommended that the MOEF shall take following action in the light of the Hon’ble Supreme
 Court’s directive to all the State Government to compulsorily teach environmental concepts in schools as per the model
 syllabus prepared by NCERT:
MOEF will collaborate with NCERT to facilitate the preparation of the textbooks by developing training modules for the
 textbook writers;
MOEF shall help the state governments in training teachers, master trainers/ resource persons by providing financial and
 technical assistance;
MOEF will play an important role in hands-on activities suggested by NCERT in the model syllabus.
Under the research funding program, guidelines are being framed to pay good remunerations to talented persons working in
 institutes, which do not receive core grant, to do research on environmental issues.

            The Committee recommends that National Mangroves Afforestation Programme should be designed so that new

Action Taken by the Ministry
The Government seek to sustain mangrove forests and Coral Reefs in the country by both regulatory and promotional
 measures. The Coastal Regulation Zone notification(1991) under the Environmental Protection Act(1986) recognizes the
 Mangrove and Coral reef areas as ecologically sensitive and categorizes them as CRZ-I(i) which implies that these areas are
 afforded protection of the highest order. Under the promotional measures the Government has identified 35 mangrove areas
 and 4 Coral Reefs areas on a country-wide basis for intensive conservation and management.
The Ministry of Environment and Forests, for the last several years has been funding research in multi-disciplinary aspects
 of Mangroves and Coral Reefs ecosystems protection, conservation and management at various universities, institutions of
 higher learning, national research institutes and non-governmental organizations. There has been an allocation of Rs. 24
 crores during the X Plan for Mangroves and Coral Reefs, of which a sum of Rs.6.50 crores has been provided for Research
 Projects. The Current year’s allocation for Research in Mangroves and Coral Reefs is Rs.5.30 crores. There is an increasing
 emphasis on close interface between Researchers and Managers in the field. The Primary objectives are to develop
 strategies, technologies and methodologies for better management of mangroves areas in the country.
