Food Biotechnology
Achievements 2005-06:
Multi-Institutional network projects have been generated in the area of Nutraceuticals & Probiotics through Brain
 Storming sessions, which were sanctioned. Initiatives would be taken for technology diffusion of micronutrient fortified
 “Ultra-Rice” and to study their biological impact in addressing nutrition deficiencies. Taking into account the beneficial
 role of Zinc supplementation in child health, particularly for the treatment of diarrhea in developing countries, a dialogue
 with W.H.O for technology diffusion of dispersible Zinc tablets would be initiated.
Proposed programmes for 2006-07
 The programme would continue with its core activities concerning major on going and new initiatives on the projects in
 the area of food biotechnology.   Programmes will be generated on food safety issues; Nutraceuticals: process
 development to obtain health foods from herbal plants and traditional foods. Biofortification issues would be addressed.
 The projects, which have been initiated, would be pursued for their logical conclusion and development of
 product/processes.  The technologies developed at the laboratory scale would be brought to the level of pilot plant scale
 and transfer to the industry.
Microbial and Industrial Biotechnology
Achievements 2005-06:
The on-going projects in the area of microbial and industrial biotechnology would be continued with emphasis on
 development of novel molecules having industrial importance and environmental friendly techniques for social welfare.
 There would be an effort to develop projects in the identified areas. Research leads will be taken up for the pilot scale
 level demonstration. The technology for production of urokinase, the enzyme useful in dissolution of blood clots in
 myocardial system under haemorrhagic conditions, in hollow fiber bioreactor by nutrient manipulation using cell culture
 engineering is standardized.  Cholestrol biosensor has been developed. Some selected projects in the area of
 bioinstrumentation would be considered.
Proposed programmes for 2006-2007:
The projects which have been initiated during the previous year(s) would be pursued for their logical conclusion and
 development of product/processes.  Emphasis would be laid on perfection and scaling-up of the research leads obtained in
 various projects supported under this scheme. The technologies developed will be supported for patenting purposes so as
 to give full protection to the process developed under Patent Act. Some new projects in the area of microbial and
 industrial biotechnology and downstream processing would be developed with emphasis on development of novel
 molecules having industrial importance and environmental friendly techniques for social welfare. Funding of R&D
 projects in the identified areas by the expert group would be continued. Gap areas especially of national importance will  
 be identified and steps would be taken to initiate programmes in these areas.

Biosafety:
Achievements 2005-06:
For making available transgenic crops and recombinant DNA therapeutics to the society at the earliest and at the same
 time not compromising on the safety of the products, the rationalized Biosafety guidelines and procedures would be
 followed. A dedicated website on Biosafety reflecting National and International Guidelines, National Rules &
 Procedures with dynamic interaction with Institutional Biosafety Committees (IBSC) is being developed. A website on
 Indian GMO Research Information System (IGMORIS) is being prepared.

            Aspect of Bio-safety and Genetically Modified Organism (GMOs)
 The advent of new molecular and cellular  techniques of genetic modifications of micro organisms  has led to the
 continuing emergence of products including organisms of bio-technology that promises substantial benefits and
 importance to the quality of life. These techniques are available but to be safely and effectively used, they must be applied
 according to a number of priniciples and with the support of a National Bio-safety Information Network and Advisory
 Service. The Committee is of the opinion that since newly introduced organisms have the potential for trans-frontier
 impacts, there is an urgent need to develop national code of conduct/practice to establish a general frame work and
 guidelines to ensure safety in research, development, production, trade and use of these Genetically Modified Organisms
 (GMOs). The Committee feels that with the development of  Comprehensive Code of Conduct and  Guidelines for Bio-
safety, the safe application of bio-technology in orderly manner would  be possible.
 
Assistance for Technology Incubators, Pilot Level Facilities, Biotechnology Parks and Biotech Development Fund
The scheme of providing financial/logistical support for establishment of biotechnology parks, biotechnology incubators,
 training and pilot projects in various States and organization has been designed to help small and medium enterprises and
 specially the young entrepreneurs who are not in a position to incur high capital expenditure in the biotech industry but
 have the capabilities to develop, design and perfect new biotech products and processes by utilizing the biotech incubators
 and pilot level facilities
While the allocations stood at Rs. 25.00 crore at B.E. in 2005-2006,  it was substantially reduced to 7.00 crore in R.E. the
 same year.  It now stands at Rs. 15.00 crore in B.E. 2006-2007.  According to the Department this budget is for Biotech
 Parks & incubators.  Since, the Biotech Parks were supported during 2005-06, there was not a high budget requirement for
 current year.  Next year, however, new parks would be supported and grant would also be required for ongoing park
 activities.
During the year 2005-06 six major projects were funded for the establishment of Biotechnology Parks & other related
 facilities in the cities/states of Lucknow, Hyderabd, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Punjab, Kerala.

More projects from State Governments and other organizations will be evaluated and suitable actions would be taken for
 establishment of technology incubators, pilot projects etc. based on the recommendations of the Expert Committee.

61.       A major success during the current year has been the launch of public/private partnership scheme - Small Business
 Innovation Research Initiative (SBIRI), which promotes highly innovative early stage, pre proof-of-concept and late stage
 development research emphasizing on important national needs. Under the SBIRI Scheme, the projects which have been
 initiated during the current year would be pursued for directive progress and development of product/processes. 
 Emphasis would be laid on perfection and scaling-up of the proof-of-concepts obtained in various projects supported
 under this scheme. The IPR developed will be supported for patenting purposes so as to give full protection to the process
 developed under Patent Act.
62.       Allocation to Public Private Partnership has been increased from Rs.20.00 cores in B.E. and Rs.16.54 crores in
 R.E. in 2005-2006 to Rs.30.00 crores in B.E.  2006-2007. The Committee has been informed that the increased grants are
 for a new Public-Private partnership scheme SBIRI that  has been launched during September, 2005.  The Committee
 observes that the private companies in different sectors of Biotechnology have shown a good response.  Since the scheme
 has been initiated only in the second half of the year 2005-06, it hopes to expect a much better response during the year
 2006-07.  It appreciates the new initiative taken by the Department in this regard and in view of its importance to promote
 innovation for product development, this schemes need to expand in a big way.
SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
1.         The Committee notes that the Department has been able to make optimum use of the funds allocation is carrying
 out its various programmes/activities.  It also notes the assurance of the Secretary of the Department that the remaining
 amount of the last quarter of 2005-2006 will be fully utilized by March, 2006.
(Para 21)
2.         The Committee notes the efforts made by the Institute  in the areas of stem cell biology, molecular neuroscience
 etc. The Committee is hopeful that the Institute will do its best to develop human embryonic stem cell lines and further
 translational research by transplanting embryonic stem cell lines in animal models of spinal cord and brain injury.  The
 knowledge derived from the above is extremely important considering its impact on clinical situations. (Para 25)
3.         The Committee further notes the importance of research in areas of computational neuroscience, system and
 cognitive neuroscience, developmental neurobiology and basic research towards understanding of neurological and
 psychiatric disorders, as such cases are on the rise in the country owing to the stressful demands of the modern civilization
 which take heavy toll of psychological well-being.(Para 26)
4.         The Committee feels that the development of new vaccines is extremely important. New vaccines and 
 immunodiagnostic kits will be required by the country to check spread of bacterial and viral diseases which either have
 become immune  to  old vaccines or are still un-tackled. (Para 31)
5.         The Committee also feels that in this age of market economics, fundamental high-end research being a high-risk
 venture requires participation from industry for distribution of risks between the research institute and the industry.
 Interaction with industry for manufacture of products developed from the research leads is extremely important to become
 commercially viable. The Committee hopes effective participation from the industry, which is also in long-term interest of
 quality research , will be encouraged  by the Department as far as possible.(Para 32)
6.         The Committee takes note of Studies that have been initiated to understand the process of differentiation of
 embryonic stem cells into cardiomyocytes and also into dopaminergic neurons which could be utilized for replacement of
 damaged neurons in neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s. The Committee feels that new discovery about bone
 marrow stem cells is of therapeutic importance and can prove important in finding better cure for diabetes.(Para 36)
7.       The Committee would also like the Institute to make more efforts for understanding the molecular basis of cancer
 using cell line and animal models as this can help understand this deadly disease better. The Committee would also like to
 emphasize the importance of studies on sequencing of the midgut cDNA library of Anopheles Stephensii, the mosquito
 responsible for spread of malaria in India as malaria is still prevalent in backward areas of the country and still require a
 lot of effort for total eradication(Para 37)                                                                
 8.        The Committee is of the opinion that automated DNA sequencing, comprehensive in silico modeling studies and
 microarray based approaches ,which have already been initiated, should be brought to their logical conclusion. The
 Committee also feels that Data bases of genetic disorders prevalent in India and  of the pathogen that causes TB should be
 completed as soon as possible as they can serve  as an  important referential  source for further studies and research.(Para
 44)
9.         The Committee observes that the research programme of NCPGR aims at contributing to the understanding of the
 structure, expression and function of genes and arrangement of genes on plant genomes and manipulation of plant
 genes/genomes to breed improved varieties of food and industrial crops for high yields of better quality products. The
 mandate of the Department becomes extremely crucial in the light of the fact the India is on the threshold of second Green
 revolution. The technological advances made in the field of agriculture bio-technology should, in the ultimate analysis,

I N T R O D U C T I O N
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred Fifty-eighth Report
 of the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2006-2007) of the Ministry of Ocean Development
 (Demand No.66).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 5
th April, 2006 the Secretary and other Officers of the Ministry of Ocean
 Development gave an overview of the various activities of the Ministry and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of
 the performance of the Ministry to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Ministry for replying to the clarifications sought by the Members
 and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Ocean
 Development.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 15
th  May, 2006.
NEW DELHI;  
May  15, 2006
                                         P. G. NARAYANAN,      
 Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on  Science & Technology, Environment & Forests.
 
 
REPORT
 
Oceans have always influenced the life and history of mankind. From time immemorial, man has been using oceans in several ways.
 According to our mythology, the Gods and Demons churned the ocean and extracted amrita, the elixir of life. Even in the present
 age, we get mineral, food and energy resources from the oceans.
           
2.         Due to its vastness and interplay of processes, oceans control the atmosphere and global climate, besides being a vast
 storehouse of resources necessary for sustenance of life on earth. Appreciating the importance of the subject, the Department of
 Ocean Development was created in July 1981 as a part of the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the charge of the Prime Minister and
 came into existence as a separate Department in March 1982. In February 2006, it has been notified as a Ministry. Ministry of Ocean
 Development has been functioning as a nodal Ministry for organising, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in
 the country, in line with the Ocean Policy Statement of 1982.  The programmes pursued by the Ministry over the years have kept
 pace with developments world over and addressed national needs and priorities.
 
3.         The programmes of the Ministry are directed towards:
 
Technology Development Programmes for future applications with strategic, industrial and economic significance.
Societal Programmes with direct/indirect benefit for the community by technology applications and pilot project demonstration with
 the participation of the community for their socio-economic prosperity, and for coastal area development/management through
 scientific tools and techniques.
Marine Resource Programmes for exploration of marine living and non-living resources, techno-economic studies to evolve strategies
 for sustainable exploration and utilisation, and resource enhancement.
(iv)       Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions with scientific and geo-
political significance.
Capacity Building Programme towards self-reliance through basic scientific research in ocean sector, human resource development
 and establishing Centres of Excellence in academic institutions.
Creation of public awareness of ocean, its potential and uses.
 
4.         The scientific research and technology development programmes are formulated, coordinated and executed through three
 autonomous institutions supported by the Ministry and two Attached offices of the Ministry. These multi-disciplinary and multi-
institutional programmes are assisted by National Research Laboratories, academic institutions and industries. Further, Marine

 Research and Capacity Building is one of the key programme areas of the Ministry to promote basic research in marine science and
 establish centres of excellence in academic institutions and for self-reliance. The oceanographic programmes have national, regional
 and global importance. With the ratification of the UN Convention on Law of the Sea, a new international order has been established
 for the oceans. India is represented in almost all the important bodies on oceans. India will stand to benefit enormously by provisions
 of the convention, if we can build an integrated approach for scientific planning, formulation, implementation and overall
 management of the programmes with a comprehensive organisational and institutional back up. The Ministry is the nodal agency for
 international programmes in the ocean sector and representing the country in Inter-governmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC)
 of UNESCO, Regional Committee of IOC in Coastal Indian Ocean(IOCINDIO), South Asian Regional Seas Programme,
 Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf (CLCS), International Sea-Bed Authority(ISBA) and the State Parties of the United
 National Convention on the Law of the Seas (UNCLOS), the Antarctic Treaty System (ATS) and its scientific and managerial organs
 – Commission on Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), Council of Managers of National Antarctic
 Programme (COMNAP), Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research (SCAR), etc. These activities have scientific, economic and
 geopolitical impacts. Hence, the activities of the Ministry address Scientific Research and Technology Development with orientation
 towards applications, capacity building and human resource development for self-reliance, and international programmes arising out
 of International obligations and bilateral and multilateral cooperative ventures.
 
TOTAL BUDGET DEMAND FOR 2006-07 AND ALLOCATION OF FUNDS FOR THRUST AREAS
 
5.         The Plan outlay for 2006-07 has been fixed at Rs. 475.75 crores (Rs. 438 crore for Plan and 37.75 for Non-Plan expenditure)
 which is Rs. 98.75 crore more than the outlay for 2005-06.  This reflects a 26% hike in the allocation over that for the year 2005-06
 which was Rs. 377.00 crores (Plan - Rs. 340.00 crores and Non-Plan - Rs. 37.00 crores).  The Ministry has maintained that the
 allocated funds would be sufficient for carrying out its activities. The Ministry has informed that in order to be better prepared to face
 devastation like that caused by the killer tsunami in December 2004, the increased allocation is for equipping the country with proper
 warning systems and for in-depth researches. Out of the allocation, Rs. 95 crore has been earmarked for Tsunami and Storm Surge
 Warning System mainly for indigenous development of Deep Ocean Assessment and Reporting systems and setting up of INSAT
 DART & INSAT Met data Reception system at Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS).
6.         The budgetary allocation for the year 2006-07 in the tabular form is given at Annexure.
           
7.         Tsunami and Storm Surge Warning System, Polar Science, National Institute of Ocean Technology, Ocean Observation and
 Information Services, Ocean Data Buoy programme, Gas Hydrates and Polymetallic Nodules programme are the major programmes
 identified by the Ministry for implementation during 2006-07.
 
8.         The head-wise quarterly statement as well as total expenditure of the Ministry for 2005-06 can be seen from the statement

rd Quarter ending December 2005 is due to the Annual

 regular infusion of funds in various projects/schemes in all quarters of the financial year and thereby maintain the uniformity in the
 pace of expenditure throughout the year.

MAJOR DISPROPORTIONATE VARIATIONS AND REASONS
                       
           
10.       The Ministry has informed that during the year 2005-06, the BE of the Ministry i.e. Rs. 340 crore had been reduced to Rs. 250
 crore. Due to this, scaling down of activities had to be made under most of the programmes. The major variations, therefore, were in
 the following programmes:
(i)         Polymetallic Nodules Programme
 
                        BE  -  Rs. 22 crore                               RE  -  Rs. 20.50 crore
 
Due to non-availability of Research Vessel, ship days were reduced leading to the reduction in anticipated expenditure.
 
(ii)        Delineation of Outer Limits of Continental Shelf
 
                        BE  -  Rs. 1 crore                                 RE  -  Rs. 0.00 crore
 
Neither additional analysis and interpretation activity nor any contingent expenditure in this regard was required as anticipated,
 resulting in savings.
           
(iii)       Comprehensive Swath Bathymetric Survey of Indian EEZ
 
BE  -  Rs. 24 crore                               RE  -  Rs. 2.50 crore
 
The reduction in the requirement is due to non-availability of Ministry of Defence clearance from for undertaking surveys.
 
(iv)       Gas Hydrate Exploration and Technology Development for Exploitation
 
                        BE  -  Rs. 30 crore                               RE  -  Rs. 15 crore
 
Non-availabilty of suitable collaboration partner for technology development of coring system and non-availability of seismic vessel
 in market due to sudden spurt in hydrocarbon exploration, resulted in reduced expenditure.
 
(v)        Acquisition of new Research Vessel
 
                        BE  -  Rs. 80 crore                               RE  -  Rs. 30 crore
 
The savings is due to rescheduling of payment for acquiring the vessel in accordance with the finalized contract.
 
(vi)       Geophysical Study of Laxmi Basin
 
                        BE  -  Rs. 1 crore                                 RE  -  Rs. 0.00 crore
 
Neither additional analysis and interpretation activity nor any contingent expenditure in this regard was required as anticipated,
 resulting in savings.
 
11.       The Ministry also informed that under Delineation of the Outer Limits of Continental Shelf, the claim for extending the outer
 limits of continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles EEZ has to be made before 2009. The claim is required to be supported by
 geophysical data, viz., bathymetric, seismic, gravity and magnetic data. The seismic data was collected & post-processing work and
 analyses are in progress and the technical report is in advanced stage of preparation with all work for the claim expected to be
 completed, during 2006-07. While the geo-physical study of Laxmi Basin programme has been completed. The study helps us to
 understand the geology specially the crustal characteristics of the Laxmi Basin in the Arabian Sea. The report submitted is under
 examination.
12.       The Committee observes that the reasons advanced by the Ministry for non-utilisation of the budgetary support in respect of
 Polymetallic Nodules Programme, Comprehensive Swath Bathymetric Survey of Indian EEZ, Gas Hydrates Exploration and
 Technology Development for Exploitation and Acquisition of new Research vessel programmes mainly related to delay in acquiring
 the clearances and finalizing the contract, non-availability of vessel and other such procedural delays. The Committee expresses
 serious concern on such delays and is of the opinion that such delays could have been avoided. The Committee, therefore,
 recommends to the Ministry to evolve a suitable mechanism to monitor the budgetary planning and its allocations and so as to avoid
 such delays in future.
 
13.       The Committee has been given to understand that during the last year of the 10
th plan, all the ongoing schemes will be
 continued and additional activities relating to Exploration of Gas hydrates & EEZ surveys, acquisition of Technology Demonstration
 Vessel that are required for exploration of non-living resources; and the establishment of a Tsunami and Storm Surge Early Warning
 System to be forewarned during impending sea disasters will be undertaken. 

158thReport of Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests

14.       Regarding the mechanism that exist in the Ministry to monitor and review the progress of ongoing schemes/projects, the
 committee has been informed that the ongoing schemes were formulated after studies/recommendations by expert groups and
 following due process of approvals of Standing Finance Committee (SFC)/Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC). The approved
 schemes have clear details of overall budget, scope of work, manpower, equipment details, schedule of activity, year-wise
 expenditure etc. The progress in all areas particularly progress in implementation vis-à-vis expenditure is monitored. Similarly, the
 expenditure incurred and physical achievements vis-à-vis overall approved limit of expenditure is also periodically reviewed. Thus,
 proposals for budgetary support are formulated and finalized.
 
15.       The Ministry further informed that the progress of the ongoing schemes like Antarctica Programme, the Ocean Observing
 System, Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS), Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM),
 are  monitored through the Governing Councils/ Steering Committees of the Programmes. The recommendations of these
 Committees are taken while finalizing the budgetary requirement of the programmes.
 
16.       All the projects under PMN programme have milestones. They are monitored regularly against the milestones. In addition,
 Standing Finance Committee on Polymetallic Nodules Programme (PMN) programme reviews the progress of work for every 3-4
 months. The formulation/finalization of budgetary support is made on the basis of the progress of the programme.
 
17.       Under CLCS programme, the Steering Committee Chaired by Secretary reviews the programme against the milestones. The
 budgetary support has been finalised on the basis of the targeted work under this programme.
 
18.       The monitoring of the MRDF programme is coordinated through 9 OSTCs of the Ministry and monitoring of MRDF
 programme funded on the recommendation of OSTC is carried out by the Management Board of each OSTC. The Management
 Board, in turn, makes available the review reports and corrective action, if any, to the Ministry for formulating the budgetary support.
POLAR SCIENCE/ANTARTIC RERSEARCH
 
19.       The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and logistics prompted the Department
 to establish the first polar research lab of the country at Goa, namely the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) in
 1998, which is responsible for carrying out all the activities relating to Antarctic expeditions. The research on polar science and
 expeditions to Antarctica was being planned, executed and launched annually on behalf of the Department by the Centre.  The Centre
 has a specific R&D mandate in the realm of polar science and to coordinate and launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre has
 a unique laboratory for low-temperature research on ice cores retrieved from Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It would also have the
 facility for the application of remote sensing techniques aimed at understanding the sea-ice-atmosphere interaction in the Polar
 Regions.  It would also have an Antarctic museum and a database repository on polar sciences.
           
20.       In response to a question regarding adequacy of the allocated budget to sustain the tempo of its activities during 2006-07, the
 Ministry informed that the actual project estimate as projected by NCAOR, Goa for the financial year 2006-07 for the
 implementation of Polar Science Programme and other research activities of NCAOR was Rs. 56.00 crores. However, due to
 reduction in overall allocation for the Ministry, based on the prioritised item of expenditure for Polar Science Programme and other
 research activities of NCAOR, an allocation of Rs. 41.00 crores is made for the year 2006-07. The Ministry expects that the major
 planned activities under this programme will be undertaken within this allocation and if required, allocation of additional funds will
 be taken up at RE stage. Targets set for the year 2006-07 are as follows :
Planning, co-ordination and execution of the XXVI Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica
Structural strengthening of Maitri
Revamping the summer huts and establishment of field huts in the Gruber Mountains
Continuation of work towards the establishment of the Third permanent Indian Base in the Larsemann Ranges
Establishment of a summer base in the Larsemann Hills
EIA studies at the site of the new Indian Station
Submission of the Initial Environmental Evaluation Report to ATCM and finalization of the Comprehensive Environmental
 Evaluation of the Larsemann site
Initiation of scientific programmes in Larsemann in the fields of glaciology, paleoclimatology, limnology, meteorology, and upper
 atmospheric studies
Analytical studies of the shallow ice-cores proposed to be collected during the XXV Antarctic Expedition
 
21.       The Committee is of the view that in addition to on-going programmes in various domains of polar sciences, National Centre
 for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) should also initiate cutting-edge experiments in such frontier areas as assessment of
 biotechnological potential of Antarctic microbes, biodegradation of organic wastes using microbial consortium and productivity and
 ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic lakes. It should also envisage initiating meaningful logistics operation with other countries,
 which could lead to operational and financial cooperation.
 
22.       The Committee is of the view that the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR), being the nodal organisationt
 to execute the Antarctic Programmes should strive to further expand its infrastructure facilities for carrying out research in the realms
 of Polar Sciences and Southern Ocean Oceanography.
           
POLYMETALLIC NODULES PROGRAMME

23.       The Polymetallic Nodules Programme (PMN Programme) is a national programme with international commitments which
 envisage eventual exploitation of the nodules from the allotted 1,50,000 sq. km. mine site in the Central Indian Ocean Basin. The
 programme consists of four components-Survey & Exploration of Polymetallic Nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB);
 Environmental Impact Assessment studies at CIOB; Technology Development for mining of nodules; and Technology Development
 for extraction of metals from nodules.
 
24.       During 2006-07, the programme is supported with an allocation of Rs. 19.00 crores. The Committee has been informed that
 the lower allocation of outlay for 2006-07 is mainly due to reduction of outlay in the Survey & Exploration component to Rs. 1.50
 crore during 2006-07 as compared to Rs. 6.00 crore during 2005-06, as only one Survey & Exploration cruise would be taken up as
 per approved programme of 10
th Five Year Plan. Hence, the provision of Rs. 19.00 cores made for 2006-07 would be sufficient to
 meet the requirements of the ongoing activities. The Ministry further informed that it has fulfilled its programme objectives and
 achieved the targeted activities during the year 2005-06. The delay in availability of Research Vessel for demonstration of mining
 system resulted in delay in Phase II of the Mining Programme. All other components viz. Survey & Exploration, EIA- monitoring,
 Technology Development (mining) & Extractive Metallurgy Programme have successfully fulfilled the target. During the year 2006-
07, major thrusts would be given to Technology Development of mining system.
 
25.       The Committee notes that the delay in availability of Research Vessel for demonstration of mining system resulted in delay in
 Phase II of the Mining Programme. The non-availability of Research Vessel, led to reduced ship days under the Polymetallic Nodules
 Programme. The Committee feels that such eventualities result in non-utilisation of the budget in fruitful manner and should be
 avoided. 
 
OCEAN OBSERVATION AND INFORMATION SERVICES
 
26.       Recognizing the need to operationalise the oceanographic services in the new areas of Science & Technology, the Ministry has
 implemented the Ocean Observation and Information Services (OOIS) programme from the beginning of the 9
th Plan.  The objective
 of the Programme is to provide ocean information services for various applications in the ocean section.  OOIS is structured around
 four major themes namely,  Ocean  Observing  Systems,  Ocean  Information Services, Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research
 (SATCORE) and Indian Ocean Modelling & Ocean Dynamic(INDOMOD).
27.       The Ocean Observing Systems envisage collection of sea truth campaigns using moored data buoys, expandable
 bathythermographs (XBT), current meter arrays and tide gauges, and designed particularly for acquisition of real-time sea surface,
 meteorological and upper oceanographic parameters from the coastal and deep waters.  Validation of the satellite sensors has also
 been undertaken using the sea truth data generated under this programme.  The Data Buoy Programme was initiated in 1996 with
 partial financial assistance from Norwegian Agency for Development (NORAD) and National Institute of Ocean Technology (NOIT)
 has been entrusted with the responsibilities for deployment, operation and maintenance of the data buoys.
28.       The Ocean information service envisages generation and dissemination of ocean data/data products on an operational basis. 
 The 14 National Marine Data Centres will be continued under the Ocean Information & Services. A dedicated centre “Indian
 National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)” started functioning at Hyderabad from 1999 for efficient development
 and dissemination of data products.   INCOIS is involved to synthesis, generate, promote, provide and coordinate various endeavours
 in the field of ocean sciences, ocean observations, satellite oceanography, and ocean information and advisory services.  INCOIS has
 a vision to emerge as a knowledge and information technology enterprise for the oceanic realm.  Synergy and knowledge networking
 with centres of excellence in ocean, atmospheric sciences, space applications and information technology as well as translating this
 scientific knowledge into useful products and services comprise the cornerstone of INCOIS.
 
29.       During the X Plan, Indian Ocean Modelling & Ocean Dynamic (INDOMOD) and Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic
 Research (SATCORE) components have been integrated to development of a wide range of ocean atmosphere models for operation
 use at INCOIS.  These include development of regional algorithms, data assimilation techniques and operational models, which
 would be transferred to the Ocean Observation and Information Services (OOIS) Centre for operational use.  The ocean modeling
 and dynamics projects address basic issues on the ocean dynamic, climate variability, ocean state forecast, sea level variations, ocean
 flux studies etc.  Some of the models generated under the programme have already been made operational at INCOIS.
 
30.       The Ministry has been given a budgetary allocation of Rs. 25.00 crores for 2006-07,as compared to last year’s Rs. 17.00
 crores. The Committee has been informed that the proposed increase in the budget allocation of Ocean Observation & Information
 Services (OOIS) for the year 2006-07 is primarily for acquiring High-Performance Computing System at an estimated cost of Rs.10
 crore for Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad, to run the ocean models for providing better
 ocean information services. The Centre is implementing these programmes through a network of reputed national research institutes.
 The ocean-atmosphere models being developed by these institutes, after validation and calibration would be transferred to INCOIS
 for making them operational for providing a variety of reliable ocean information services. In meeting the major aims of acquiring
 data from the sea for the use of various operational and research purposes, infrastructure is established at INCOIS by way of new
 campus and setting up of Satellite Data Acquisition System for real-time reception of satellite data for operational services such as
 generation and dissemination of Potential Fishing Zone information to the fisherman community.
 
31.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that the programmes under the Ocean Observation Information Service have been
 progressing in the right track. However, the Committee feels that the National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS),
 being the nodal agency for providing coastal and ocean data and value added products to the users should monitor its performance
 and work-mechanism to process and disseminate ocean data and data products to user communities like fisheries, weather, climate,

 ports, shipping etc. on a regular basis so that ocean weather forecasting is timely and precise. The Committee hopes that the High
 Performance Computing System at INCOIS, Hyderabad would be in place at the earliest for which a budgetary allocation of Rs. 10
 crores has been made for the year 2006-07.
MARINE RESEARCH AND TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT
 
32.       The objectives of the programme are to foster the concept of stewardship through education, training and human resource
 development and increasing awareness at all levels. The activities proposed in the programme include promotion of research under
 the basic categories of marine ecology, marine biology, marine microbiology, marine benthos, coastal marine culture systems, marine
 geology/geophysics and ocean engineering & underwater robotics.  Besides the ongoing programme of award of fellowships to
 students for pursuing higher studies in academic/educational institutions in various disciplines of ocean science and technology,
 organizing exhibitions and fairs to create awareness among the public on the oceans would continue.
 
33.       The Scientific Research and Technology Development programmes for exploration and sustainable use of the marine
 resources are multi-disciplinary and multi-institutional.  Basic research and developments are required in a wide spectrum of areas to
 gain adequate knowledge and expertise.  Required infrastructure and trained personnel are essential for successfully implementing
 different programmes.  There is need for effective interaction between R&D institutions, academicians and industries.  The sub-
programmes under this programme are as under :
(i)         Assessment of Marine Living Resources and FORV
 
(ii)        Drugs from Sea
 
(iii) Assistance for Research Projects and Manpower Training
 
(iv)       Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS)
 
(v)        Ocean Awareness (Exhibitions & Fairs, Seminars/Symposia)
(vi)       Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM)
(vii) Deep Sea Mineral Exploration
 
(viii) BENFAN – project related to Bay of Bengal
 
 
34.       The Ministry has sought an enhanced budgetary allocation of Rs.1.00 crore for the Drugs from Sea programme during 2006-
07 as compared to the year 2005-06. It has been informed by the Ministry that it is projected to meet the demand for ongoing projects,
 which are being implemented at 10 different research laboratories/ Universities. There has been continuous interaction with
 pharmaceutical industry for transfer of technology towards commercialization of products. There are two new compounds discovered
 recently under this programme for anti-diabetic and anti-hyperlipidemic activities. The Phase-I clinical Trial of CDR-134, an anti-
diabetic compound, has been completed and Phase-II is under commencement. The second preparation has been found safe in the
 subacute monkeys chronic toxicity. The negotiations are progressing well with (Indian & Foreign) pharmaceutical industries towards
 technology transfer of these new products.
 
35.       Under the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) Programme, the Ministry of Ocean Development
 takes up scientific monitoring of pollution at different locations. The programme aims at assesing the status and likely trends in
 coastal marine environment quality and contribute directly to the development of strategies for maximising the economic benefits
 derived from the intelligent and sustainable use of marine environment and resources. The programme envisages systematic
 collection of data on pollutants such as heavy metals and pesticide residue in water, sediment and biological organisms at 82 stations
 along the coastline of the country. The data collected under the programme is made available to the Pollution Control Boards and
 periodically discussed with them. Any significant increase in pollutants at a particular location is brought to the notice of the Central
 Pollution Control Board for control as well as remedial actions.  The main objective of the Programme is to constantly assess the
 health of India’s marine environment and indicate areas that needed immediate and long-term remedial action. 
 
36.       In response to reduced budget for the programme COMAPS, the Ministry maintained that the Departmental Committee during
 its review, suggested to restrict monitoring of all the stations as there is no change in the water quality but these stations are only to
 be monitored once in two years. Hence, the expenditure has been reduced by Rs.30.00 lakh. However, only the hot spots would be
 now monitored intensively. The reduction in allocation does not reflect reduced priority and the Coastal Ocean Monitoring and
 Prediction System programme continues to be a key programme to assess the health of the entire Indian Coastal waters and needs
 long-term monitoring. Based on the data collected, the water quality along the coast is found clean and healthy beyond 2 km from the
 shore except Mumbai, where it is beyond 5 km.
 
37.       The Committee observes that the efforts of the Ministry to monitor pollution in the coastal areas on vigorous basis should not
 be restricted to hot spots only. The Ministry should keep on identifying locations for periodical monitoring alongwith stipulated
 parameters for diffusion and dispersion characteristics. Besides, the samples collected at these locations should be forwarded to State
 Pollution Control Boards for taking remedial measures.
 
38.       The Committee feels that the Ministry should also focus its efforts in assisting Universities to create infrastructure facilities
 and building up a skilled human resource base in Marine Sciences. Besides, the Ministry should also participate and showcase its

 activities in national and international level exposition, exhibition, fairs etc. from time to time. Inter-active computer generated

39.       The Committee observes that the sea's potential as a medicine storehouse remains largely in the realm of experimentation. It

 the products. The Committee recommends that under this programme, the extraction and development of other potential drugs and

NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY (NIOT)
 
40.       NIOT was established in 1993, as a society, under the Ministry, for development of ocean related technologies. The activities
 of NIOT cover five missions, viz. Energy and Freshwater from the Sea, Deep Sea Technology and Ocean Mining, Coastal and
 Environmental Engineering, Marine Instrumentation and Ocean Science and Technology for Islands. NIOT is also the nodal agency
 for deploying floats under the Indian ARGO programme, for implementing the National Data Buoy programme, and for running and
 maintenance of two Coastal Research Vessels. NIOT is entrusted with implementing mining technology development work under
 Polymetallic Nodules programme, development of Submersibles, and with part of the work under Drugs from Sea scheme. It has
 commissioned on May 25, 2005 a one lakh litres of drinking water/day capacity desalination plant at Kavaratti, Lakshadweep and a
 floating, barge-based 10 MLD demonstration plant off Chennai/ Ennore is being designed for main land requirement.
 
41.       During the year 2005-06, NIOT has successfully commissioned the first ever Desalination Plant in India to produce one lakh
 litres per day freshwater based on Low Temperature Thermal Desalination principle at Kavaratti, Lakshadweep islands. The plant has
 produced close to 2 crore litres of water so far and distributed to the Island community by Lakshadweep Public Works Department,
 Kavaratti. The plant also achieved the production rate of 130% during the campaign. In addition, NIOT is working on development
 of desalination plant with a higher capacity of 1 million litres per day and 10 million litres per day during the year 2006-07. NIOT
 would also be developing the wave front facility as a part of capacity building measure during the year 2006-07. The enhanced
 allocation during the year 2006-07 is primarily on these accounts.
42.       The thrust areas under this programme for the year 2006-07 are as under :
(i)         Technology Development for Energy and Freshwater from sea (Desalination)
(ii)        Deep-sea Technology including mining (funded partly under PMN programme)
(iii)       Technology for Coastal and Offshore applications including Environmental Engineering
(iv)       Technology for Marine Instrumentation System
(v)        Ocean Science and Technology for Islands
43.       The Committee commends the efforts of the Ministry on the successful commissioning of the first ever Low Thermal
 Desalination Plant in Kavaratti, Lakshadweep by National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT). The Committee, however feels
 that despite above initiatives by the Ministry, there is still enough scope left to commission such Plants in other coastal areas of the
 country. The Committee, therefore, feels that it should be one of the prioritized areas of the Ministry.
44.       The Committee observes that Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) has a rich potential to provide pollution free
 renewable energy to meet the power needs of coastal region as well as island groups. Therefore, it recommends to the Ministry to
 build energy plants of higher capacity as this might lessen the demand on fossil fuel for power generation. 
45.       The Committee would like the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) to ensure that its activities especially in the
 area of Deep Sea Mining should not pollute the ocean floor and depletion of fish stocks from their habitats, which could affect the
 fishing communities.
 
COASTAL RESEARCH VESSELS
 
46.       Two research ships ORV Sagar Purvi and FORV Sagar Paschimi have been carrying out oceanographic surveys for the
 exploration of non-living and living resources in the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and beyond, around Indian Ocean region since
 1984.  These vessels were being utilised for multi-disciplinary research on the physical, chemical, geological and biological aspects
 of the Indian Ocean.  The vessels were also engaged in campaigns for validating satellite oceanographic data, assessment of marine
 living resources and for various technology demonstration activities. The vessels facilitate systematic collection of samples and
 immediate analysis of the mandatory parameters like nitrate, phosphate etc. for the Coastal Ocean Monitoring  & Prediction   System 
 (COMAPS) programme.   Both    the   vessels   are equipped with sophisticated scientific facilities for onboard analysis and
 navigational equipments along with communication facilities. In order to strengthen the programme on monitoring of marine
 pollution along the coastal waters of the country and to promote research on near shore phenomena, the two vessels do sampling at
 desired locations of the transects identified for potential hot spots. The National Institute of Ocean Technology, Chennai through its
 Vessel Management Cell is maintaining these vessels. During the year 2006-07 an allocation of Rs. 5.00 crores has been earmarked
 for the programme. Sagar Purvi and Sagar Paschimi will undertake cruises for COMAPS (Pollution monitoring) across the eastern
 and western coasts of India and the physical oceanographic observations & microbiological studies for the waste load allocation
 project under ICMAM will continue during this year. The proposed activities under the programme for the year 2006-07 are as
 follows :
Sagar Purvi and Sagar Paschimi will undertake cruises for COMAPS (Pollution monitoring) across the eastern and western coasts of
 India
Continuation of physical oceanographic observations & microbiological studies for the waste load allocation project under
 ICMAM      
Monitoring of pollution in the hot spots
Continuation of Consultancy works for public and private sector undertakings using the vessel

GAS-HYDRATE EXPLORATION AND TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT FOR EXPLOITATION
 
50.       With ever increasing gap between demand and indigenous production of natural gas and the huge import bill incurred by
 India, it is necessary to look for alternative resources and Gas hydrates have the potential in this direction.  The Gas hydrates
 programme consists of both scientific & technology development for gas hydrates. The steps in this programme will be to understand
 the generation and accumulation of hydrates in sediments, estimate impact of gas dissolution on geological environment and climate,
 develop or adopt environmentally safe technology for production and transportation of gas from hydrates, draw up plans to monitor
 and manage environmental perturbation during hydrate harvesting. The allocation of Rs.30.00 crores during the 2006-07 is required
 to continue with survey and fine tuning the SS2500 at gas hydrate site in Krishna - Godhavari and Mahanadi basin  and design of
 ACS for gas hydrates sampling.
 
51.       The Committee during its interaction with the Secretary, Ministry of Ocean Development had observed that the country
 needed alternative sources of energy and gas hydrate was an important discovery. To which the Secretary replied….. “We believe gas
 hydrate is a kind of intermediate solution to energy in the world. When I say that, I mean that once the gas and petroleum are over,
 then gas hydrate will get before the so-called non-conventional and non-hydrocarbon kind of alternative energies, maybe by 2050.
 Now, in this area, we are keeping track of what others are doing. We are not far behind the world. We have not done much research
 because we could not get the permission to use foreign vessels for gas hydrates. We have now got the clearance form the Ministry of
 Defence. Technology development is important and we are concentrating on that like development of remotely operated vehicle. This
 is essentially to further the science of gas hydrate because then equipment will actually be going near to the sea surface and take
 measurements. We know from the science that in case there is a gas hydrate present, we should have significantly very low
 concentration of oxygen locally. We cannot do this unless we have a moving laboratory inside the ocean. We are not far behind from
 rest of the world”.
52.       The Committee is of the view that Fossil Fuel reserves are continuously depleting and will not last long. However, Gas
 Hydrates have the potential of providing energy security to the country, as it is an alternative source of energy. The Committee is
 however, constrained to observe that budget that was allocated under this programme was not fully utilized. The Ministry should
 encourage excellence in national laboratories to focus on niche areas of hydrate research with special emphasis on resource extent
 evaluation and environmental impacts and development of technology for detection of gas hydrates in sediments. The Committee,
 therefore, feels that this programme should be a high priority area for the Ministry in the years to come.

 Warning System during the year 2005-06. The objective of the project is to establish a warning system for the oceanogenic disasters

 directly coming to INCOIS Tsunami Warning Centre shall be established during the year.

 Government for the planning, promotion and coordination of environment and forestry programmes. Within the overall
 framework of its mandate, the main activities of the Ministry include conservation and survey of flora, fauna, forests
 and wildlife, prevention and control of pollution, afforestation and regeneration of degraded areas, protection of the
 environment and ensuring the welfare of animals. These tasks are sought to be fulfilled through environmental impact
 assessment, eco-regeneration, assistance to organizations implementing environmental and forestry programmes,

            REASONS FOR SHORTFALL IN UTILISATION OF THE OUTLAYS
 
18.       The broad reasons for shortfall in the utilisation of the outlays during 2005-06 were as follows:
Delays in approvals/investment approvals of schemes and other procedural delays including delay in receipt of
 proposals from implementing agencies. 
Non receipt of sufficient proposals/detailed project reports and delays in submission of utilization certificates.
Delays in appraisal process of sanction/completion of procedural requirements.
In many schemes, implementing agencies are state governments/ Forest Departments whose performance depends on
 timely release of matching grants.
Under e-governance the shortfall was due to the methodical and well-defined process of selection of consultant adopted
 by the Ministry with the assistance from National Institute for Smart Governance (NISG) for SR specifications and
 software development.
Delays in tender/land acquisition /litigation process by the project implementing agencies in river conservation projects.
 Non utilization of externally aided component of river conservation plan was on account of time taken by states in
 appointment of consultants for various sewerage and non sewerage works. The actual physical works are likely to start
 in 2006-07. 
 
19.       The Committee observes that the reasons cited by the Ministry for shortfall in utilization of the budgetary
 outlays during 2005-06 are mainly attributed to delay in getting approvals, appraisal, finalizing of contracts and non-
receipt of sufficient proposals and other such procedural delays. This reflects the lackadaisical approach on the part of
 Ministry to implement its programmes on timely basis. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should make
 every effort to avoid such procedural delays for effective and timely implementation of the schemes. It needs to have a
 pro-active approach in this regard.
MECHANISMS DEVELOPED BY THE MINISRTRY TO MONITOR AND REVIEW THE PROGRESS OF
 ONGOING SCHEMES/PROJECTS
 
20.       The Committee was informed that the performance of the schemes were reviewed by the Secretary (Ministry of
 Environment & Forests) regularly in senior officers’ meeting of the Ministry. Planning Commission also conducts
 Quarterly/Half Yearly review meetings with the Ministry, to monitor progress of various schemes/projects. Further, the
 Ministry has designated senior officers of the Ministry as Nodal officers for each State/UT, and these Nodal officers
 visit their designated States/UTs regularly to, inter alia, monitor and review progress of schemes/projects in these
 states/UTs. Finally, subject Divisions in the Ministry executing/implementing the schemes also undertake regular field
 visits to carry out monitoring and review of various schemes/projects. 
 
21.       Proposals received in the Ministry are thoroughly examined, both inhouse and also through external evaluators
 like independent experts, peer review, expert committees etc., before being posed for funding to the Planning
 Commission. Most of the Schemes posed for funding in 2006-07 Plan are ongoing schemes.

RESEARCH
23.       The Research programme of the Ministry aims at promoting research in multi-disciplinary aspects of
 environmental protection, conservation and development. The objective of the scheme is to generate information
 required to develop strategies, technologies and methodologies for better environmental management. It also aims at
 attempting solutions to practical problems of resource management, conservation of natural resources and eco
 regeneration of degraded areas. Further, the scheme also seeks to strengthen facilities to facilitate research and
 scientific man-power development. During 2006-07, the allocation for the Research Programme is made in respect of
 Indian Council of Forestry Research & Education (ICFRE), Dehradun and Indian Plywood Industries Research Institute

GREGARIOUS FLOWERING OF MULI BAMBOO
61.       The specter of gloom is haunting the North East region once again with reports of the natural phenomena
 occurring in different parts of the north-east India. Experts at the Rain Forest Research Institute (RFRI), Jorhat has
 anticipated another gregarious flowering of Muli bamboo between 2005-07 over an area of 18,000 sq. kms in India’s
 north-eastern states of Mizoram – the epicentre, Tripura, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and in parts of
 Assam. Manipur’s Tamenglong district is already reeling under a rodent menace, the outcome of bamboo flowering.
62.       For the people of the region, the flowering of the bamboo blossoms means that the inevitable famine is not far
 behind. As per records, flowering of this very species of the bamboo (Muli bamboo) led to famines in 1862, 1881,
 1911-12 and 1959. The 1959 famine claimed between 10,000 and 15,000 lives in Mizoram, Tripura, Manipur and
 Barak Valley of Assam. Based on this, the projections have been made that the next flowering cycle is expected to
 occur during 2004-2007. The phenomenon can be explained as a chain of events occurring in the following sequence.
 The gregarious flowering of bamboos produces large quantities of seeds, which in turn causes sudden population
 explosion in rats. However, the quantity of seeds available for rats diminishes soon on the germination of seeds after
 the rains. The resultant short supply of bamboo seeds on the one hand and a large population of rats on the other, makes
 rats heading towards the farmlands in the adjoining areas and causing wide spread loss to the crops. Such a chain of
 events has the potential to cause famine. 
63.       Most species of bamboo in India — home to the world’s largest bamboo forests — flower simultaneously every
 50 years, then the bamboo germinates its seed and dies subsequently. In previous years, the simultaneous production of
 seeds by millions of bamboo plants has caused a surge in the number of seed-eating rodents. The rodents then move to
 nearby paddy and potato fields in search of food, with a devastating effect on staple crops. Rats literally thrive on the
 seeds of bamboo flowers. Experts say the rodents multiply at a tremendous rate as they get enough food to sustain a
 large population from the bamboo flowers and seeds. The flowers and seeds also enhance the estrogen level of rodents,
 leading to a spurt in the rodent population.
64.       The gregarious flowering of muli bamboo is a natural ecological phenomenon having high social and economic
 implications.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the Ministry of Environment & Forests should collaborate with the
 State Governments to gear up for the impending catastrophe, since the magnitude of the disaster could be very large.
 The Committee recommends that the focus areas in this regard should be harvesting, regeneration of the area and
 rodent control.
INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION
 
65.       The Committee has been informed that there has been an increase of Rs. 2.05 crores in the proposed budgetary
 allocation in BE 2006-07 over RE 2005-06.  Similarly, there has been an increase of Rs. 2.40 crore proposed in the next
 financial year in relation to BE 2005-06. The proposed enhanced allocation in BE 2006-07 is mainly due to increased
 allocation for Contribution to Other International Organisations (Rs. 102.00 Lakhs), Foreign Travel Expenses (Rs.
 102.5 lakhs) and UN Contributions (Rs. 00.27 crore).
 
66.       The Committee feels that the Ministry has not done enough to persuade the international community to adopt

 stringent measures and provide enough cooperation in curbing illegal trade in wildlife parts. The international
 community has not been successful so far to put effective check on illegal trade in wildlife parts, especially tiger parts.
 Therefore, it is very important for the Ministry to take proactive and strong measure on this matter.  It should take up
 this common issue with the international community through Convention on Trade in Endangered Species on Wild
 Fauna and Flora (CITES).
 
WILD LIFE PRESERVATION
           
67.       Under the Wild Life Preservation Programme, the Ministry has sought a budgetary allocation of Rs. 142.98
 crores for the year 2006-2007. The major Centrally sponsored schemes under this Programme are Project Tiger, Project
 Elephant and Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries. Out of this budgetary allocation of Rs.142.98 crores,
 Rs.29.50 crores has been sought for Project Tiger for the year 2006-2007, while for Project Elephant it is Rs. 13.09
 crores and for Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries, Rs.49 crores have been sought. These schemes aim not
 only at protecting the endangered species of wild life, but the entire eco-system.
           
68.       Although the sum sought for budgetary allocation is quite impressive, the basics of wild life conservation cannot
 be successfully accomplished unless certain ground realities are improved.
           
69.       In this connection, the Committee while examining some of the important recommendations in the Report of the
 Tiger Task Force appointed under the direction of the Prime Minister of India following the Tiger fiasco in the
 protected reserve of Sariska in Rajasthan has noted that about 18.2 per cent of the posts for field staff i.e., forest guards,
 foresters and rangers across 28 Tiger reserves are vacant. Among these, the vacancy in the post of guards is
 comparatively higher than other field staff position.
 
70.       The Task Force in its Report has also observed that the training position for foresters and guards is far from
 satisfactory in most of the reserves. 
 
71.       Keeping in view the aforesaid observations made by the Tiger Task Force in its Report, it is observed that the
 basics of the wild life conservation demand for extremely devoted, trained and high quality performance of existing
 staff alongwith strong law enforcement.
           
72.       Another factor, which the Committee feels is very important, is to provide special package for staff, amenities
 and incentives like hard area allowance, free rationing etc. for the forest protection guards combined with provision for
 basic infra-structure, such as wireless sets, cell phones, vehicles etc. so that these could be effective incentives to boost
 wild life conservation. Fast track courts for quick judicial settlements of wild life crime cases, in the opinion of the
 Committee, can also do great justice towards conservation of endangered species in India like Tigers, Elephants,
 Rhinos, etc.
           
73.       For mitigation of human- tiger conflict, the minimisation of livestock killings is an effective countering method
 towards socio-ecological constraints which may stand in the way of wild life conservation. To minimise the ill-effects
 of livestock killings on people, education and awareness programmes related to ecology and  behaviour  of   tiger, 
 genesis  of  tiger menace, possible   mitigation  strategies, need to be framed for  the villagers in the important areas
 with a package for effective  and quick compensation in genuine cases and effective participation of the village
 populace at the ground level which can immensely contribute for wild life conservation of endangered species.

 during the Tenth Plan and evolve suitable mechanism in this regard to avoid such situation in the Eleventh

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
 Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf present this
 Sixteenth Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the problem of environmental pollution and other related
 issues which fall within the mandate of the Ministry of Environment and Forests.

            2. The Committee held, in all, 7 meetings on September 7, 8, 19, 20, 29, 30, 1994 and March 6, 1995. In the
 meetings held in the month of September, 1994, apart from listening to the presentation made by the Secretary,
 Ministry of Environment and forests, the Committee heard the views of the Chairman of the Central Pollution Control
 Board and Chairmen/Member-Secretaries of some of the State Pollution Control Boards/Committee. Besides, the
 Committee also heard the representatives of some of the voluntary organisations which are working in the
 environmental sector, representatives of Indian Industry, representatives of companies which are manufacturing
 pollution control devices, representatives of the Transport Department of the Government of National Capital Territory
 of Delhi and experts on environmental matters which included representatives of some of the premier institutions in the
 field.
            3. The Committee thanks the officials of the Ministry of Environment and Forests for giving the necessary
 information and placing before it the relevant background note/papers which facilitated the work of the Committee in
 examining the problem of environmental pollution and to consider related issues in detail. The Committee also thanks
 the experts and representatives of various organizations Institutions who appeared before the Committee and gave
 valuable Suggestions. The papers/memoranda submitted by many of them were found very useful by the Committee.
            4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on March 6, 1995.

REPORT
General Background
            Advances in science and technology clearly demonstrate how all aspects of nature, living and non-living, are
 interconnected. Nature sustains us. It is in our own interests not to cause damage to it. Resources of the earth must be
 made use of in a sustainable manner. If we $o on destroying natural resources, it would lead to our own extinction
 ultimately. There is no doubt that we have to feed and meet the basic human needs of our population; but at the same
 time we have to remember that our environment should not be damaged to such a great degree that the existence of
 future generations of humanity is threatened. We are increasingly aware of the need to ensure equity in our generation;
 but we should also ensure inter-generational equity. The entire world community has been expressing itself in favour of
 development in harmony with environmental imperatives; and this was the raison-de-etre for holding the UN
 Conference on Environment and Development at Rio de Janiero in June 1992.
           
            1.1 The Earth Charter adopted at that Conference represents the agreement of the various Governments of the
 world to bring humanity back on the path of sustainable development.
1.2 Agenda-21, which was agreed at the Rio Conference, addresses itself to the major environmental and developmental
 priorities important for achieving sustainable development. It was a text agreed to unanimously, after having been
 discussed threadbare, sentence by sentence, word by word and comma-by-comma. It is, therefore, a working document
 of great importance which we as a nation should implement as well as we can.
           
            2. The Constitution casts on us a duty to preserve and protect the environment. The Directive Principles of State
 Policy, contained in Part IV of the Constitution, provide in unambiguous terms for the protection of the environment.
 Article 48A :of the Constitution deals with the protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests
 and wild life. To protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have
 compassion for living creatures, is one of the fundamental duties enshrined i~ "Part IV A of the Constitution, which
 every citizen of this country must abide by. In order to fulfill this Constitutional duty a number of laws have been
 enacted by the Government which aim at protecting and promoting environment and controlling pollution. The water
 (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act', 1974 provides for the prevention and control of water pollution; the Air
 (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 provides for the prevention, control and abatement of air pollution; and
 the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977 provides for the collection of cess on water and
 discourages indiscriminate consumption of water. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella legislation
 for the protection and improvement of environment which also covers protection of environment from hazardous and
 toxic substances. The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 provides for immediate relief to persons affected by

            3. For the management of environment in the country, which includes the prevention and control of pollution,
 the Department of Environment was set UP at the Centre in 198o and was made a fullfledged Ministry of Environment
 and Forests in the year 1985 Present all the States and the Union Territories have set up Departments of Environment,
 under the Water and Air Acts. Central and the State Pollution Control Boards/Committee are also functioning in the
 country.
           
            4. In view of the magnitude of environmental degradation, the Committee thought that it should take stock of the
 strategies of Government with regard to the prevention and control of environmental pollution and other related issues,
 so that a clear picture may emerge about the endeavors which the Ministry of Environment and Forests is making
 towards providing a cleaner environment. The Committee accordingly, on the basis of the Annual Report (1993-94) of
 the Ministry, took up detailed examination of environmental pollution and related issues.
 
            5. As per the "information supplied by the Ministry to the Committee, water quality monitoring is being carried
 out under the Global Environmental Monitoring Systems (GEMS) and Monitoring of Indian National Aquatic Resource
 Systems (MINARS): A network of 480 Water quality monitoring stations has been set up at various locations;, these
 include revivers, lakes, ponds, etc. 37 polluted river stretches have also been identified which require immediate
 attention for restoring the water quality.* An inventory of large and medium polluting industries has also been
 compiled; and the Government has identified 17 categories of highly polluting industries.**         
 
            6. Fiscal incentives are provided to industries which install pollution control devices; and also for the setting up
 of common effluent treatment plants. Epidemiological studies are also being initiated to chalk out proper strategies to
 ensure maintenance of health in the case of people who are exposed to various risk factors clue to environmental
 pollution.
 
            7. In his presentation, the Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Forests made mention of the various factors
 which lead to the degradation of environment. He emphasised the need to chalk out a policy to ensure environmental
 preservation and conservation compatible with the developmental needs, imperatives and priorities. He also informed
 the Committee about the policy statement for abatement of pollution which was brought out by the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests in 1992. He gave the Committee an idea about the working of various environmental laws and
 regulations. About the Central and the State Pollution Control Boards, the Secretary emphasised the need to strengthen
 them and to have environmental experts on their staff so that they are able to discharge their functions more effectively.
 The Secretary also informed the Committee about the methods of environmental impact assessment developed by the
 Ministry and talked of environmental audit and need to have clean technologies which will help in environmentally
 sustainable development.
 
            8. According to the Ministry, while the economic liberalisation process eases the access to technologies from
 abroad, it is essential that Indian firms acquire the best technologies that are also environmentally sound. A clean
 technology or environmentally sound technology (EST), is more efficient technology as demonstrated so strikingly by
 Japan. It involves processes and equipment ~hat ensure optimal utilisation of natural resources and adopts a preventive,
 rather than a corrective approach to pollution abatement; as a result it minimizes waste, and emissions/effluents that
 lead to air/water pollution. To encourage identification, acquisition, development and promotion of cleaner
 technologies at all levels, the Ministry underlined the need to set up a network of Clean Technology Centres with a
 National Centre which would look after coordination functions. While identification, design development and
 promotion of clean technologies in different sectors has to be undertaken by agencies who are specialists in those
 sectors and participate in the network, the central clearing house for clean technologies would perform the following
 functions:
 
Identify areas where introduction of clean technologies is possible and needed;
 
identify sources from which clean technologies and associated datfi can be obtained;
 
assess the technologies, both domestic and imported;

            9. Besides, the presentation made by the Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Forests and other
 representatives of the Ministry, the Committee got valuable feedback on the subject from the Chairman of the Central
 Pollution Control Board. Chairmen/Member-Secretaries of the State Pollution Control Boards of Uttar Pradesh,
 Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, of the Delhi Pollution Control Committee. To obtain the views of Indian
 industry, the Committee invited the representatives of the Confederation of Indian Industry, (CII), New Delhi.
 Representatives of the All India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health,,, Calcutta, Industrial Toxicology Research
 Centre, (ITRC) Lucknow, National Environmental Engineering Research institute, (NEERI) Nagpur, and Central Road
 Research Institute, (CRRI) New Delhi gave very valuable information to the Committee. The Committee also benefited
 from the. views of the representatives of the Bombay Environmental Action Group, Bombay and the Indian Council for
 Enviro-Legal Action, New Delhi who were invited by the Comlfiittee to appear before it. The Committee also heard the
 representatives of the Transport Department of the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi. In order to hear
 the viewpoint of the manufacturers of the pollution control devices, the Committee invited the representatives of M/s
 Bharat Heavy Electrical Limited, Voltas Limited, Andrew Yule and Company limited, Batliboi & Company Limited
 and Envirotech Instruments Private Limited. The Committee also benefited by the views of Prof. Padmanabhamurthy,
 School of Environmental Sciences, Jawaharlal Nehru University who appeared before the Committee on a request
 made by it:. When the representatives of the Ministry of Environment and Forests again appeared before the
 Committee, the Additional Secretary of the Ministry answered the points arising out of the discussion which the
 Committee had held with the experts and representatives of the aforementioned organisations/institutions.
 
            10. The representatives of industry, and some of the experts, demanded that greater incentives be given to
 industry for, installing pollution control equipment, and more duty concessions be given to the units engaged in
 manufacturing pollution control devices. Besides, some of them stated that the environmental standards which have
 been laid down are too strifigent; the efforts have been to conform to western standard, but taking a pragmatic view of
 Indian conditions, a second look should be taken so as to make them more acceptable to Indian industry in terms of its
 present financial and technical capabilities and ultimate product/service c0st~. A point was also made that degraded
 forest areas could be given to industry for plantations so that the forest produce is available both to the industry and the
 people in' the region.
 
            10.1 The Committee is of the view that the idea relating to the involvement of industry in afforestation on
 degraded forest land merits consideration by Government, subject to a suitable regulatory mechanism being evolved to
 ensure  that rights  of local  people are fully  protected.
 
            10.2 The Committee would also e to emphasise that quite a few industrial units in the country are manufacturing
 pollution control devisees and it is necessary that these units are given due encouragement to produce these at low cost
 and ensure their effectiveness.
 
            11. On the basis of the discussions which took place, the Committee has come to definite conclusion that
 environmental pollution in the country is rising. In the cit vehicular pollution is increasing and the quality of air and
 water is deteriorating. T¢ elements are entering the food chain on an increasing basis. This and noise pollution in rural
 areas are risk factors affecting human health. Improper water management is leading to increase in various
 communicable water borne and vector borne diseases. Though a v organisational network exists in the country, which
 has been mandated to protect a preserve the environment yet the Committee feels that the strategies devised so far to
 protect and regenerate environment and to Control pollution have not led to tangible improvement there situation that is
