 Department is gradually shifting to society-related programmes such as Marine Satellite Information System, Coastal
 Zone Monitoring and Prediction System, Sea Element Monitoring & Modelling System, development of islands areas,
 communications, information network and acquisition of coastal research vessels. But this thrust has not to be at the
 cost of development of technologies and oceanographic research. The Committee feels that the programmes of the
 Department which are targetted at benefiting the coastal community which constitutes a significant segment of our
 society, have no doubt been given priority, but these programmes can not make major progress unless matching
 technologies are developed. The Secretary of the Department has conceded that the budgetary allocations for basic
 research do not reflect a priority for this sector and there is imperative need to substantially enhance budgetary outlays
 for R&D projects in the ocean sciences. The Committee appreciates that with a modest Plan outlay of Rs. 52 crores, the
 bulk of which would go on Committee programme of Antarctica research, Poly-Metallic Nodules Programme, Data
 Buoys Programme and in acquiring coastal research vessels, the Department has very limited options, especially when
 it is borne in mind that against the projected demand of Rs. 656.05 crores by the Department for the entire 8th Five
 Year Plan at 1992 prices, only Rs. 130 crores had been approved; of course, during the first 4 years of the 8th Plan
 actual allocations have been to the tune of Rs. 180 crores but this is a far cry from Rs. 656 crores. The Committee
 would, therefore, like to emphasise that, keeping in view the importance of an area like our marine environment,
 budgetary allocations of the Department, particularly for R&D projects and basic research, should be given greater
 priority. Some of the programmes of the Department like Coastal Zone Mapping, installation of Coastal Bathymetry
 System, MET--Ocean Data Buoys Network, National Ocean Information System, in the opinion of the Committee, are
 not getting the necessary coverage for want of financial allocations.
8.A related question was put to the Secretary of the Department about the feasibility of the Department augmenting
 its resources for technological development through external funding. The information given to the Committee was that
 the Department has made efforts to mobilise money through external funding, but the results have not been too
 encouraging. There is, however, a possibility of NORAD funding for its Data Buoys and sea bed mining programmes.
     
      9. The Committee had, in the course of examination of the Demands for Grants of' the Department for the year
 1994-95, earlier noted that a substantial expenditure was being incurred by the Department for chartering/renting of ice-
breaker ship for Antarctica expeditions, and its two oceanographic research vessels, namely ORV Sagar Kanya and
 FORV Sagar Sampada, seemed to have outlived their life and needed replacement. The Department's plan was to
 acquire a multi-purpose vessel which would be useful for the Antarctica expedition, and could also be utilised for
 oceanographic research during the intervening period. The Department had drawn up necessary specifications and even
 floated a global enquiry to ascertain the availability of such a ship which could be modified to the country's
 requirements. The anticipated cost of this multi-purpose vessel was expected to be in the Vicinity of Rs. 75 crores. The
 Department was also exploring the possibility of having such a vessel on lease basis. The Committee was, therefore,
 interested in knowing, the progress towards acquiring this multi-purpose vessel, which could serve the purpose of both
 Antarctica expeditions as well as Oceanographic research and result in substantial savings over a period of time. The
 Committee was informed that the specifications of the proposed multi-purpose, vessel were put out floated through our
 embassies, and as per the advice of the Indian Embassy in Moscow, a delegation also visited Russia to explore the
 possibility of getting an existing vessel which can be modified to suit our needs. So far, there is, only one such
 Antarctic vessel which is being examined in consultation with the technical experts. The Department has also to look
 into the financial aspect of an outright purchase or of going in for a lease. The Committee feels that a major part of
 budgetary allocations for Antarctica research every year is being spent on chartering of an ice-breaker ship and the
 Department's efforts to acquire such a vessel have yet not been successful. There are a number of countries engaged in

19th Report of Committee on S & T

 research in Antarctica who must be using vessels of this nature, and the Department has been encountering little
 difficulty in chartering such vessels. The Committee fails to understand the reasons for the Department failing to
 acquires multi-purpose vessel even after floating a global inquiry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that vigorous
 efforts be made in this direction and the multi-purpose yessel/ice breaker ship be acquired expeditiously to obviate the
 possibility of escalation in its cost in case the matter is delayed any further. Such a purchase will call for increased
 finance allocations for the Department during this plan period.
 
10. The new schemes which are to be initiated by the Department relate to: (i) setting up of a marine
 acquarium/oceanarium; (ii) Data Buoys Programme for which the budgetary outlay has been enhanced from Rs. 0.10
 crores to Rs. 2.20 crores; and (iii) acquisition of coastal research vessels. The Committee has noted that these schemes
 are not entirely new, as budgetary provision for all of them had been made in the outlay for 1994-95, though none of
 these could take off in that year. Responding to a query from the Committee about the progress made in regard to
 setting up of oceanarium, the Secretary of the Department stated that the project involved an investment of about Rs.
 100 crores and, therefore, participation by the private sector was considered necessary. A national and global inquiry
 was floated by Engineers India Ltd. inviting proposals from the private sector to set up the oceanarium at Goa on a
 Build, Own, Operate and Maintain (BOOM) basis. No response has been received from any private parties. The
 feedback received revealed that more informations about the sites in Goa, particularly on the ecology, accessibility,
 infrastructural facilities available, likelihood of approvals other tourist attractions nearby, tourist flow and likely
 number of local visitors, etc. are required by the private parties in order to work out the economic viability of the
 proposal. It was also pointed out that there would be need for Government to participate in the project. These issues are
 being examined by the Department, and after collecting all the required information, it is proposed to invite fresh
 proposals. The bidders will be provided with the above information.
 
11. Explaining the importance of the Data Buoys Programme, the Secretary of the Department stated that the Met
 Ocean Data Buoys will provide reliable, time series, in situ data on critical oceanographic and meteorological
 parameters for understanding oceanic processes around India, which are important for exploration and sustainable
 development of living and non-living ocean resources, sea truth support for satellite data, etc. The Department has plans
 for taking up the implementation of the data buoy programme, and has moved NORAD for financial assistance. The
 financial assistance may be in ~e form of part credit and part loan. The provision of Rs. 2.2 crores in the financial year
 1995-96 is for meeting the Xocal (Indian) expenditure.
12. As regards the coastal research vessels, which would be needed for monitoring the health of marine environment
 of the country, and monitoring marine pollution along the coastal waters, as also to promote research on near shore
 phenomena e.g. coastal circulation, the information given to the Committee was that the vessels are under construction
 and the stipulated time for the delivery is April, 1996.
 
13. The Committee found that in the Budget estimates for 1995-96, the allocations for Marine Satellite Information
 Service (MARSIS), National Oceanographic Data and Information System, National Institute of Ocean Technology and
 Island Development have been reduced as compared to the allocations for these programmes during the year 1994-95,
 whereas the allocations for Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System and assistance for research projects,
 seminar, symposia, etc. have been increased. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for these variations. It was
 clarified by the Department that the actual requirement for 1995-96 for MARSIS, according to EFC approval, is Rs.
 480 lakhs; against this a Budget provision of Rs. 400 lakhs has been made. The reduced outlay is due to delay in
 launching of the American Sea Star Satellite. Similarly, as regards the National Oceanographic Data and Information
 System, during the year 1994-95, strengthening of 11 out of 13 National Marine Data Centres was completed with a
 budget estimate of Rs. 1 crore. During 1995-96, funds are required to strengthen the remaining two Data Centres and to
 meet the recurring expenses of the created Data Centres, which will need a lesser requirement in the year 1995-96. Data
 is at present exchanged between Government institutions and agencies, and large scale selling of data to private sector
 is yet to commence; but matters relating to security aspects of Data release are being sorted, out in consultations with
 Defence. The reduction in the Budget allocation for the National Institute of Ocean Technology for 1995~96 is due to
 tapering of non-recurring expenditure and infrastructure development. The Institute would, nevertheless, be able to
 continue to work on wave energy coastal zone processes and marine instrumentation during the year 1995-96 as
 targetted.
 
14. Explaining the reasons for the enhanced allocations for the Coastal Ocean Monitoring Prediction System

 (COMAPS) and assistance for research projects etc., the Secretary of the Department submitted that a project for
 development of a mathematical model to study the dynamics of pollutants in the Thane Creek is in progress; and in
 order to validate the model, data on physical and chemical parameters are needed for which an additional requirement
 of Rs. 65 lakhs is proposed in the Budget of 1995-96. The increase in the Budget estimates from Rs. 2.30 crores in

 due to the new thrust being given to increase the assistance to universities and other research institutions for human
 resource development in the area of marine sciences and technology. The Committee feels that the reasons for
 reductions in allocations on the earlier indicated 3 programmes of the Department are quite understandable. It is of the
 view, however, that MARSIS, COMAPS, data buoys programme, support for research and development and for human
 resource development in the area of marine sciences and Island Development programme are all priority areas calling
 for greater thrust and financial allocations. Ocean Sciences is an emerging area which needs to be given necessary
 support and attention. Educational institutions particularly in the Coastal Zone which have the Infrastructure for
 relevant research in ocean sciences need to be given an impetus. The Committee also notes that the Scientific
 Departments are exempt from consultation with UPSC and the Committee would, therefore, like the Department of
 Ocean I Development to expedite filling up of posts including absorption of those on contract basis.
 
15. The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier view that the Department of Ocean Development cannot just
 carry out some marine related programmes that the agencies of government are not handling. It is the nodal department
 to lay down ocean policy and to promote an integrated, coordinated approach to the whole area of marine science and
 technology and exploration and utilization of marine resources. The Committee would like to see the Department play
 this role effectively.

REPORT
The Department of Biotechnology which was established as an Independent Board in
1982, and became a full-fedged Department in 1986 has completed more than two decades of
existence. During this period the focus has been on enhancing the knowledge base and generating
highly skilled human resource, nurturing leads of potential utility and bringing bio products to the
market place. In the area of HRD, the Department has implemented an integrated programme to
generate adequate and appropriately trained manpower. The Department has established about 35
Biotech facilities during the Tenth Five Year Plan for production and supply of biological
reagents, culture collections and experimental animals which are available to scientists, industries
and students. An extensive Bio-Informatics Network covering 65 Institutions spread all over the
country has been established. Some of the Important achievements in the field of Crop
Biotechnology include transformation technology for rice for salinity and drought tolerance,
molecular marker for wheat quality trades; Bt novel Cotton Technology; Transgenic virus
resistant Tomato; GM Mustard with higher yields, etc. In the area of Animal Biotechnology a
technology for recombinant anthrax vaccine has been developed and transferred. In the field of
Medical Biotechnology, development of new technologies for affordable vaccines for Malaria,
Tuberculosis, Cholera, HIV , Filariasis, etc. have been undertaken. Stem Cell Research is also
being promoted for basic and translational research. In the area of Environmental Biotechnology,
several technologies are ready for commercialization like Hioremediation of mine spoil dumps;
technology for mangrove afforestation, etc. Various technologies have also been developed for
manufacture of nutrient supplements, health food, fruit juice processing, oil and fat modification,
ensuring food quality/safety etc.
1.1 The National Biotechnology Development Strategy was approved by the Government of
India during the current year. The strategy is an outcome of a two-year-long nationwide
consultation process with multiple stakeholders including concerned ministries, universities,
research institutes, private sector, civil society, consumer groups, non-government and voluntary
organizations and international bodies. The draft strategy, which was posted on the web, received
over 300 comments from all sections of the society. The strategy, while enabling the full utilization
of currently available opportunities in manufacturing and services, will lay a strong foundation for
discovery and innovation, effectively utilizing navel technology platforms with potential to
contribute to long terms benefit in agriculture, animal prductivity, human health, environmental
security and sustainable industrial growth.
1.2 The autonomous institutions like National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi, National
Centre for Cell Science, Pune, and Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and diagnostics, Hyderabad, etc.
under the fold of DBT have made significant achievements. Four International and ten Indian
patents were granted to National Institute of Immunology. The repository at the National Centre for
Cell Science is the only repository that houses human and animal cells in India. The Centre has
a total of 155 publications and has obtained 6 US and 3 Indian patents. The Department has
supported setting up of biotech parks at Lucknow and biotech Incubation Centre at Hyderabad,
Bangalore, Kochi, Chandigarh and Solan. The Department has launched Small Business Innovation
Research Initiative (SBIRI) to boost Public Private Partnership in the country.

4. BIOTECH FACILITIES AND PROGRAM SUPPORT
4.1 The Committee was informed that the strength of biotechnology development in the country
lies in up scaling a number of proven technologies-diagnostic, vaccines, products, and processes
for fine-tuning and large-scale production. While Indian industry is strong in product development
and marketing for commercial benefits, biotechnology in India still lacks necessary infrastructure
for R&D in molecular modeling, protein engineering, drug designing, immunological studies, pre-
clinical studies, clinical trials, etc. The public investment in major equipment required for research
and development in biotechnology should be directed so as to maximize access not only within the
institution but also for other institutions and industry both in public and private sectors for optimum
utilization of resources.
4.2 It was further informed that the Department has been supporting establishment of Biotech
Facilities in Institutes/Universities to undertake production and supply of biological, reagents,
culture collections and experimental animals. These facilities also conduct regular training
programmes for capacity building in the areas of instrumentations, handling of small animal house,
bio-processing, microbial taxonomy and molecular biology.
4.3 Till the end of the Tenth Plan (2002-07) the Department had established about 35 facilities
across the country. A major review at the end of Tenth plan on the performance and relevance of
these facilities was carried out. Most of the facilities are now operated by the host institutions and
their agencies while others were continued for support through remodeling and up gradation to suit
contemporary needs. New facilities are being continuously established keeping in view the National
Biotechnology Development strategy of the Department.
4.4 Allocation made for ‘Bio-Tech Facilites’ has shown an increase from Rs. 22.50 crores at
BE and RE stages in Budget 2007-08 to Rs.25.00 crores in Budget 2008-2009. The Department
has informed that the increase is due to implementation of a newly proposed programme in the
Eleventh Five Year Plan aimed at remodeling/reengineering of university departments of Life
Sciences for taking up new research agenda for global competitiveness. The programme envisages
faculty induction, upgradation of postgraduate laboratories/fellowships, providing common
sophisticated instrumentation facilities.
4.5 The Committee is of the view that remodeling/reengineering of university
departments of Life Sciences is of utmost importance in order to remain globally
competitive. The Committee expresses its concern over the lack of infrastructure for R&D
in molecular modeling, protein engineering, drug designing, immunological studies, pre-
clinical studies, clinical trials, etc. as without a strong R&D base success of the Department
will remain short-term and would fail to sustain itself in the long run. Therefore, the
Committee recommends that infrastructure for R&D needs to be built up adequately to
achieve the desired targets fixed in the Eleventh Plan period.
5. Research and Development
5.1 Allocation made for ‘Research and Development’ has been increased from Rs.237.56 crores
at RE stage in Budget 2007-08 to Rs.315.00 crores in Budget 2008-09. When enquired about the
new programmes that have been initiated by the Department with the enhanced allocation, the

5
Department has informed that besides reviewing of the ongoing programmes for logical conclusion
and continuation, other R&D projects in following new areas will be initiated:
• Fine mapping of genome region harboring useful genes to help marker-assisted precision
breeding in wheat, chickpea, pigeonpea and groundnut.
• Molecular characterization of genes involved in apomixes in crops.
• Transgenic for pest and disease resistance, drought along with development of RNAi
technology applications in:

*Forestry species with a thrust on secondary metabolites and non-timber forest

chromosome 5 (12Mb) of tomato. Sequencing of 5 Mb is expected; efforts will be
strengthened.
• Construction of BAC genomic library for the buffalo genome.

aqua/shrimp genomics and wheal functional genomics.
• New R&D based wellcome Trust-DBT fellowships will be launched for enhancing

• Cell-based approach in product and process development and marine extremophiles
• Joint projects with industries on isolation and characterization of therapeutically active
compounds (NCE) from medicinal plants for metabolic syndrome, neurodegenerative

• Programme for development of antiviral agents- Hepatitis C; Dengue, Influenza.
• Animal vaccines and diagnostics, brucellosis, Pow vaccine, Johns disease and swine
fever.

• Development of cancer biomarkers.
• Biomarkers for Neuro degenerative disorders
• RNAi technology based programmes.
• Nanotechnology based programmes.

Diarraheal, Tuberculosis, Hepatitis B & C, Nanotechnology based Sexually Transmitted
Diseases related with improved sensitivity, HIV/AIDS and acute lower respiratory

• Development of Diagnostic Methods in Chronic Diseases
5.2 The Committee is of the opinion that State Agriculture University should be given
required support to start interdisciplinary translational research centres so as to enable
them to emerge as solution providers for local agricultural needs. The Committee
recommends that the Department engages itself in exploring the possibilities for the use of
barren land for agricultural or horticultural purposes with the help of bio-technology, as this
would help bring a vast unutilised area under productive cultivation in the country. The
Committee would be happy to see progress in potential application of nano-biotechnology in
agriculture, medicine and environment. Special emphasis needs to be paid for use of
technology in preserving our environment which has seen large scale degradation. This
would go a long way in conservation of lakes which are getting polluted everyday. The
Committee would also like the Department to establish specialized virus research centres
to address viral biology, pathogenesis, biomarkers, etc. within a reasonable time-period.
5.3 The Committee would also like the Department to focus and channelise its R&D
activities on programmes for using algae and jatropha as a source of biodisel and producing
ethanol from cellulose because the sources of fossil fuel are depleting fast but yet constitute
the major source of energy. This should be done in a targeted manner so as to make early
breakthroughs.

plan and women component plan.
Rural Component of the Programme
6.2 Proven and field tested technologies shall be demonstrated to help the target population in
their skill development, employment and income generation in the field of agriculture, sericulture,
production and manufacture of biopesticides and biofertilisers, awareness programmes on
health and nutrition diet. Rural bioresource complexes established in five states shall be
continued.
(a) Details of Tribal Sub-Plan and Special Component Plan: Resource based programme
will be implemented for employment generation, skill development and awareness. Self

Help Groups will be supported for cultivation and marketing of medicinal and aromatic
plants, fodder cultivation, animal rearing, promotion of handicrafts, piggery, food
processing, aquaculture and dairy, health care and nutritional interventions.
(b) Details Regarding Women Component Plan: The programmes include several field
based extension, demonstration and training projects on proven and field tested
technologies for women. Some examples include: value added floriculture; processing
of horticulture produce; cultivation and processing of medicinal and aromatic plants;
production and application of vermicompost. Biopesticides and biofertilisers; high value
mushroom cultivation, aquaculture, poultry and rabbit rearing for wool extraction and

for awareness and counseling on genetic disorders and creating awareness on nutrition

6.3 Allocation under the Head-Biotechnology for Societal Development has been reduced from
Rs. 11.20 crores at RE stage 2007-2008 to Rs.10.00 crores. The marginal reduction has been due
to the fact that 10% of the RE level of Rs. 11.20 crores of 2007-2008 was to be reflected under
allocation for North Eastern Region during 2008-2009 for the same purpose.
6.4 The Committee would like the Department to disseminate proven and field tested
technologies to help the rural population in their skill development, employment and
income generation in the field of agriculture, sericulture, etc. This has a potential not only
to provide self-employment and raise farm incomes but also to check migration to the
cities, which are already under stress. Self Help Groups along with other civil society groups
need to be roped in big way to make such programmes reach tribal, women and other
weaker sections of the society.
7. HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
7.1 An exercise to formulate model undergraduate and postgraduate curricula in life sciences
and in translational science keeping in view, future needs, new PG teaching programmes in the
areas of food and nutrition biology, clinical pharmacology, bioenterprise management, biofinancing
and regulatory efforts shall be initiated. M.D/Ph. D programmes will be supported in some medical
colleges/ institutions. At least five star undergraduate colleges in biotechnologies/life sciences will
be in place. Few teacher and technician training centres will be setup. The existing programmes
like Ph.D., Post-doctoral Fellowships and others will be scaled up. Besides continuing
and expanding the fellowship, need based new fellowships to promote innovation will be
instituted.
7.2 The Committee has been informed that the country produces lesser number of PhDs,
in comparison to other developing countries like Brazil and China except in engineering.
This has grave implications for Scientific Research in future. The committee recommends
that this situation be rectified so as to create a good research base in the country and that
the Department must play a pro-active role in this regard. The number of PhDs is bound
to be less unless and until students are initiated in the subject at a young age. The
Department should evolve a suitable long-term mechanism for the purpose. But the
Committee feels that this would not be possible as the allocation under this programme is

8
Rs. 30 crores as against Rs. 70 crores proposed. The Committee is of the opinion that
adequate resources should be earmarked for Human Resource Development.

at RE stage in Budget 2007-08 to Rs.60.00 crores in Budget 2008-09. The Department has
informed that as proposed in the Eleventh Five Year Plan, the department will be launching a new
Public-Private Partnership (PPP) scheme ‘Biotechnology Industry Partnership Programme (BIPP)’
aiming at development of futuristic technologies and to address un-met national priorities in
agriculture and healthcare. Besides, it is proposed to establish 'Biotechnology Industry Research
Assistance Council ‘(BIRAC)’ for managing PPP programmes of the department, technology
management and licensing and catalyzing growth of small and medium enterprises.
8.2 The Committee is of the opinion that financial and technical support should be given
to individual innovators as good innovations many a times come from the unorganised
sector.The Committee is of the opinion that the Department should do all needful in
spreading the culture of knowledge based entrepreneurship.

Biotech Development Fund’ has been increased from Rs. 7.01 crores at RE stage in 2007-08 to

Plan 2008-2009 of the Department. During 2007-2008, the Department was informed of the
non-exemption from this allocation at the final stages of budgetary exercise in the Ministry of
Finance leaving no scope for planning the schemes/programmes in advance. Even though,

the same. The Committee is of the view that post-doctoral fel1owships are very low and

environment, quick decision-making is the key to success. Owing to involvement of several

ministries in decision-making process, initiation and implementation of schemes gets
considerably slowed down in our country. It is, therefore, required that a better coordination

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and
Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred Ninety-first Report of the Committee. This Report
deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2008-09) of the Department of Atomic Energy
(Demand Nos. 4 & 5).
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on 1st April, 2008, the Secretary and other Officers
of the Department of Atomic Energy gave an overview of the various activities of the Department
and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the performance of the Department
to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
3. The Committee express its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the
clarifications sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the
Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Atomic Energy.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 23rd April, 2008.
DR. V . MAITREYAN

EW D ELHI; Chairman,
April 23, 2008 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.

1
REPORT
The Indian Atomic Energy programme aims at utilisation of Atomic Energy for peaceful
purposes—electricity generation, development of radiation technology and application of Atomic
Energy in the field of medicine, agriculture, industry, national security and research. The policies
and programmes are administrated through the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE).
2. The Department’s Plan programmes are multidisciplinary in nature. For their execution, DAE
has evolved itself as a broad based organisation comprising research centres, industrial units, public
sector undertakings and fully aided autonomous institutions, along with service organisations. There
are five Research and Development units, three industrial units, three service organizations and five
public sector undertakings besides eight aided institutions under the Department of Atomic Energy.
These organisations are engaged in research, technology development and commercial operations in
the areas of nuclear power and associated technologies, radiation technologies and their
applications, and basic research. These also enrich university system through beneficial interaction.
3. The detailed budget allocation of the Department of Atomic Energy for the year 2008-09
was considered by the Department-related Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and
Forests at its meeting held on the 1st April, 2008 and the Demands for Grants of the Department
has the following provisions.
4. BUDGETARY OUTLAYS
The budgetary outlays of the Department (Plan and Non-plan) as per the guidelines of the
Planning Commission/Ministry of Finance, fall under the following Demand numbers:
• Demand No.4 - Atomic Energy
It covers expenditure of DAE and its organizations (Research and Development, and
Minerals Sectors), as well as DAE Secretariat and Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB).
• Demand No.5 - Nuclear Power Schemes
It covers expenditure towards (i) Russian credit to Nuclear Power Corporation of India
Ltd., (ii) Investment in equity to BHAVINI, (iii) Waste Immobilisation Plants, (iv) Other work
related to PFBR and (iv) Operational expenses of RAPS Unit-I and Fuel Inventory.
4.1 The Department informed the Committee of the following shortfalls in approved allocations
(Plan and Non-plan) as compared to the proposed allocations for the year 2008-09:
(i) Plan Allocation
The shortfall in allocation under the Plan schemes of Demand No.4 – Atomic Energy is
Rs.916.62 crore. The shortfall under Demand No.5 – Nuclear Power Schemes is Rs.263.11 crore.
Thus the total shortfall under Plan is Rs.1179.73 crore. Major portion of this is intended for the
plan project under Research and Development Sector under Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Indira
Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre, Raja Ramanna Centre for
Advanced Technology, Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research and under the
fully aided Autonomous Institutions like Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Institute of Plasma
Research, Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, Tata Memorial Centre, etc and also for the projects
under Industrial Sector in Nuclear Fuel Complex, Heavy Water Board, Bhabha Atomic Research
Centre, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Board for Radiation and Isotope Technology and

2
for the investment in equity in Uranium Corporation of India Ltd under the Minerals sector.
Shortfall under the Power sector is for the ongoing Nuclear Power Project under the Bharatiya
Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd. The Department, however, stated that the shortfall will be reviewed
at Revised Estimates stage depending on the necessity of funds and if required, request for
augmentation through Supplementary Grants, will be sought.
(ii) Non-plan Allocation
The shortfall under Non Plan side of Demand No.4 – Atomic Energy is Rs.255.29 crore.
Major portion of this is intended for the operational budget in Industrial Sector in Heavy Water
production, Nuclear Fuel Complex, Board for Radiation and Isotope Technology, etc.
4.2 The Committee enquired about the drastic cut ( i.e. Rs. l444.l5 crores) resorted to in the
allocations under the head ‘Nuclear Power Schemes’ in Demand No.5., from Rs. 2333.15 crores
in B.E.2007-08 to Rs. 889.00 crores in B.E.2008-09, to which the Secretary of the Department
clarified that this cut is due to the phasing out of some of the projects. So far as the Nuclear
Power projects of the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) are concerned, these
projects will be mostly supported on the basis of Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR)
and may require only a small amount of Budgetary Support(BS). The Ministry further informed that
two 700 and 1000 megawatt projects each were planned to start in the Tenth Plan subject to the
fuel linkage and also the possibility of international cooperation. In the absence of these conditions
being fulfilled, these projects have to be deferred. Another crucial factor that contributes to the
requirement coming down is that out of the three ongoing projects, two are nearing completion.
This is how the total requirement has come down drastically.
4.3 The Committee, however, notes with serious concern the curtailment of funds under
the Plan schemes in Research and Development Sector for premier institutions like Bhabha
Atomic Research Centre, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Variable Energy
Cyclotron Centre, Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology, Atomic Minerals
Directorate for Exploration and Research, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Institute
of Plasma Research, Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics, Tata Memorial Centre, etc. The
Power sector which is responsible for undertaking the ongoing Nuclear Power Project under
the Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd. has also experienced a cut in allocation. The
Committee also notes the cuts in budgetary allocation under the non-plan schemes which
were intended for the operational budget in Industrial Sector in Heavy Water production,
Nuclear Fuel Complex, Board for Radiation and Isotope Technology, etc.
4.4 The Committee is of the opinion that curtailment of funds for premier Institutions
engaged in comprehensive research and development of frontline technologies, for
harnessing nuclear energy for the benefit of the society, would delay the endeavour of these
institutions in achieving their goals. The Committee fails to understand as to how the
Department will manage to achieve its targets, in the field of Atomic Energy, which is
highly capital intensive with such meager budgetary allocations. The Committee hopes that
in future the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance would exercise utmost
precaution before finalizing allocation for the Department.
5. MONITORING MECHANISMS FOR ONGOING PROJECTS
5.1 The Committee was informed of the following structure of monitoring and reviewing
mechanisms of projects in the Department of Atomic Energy:
(i) Project Co-ordinator and his group of people review and monitor the progress of
ongoing projects on day to day basis.

3
(ii) Unit Head reviews and monitors the projects on month-to-month basis and tries to
remove constraints/lacuna, if any, and monitors the financial and physical progress of
projects.
(iii) At the Department level, Principal Adviser/Secretary monitors and holds quarterly
review meetings to assess the physical and financial progress of the projects and tries
to remove any procedural bottleneck amongst the Units/Divisions for smooth progress
of projects so that there is no time/cost overrun.
(iv) After the above review process the Department assesses the requirement of funds in
each project and formulates the proposal for budgetary support in the form of RE for
the current year and BE for the next financial year.
5.2 In addition to the above steps, the Department has taken concrete steps to ensure that the
Plan targets are achieved. The mechanism of formulation of projects is now based on the concept
of Major Programmes. Further, Steering Committee, Internal Working Group and Specialist Group
have been constituted to review the project report prior to their sanction and also to review the
progress of the projects. Thereafter, their recommendation provides the realistic input to the budget
planning process. In the R&D Sector, the overall programme of the Department has been divided
into twenty themes and Specialists Groups have been formed for each one of them to oversee the
activities during Eleventh Plan. Thus monitoring of projects under R&D Sector is done at three
levels. The first level monitoring is at Section or Group level in the Unit, the second level is by
the higher level of management in the Unit and the third level is the monitoring by Specialist Group
at DAE level.
5.3 The Committee desires that the existing monitoring mechanisms developed by the
Department to monitor and review the progress of the ongoing schemes/projects before
formulating/finalizing proposals for budgetary support should be effectively used to
eliminate any scope of shortage or surrender of funds at a later stage.
PROGRAMMES
The programmes of DAE have been divided into four Sectors for the purpose of allocation
of Funds viz.: Research and Development Sector, Minerals Sector, Industrial Sector and Power
Sector. The major programmes are discussed below.
6. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT SECTOR
6.1 The Research and Development Sector includes research support for nuclear power
programme as well as research and development in non-electricity areas. It covers research and
development for new power reactor concepts and long term research, radioisotope technology with
applications in medicine, agriculture, industry and research; advanced technologies relating to
accelerator, laser, computers, materials and others, and basic and applied research in frontier areas
of science and technology.
6.2 There are Five Research Centres under the Department namely, Bhabha Atomic Research
Centre (BARC) – Mumbai, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) – Kalpakkam, Raja
Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) – Indore, Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre
(VECC) – Kolkata, and Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD)–
Hyderabad. The main functions of these centres are given below:
• Bhabha Atomic Research Centre pursues comprehensive research and development
(R&D) programmes in the fields of nuclear sciences, engineering and technology, basic
sciences and allied fields for harnessing nuclear energy and also its utility for the benefit
of the society.

4
• Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research is the second largest R&D centre of the
Department engaged in basic research in nuclear sciences and allied areas, technology
development in the field of nanomaterials and nanotechnology and has designed the
500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR).
• Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology is engaged in development of particle
accelerators and lasers along with their applications, besides carrying out substantial
activities in cryogenics and materials research.
• The V ariable Energy Cyclotron Centre is operating the nation's largest and the first
indigenously built Cyclotron and has been produced for the first time in India, the
energetic Neon 20 and Argon 40 beams required for conducting research in Nuclear
Physics.
• Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration & Research carries out survey, prospecting
and exploration of atomic minerals required for the nuclear power programme of the
country.
6.3 The major programmes under the R& D Sector for the Eleventh Five Year Plan are as
follows:
(i) Intensifying of Uranium exploration including development of aerial electromagnetic
survey capability for locating concealed deposits having no surface manifestation.
(ii) Launching of :
• A high flux Multipurpose Research Reactor at Visakhapatnam.
• Upgraded APSARA reactor by enhancing reactor power up to 2 MW.
• A first of its kind in the country 250 MeV Superconducting Cyclotron for
proton beam to be constructed at VECC, Kolkata.
• Demonstration unit of a Compact High Temperature Reactor at BARC, Mumbai.
• Plant for special materials for High Temperature Reactors at Visakhapatnam.
(iii) U pgradation and modernization of scientific infrastructure of all the major R&D
Centres like BARC, IGCAR, RRCAT, VECC, and autonomous institutions like TIFR,
SINP, HRI, IMSc, AEES etc. for overall improvement, pursuing mega science projects
and for staying internationally competitive in S&T.
(iv) Setting up of major large size experimental facilities at Tarapur, supplemented by the
programmes at Trombay to facilitate continued development of advanced technologies
for next generation reactor systems.
(v) Development of Cancer Care facility at Shillong and Ranchi.
(vi) Augmentation of R&D for 700 MWe PHWR and life extension programme for existing
PHWRs including improvement in capacity utilization, safety, control instrumentation,
corrosion, materials etc.
(vii) Strengthening R&D on back end fuel cycle including long term radioactive storage
strategies.
(viii) Development of indigenous technologies related to fuel development for light water
reactors.

5
(ix) R&D for further development of metallic fuel for fast breeder reactors and associated
fuel cycle.
(x) Thorium fuel cycle development.
6.4 As regards the Budgetary allocations for the year 2008-09, the total allocation is
Rs. 2448.14 crores; while the Plan allocation is Rs. 1228.00 crores and the Non-plan allocation is
Rs.1220.13 crores.
6.5 The Committee was informed of the following demand projected by the Department to the
Planning Commission for its various programmes and the allocation that has been agreed to by the
Planning Commission under the R&D Sector:

6.6 The Committee feels that the reduction in the approved allocation vis-a-vis  the
proposed one would somehow affect the programmes envisaged by the Department during
the Eleventh Plan some of which like upgradation and modernization are very crucial. The
Committee is of the opinion that the Department is in a better position to judge its
requirements and hence surreptitious or perfunctory reduction is untenable. Any
compromise on major research programmes is not acceptable to the Committee. This issue,
therefore, needs to be seriously looked into by the Government.

6
7. NUCLEAR IRRADIATION IN AGRICULTURE AND FOOD PROCESSING
7.1 The Committee was informed that the incidence of diseases in seeds and food-borne
diseases can be reduced by food irradiation techniques. It can also inhibit post-harvest sprouting
in potatoes and onions—disinfect fruits and vegetables, delay ripening in fruits, can eliminate
outrightly the food-borne pathogens which can be kept for a long time without refrigeration before
substantial consumption. In addition, the irradiation technology can be used for eliminating pests
nuisance etc.
7.2 The Committee was also informed that presently more than 51,000 consignments of various
isotope products and processing services were provided by the Board of Radiation and Isotope
Technology (BRIT) to institutions all over the country and also some of them located abroad,
bringing in a sales turnover of Rs. 45 crore. Eight new irradiated ‘‘Trombay crop’’ varieties—two
in Mungbean and one each in Groundnut, Soyabean, Mustard, Sunflower, Cowpea and Pigeon pea
were released for commercial cultivation in various agro-climatic zones of the country. So far 35
Trombay crop varieties have been released and notified for commercial cultivation. As regards food
processing BRIT’s Radiation Processing Plant at Vashi, Navi Mumbai continued to offer radiation
processing services to its customers spread all over the country. More than 1000 MT of spices
and allied products were processed at this plant upto November, 2007.
7.3 The Committee was also informed that although irradiation technology could have outright
advantages, there could be certain health risks that might be involved in the application of the
technology of the following nature:
• Irradiation can result in loss of nutrients.
• When food/seeds are exposed to high doses of ionising radiation, the possible changes
in chemical composition and nutritional content of food damage DNA in humans.
• Irradiation does not necessarily inactivate dangerous toxins which have already been
produced by bacteria prior to irradiation.
• Irradiated food products like chicken, meat, etc. could mislead consumers into thinking
that they are biologically safer for consumption.
7.4 The Committee is of the opinion that some precautionary measures should be taken
by the Department of Atomic Energy while irradiating food so that the possible health risks
involved before consumption of irradiated food could be effectively dealt with. In this
connection a timebound programme for evaluation of Radiological Safety, Microbiological
Safety, Nutritional adequacy and Toxicological Safety may be initiated since the irradiation
of seed/food products is in a nascent stage.
8. NUCLEAR MEDICINE
8.1 The Committee was also informed that the Department through its Nuclear Medicine
Centres such as Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Tata Institute of Fundamental Research
(TIFR), Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT), etc., is also engaged in the production
of diagnostic Radiopharmaceuticals viz. lodine-I3I, phosphorous-32, Chromium-51 etc. which are
quite useful in the treatment of various diseases.
8.2 The Committee feels that diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals are an important constituent of the
various diagnostic tools used for the detection of life threatening diseases like cancer, thaleseemia,
tumors etc. and therefore desires that efforts should be made by the Department to produce
sufficient radio pharmaceuticals in the country itself and provide it to the hospitals at cheaper rates
so that the poor patients can avail of the facility.

7
9. TATA MEMORIAL HOSPITAL AND CANCER TREATMENT THROUGH
TELEMEDICINE
9.1 The Committee was informed that Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) is wholly engaged in
diagnosis, treatment and in basic/advanced researches in the field of Oncology as well as training
and education in cancer to provide highest standard of cancer treatment not only in the country
but even in Asia and has gained specialization in Nuclear Medicine. The TMC is mainly composed
of Tata Memorial Hospital (TMH) and the Advanced Centre for Treatment, Research and Education
in Cancer (ACTREC). A telemedicine network connecting all the Regional Cancer Centres across
the country with TMC has been commissioned. So far 19 cancer hospitals including seven in the
North East and two from abroad have been connected with Tata Memorial Hospital.
9.2 The Committee is of the opinion that cancer is one of the most prevalent diseases in
India afflicting the population across the country and the treatment for the disease is very
costly. Telemedicine is one of the tools of reducing the treatment cost, as it can provide
specialised treatment even at the backward and remote regions of the country. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made to spread the telemedicine
network by connecting more hospitals across the country with the Tata Memorial Hospital.

12. URBAN SOLID W ASTE MANAGEMENT
12.1 The Committee was informed that the Department has taken the initiative of solving the
problem of management of urban waste through technology. The department informed that a part
of the urban waste is biodegradable and while the rest is non-biodegradable. The biodegradable part,
which is normally sent to the landfill, contributes a lot towards bacterial pollution, which in turn
results in common ailments like cough and cold and thereby increases the cities’ health management
expenditure. Also, there is a major energy expenditure on collecting this waste and carrying it to
the landfill across the city. To process the bio-degradable waste, the BARC has developed a
technology, namely, the bio-digester, to convert all biodegradable waste into organic manure and
methane. The bio-digester digests kitchen waste, abattoirs waste, vegetable market waste,
agricultural residues and converts it into manure and methane on which even generators can be run
to produce power. The sludge can be used as organic manure. It also provides livelihood to a large
number of poor people who are involved in waste segregation. Such a plant is presently under
operation in Vadodra.
12.2 The Committee feels that both these technologies can prove to be boon for
conservation of nature and environment and for the society at large which is grappling with
the problem of disposal of sewage as well as solid waste generated in metropolitan cities and
small towns. What is required is the propagation and popularization of these technologies
because their efficacy lies in their use on a large scale. In view of the fact that
environment protection is the need of the hour as hazards of global warming and climate
change are looming large, the urgency of such a step becomes more prominent.
12.3 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should. take effective
steps for marketing these technologies, if possible by creating a special cell for the purpose,
within Radiation Technology Development Section of Bhabha Atomic Research Centre. The
cell should interact with. the municipalities/corporations/State Governments/Ministry of
Urban Development, Ministry of Environment and Forests, etc. to demonstrate the merits
of the technology.

14. HEALTH HAZARD OF URANIUM MINES
14.1 The Committee raised the issue of the health hazard created by mining of Uranium ore,
specially in open-cast mines, which are causing tremendous concern to the local population and
desired to know about the steps that have been taken to minimize their impact on the local
population.
14.2 The Department clarified that apart from the steps taken by the Uranium Corporation of
India Ltd., which is responsible for mining, a separate programme in the Health Safety and
Environment Group of the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre is functioning, where a lot of research
regarding minimizing health hazards is conducted and their advice in terms of the protection
measures is being implemented. Further, health audits are also being conducted regularly in the
population affected by the mining. However, the problem of lack of public awareness still exists.
The department also ensures that the mines are covered with greenery once they have been
exhausted. The Department assured the Committee that in DAE, safety comes first and production
next. Safety means industrial safety, radiation safety, health issues connected with mine workers,
connected with the people in the surrounding area, and also issues connected with environment.

16. ENRICHMENT AND UTILISATION OF THORIUM FOR NUCLEAR ENERGY
16.1 The Committee raised the issue of enrichment of Thorium as fuel for utilization in nuclear
reactors instead of Uranium, in view of the fact that India possesses large deposits of Thorium
as compared to Uranium and self-sufficiency can be obtained so far as fuel is concerned, in case
Thorium is used as fuel.
16.2 The department clarified that the nuclear energy programme of the country has been
consistent with the nuclear resource profile and the three stage nuclear energy programme has been
designed accordingly. Though the programme to use Thorium as fuel has been delayed, yet it is
on course right now. The Committee was also informed that since Thorium is not fissile, firstly,
it has to be converted into fissile Uranium-223 and that requires fast reactors where there is excess
of neutrons. In fact, blanket production of Thorium for the fast reactor and its processing has
already been done. However, Thorium utilization in a major way for nuclear energy, will begin only

14
after our fast reactor programme reaches the level of a fairly high megawatt capacity, of the order
of 50,000 to 1,00,000 MWes. As far as technology development is concerned such as Thorium
processing, Thorium fuel-making, the process has already been perfected and the BARC has
developed a 300 MWe Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) that aims at developing expertise
for thorium utilization and demonstration of advanced safety concepts.
16.3 The Committee is of the opinion that to gain self-sufficiency in the country’s
requirement of nuclear fuel, the Department has to make concerted efforts towards
development of technology which uses Thorium as Nuclear fuel instead of Uranium, keeping
in view the vast reserves of Thorium. The use of Uranium, makes the country dependent
on other countries and also results in outgo of foreign exchange.
17. REMUNERATION OF SCIENTISTS
17.1 So far as the remuneration of the scientists is concerned, the Committee Was informed that
a plea for a special allowance, over and above the normal salary, was made to the Sixth Pay
Commission, for attracting scientists in the field of Atomic Energy. The Pay Commission has not
agreed to that and instead, they have agreed for getting scientists on contract basis, where market
salaries can be given. However, since the scientists who join the institutions under Atomic Energy,
have a tradition of nationalist feelings, wherein they retire from the institutions after serving for
over 30 years, the contract appointment terms does not fulfill the requirements of the Department.
Secondly, as regards the promotion prospects, the fraction of the scientists who will go to the
topmost posts in the Department are very less as compared to the civil services, which leads to
high level of attrition among the scientists.
17.2 The Committee expresses its serious concern at the fact that the present
remuneration being paid to the scientists is not attractive enough to attract the best of
scientific talent available in the country. Further, to make matters worse, there is a high
level of attrition of scientists from the department, who move towards the private sector for
better salaries and promotion prospects. The Committee recommends that the case for
grant of special allowance over and above the normal salaries may be taken up emphatically
with the Government, keeping in view the the special requirements of the department, and
the scientific community at large, specially in view of the tremendous contributions of the
scientists in the field of Atomic Energy.
18. INDO-UNITED STATES JOINT CIVILIAN NUCLEAR ENERGY AGGREMENT
18.1 The Committee was informed that during the visit of Prime Minister of India to United
States of America (USA) in July 2005, a Joint Statement was signed in which both countries
agreed to work together to achieve full civil nuclear energy cooperation. India was recognized as
a responsible state with advanced nuclear technology and it was agreed that India would acquire
the same benefits and advantages; including full civil nuclear cooperation and have access to the
international fuel market. In turn, India reciprocally agreed to assume the same responsibilities and
practices such as separating its civilian and military nuclear facilities in a phased manner and filing
a declaration regarding its civilian nuclear facilities with International Atomic Energy Agency(IAEA);
taking a decision to voluntarily place its civilian nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards etc.
18.2. The Committee was also informed that in March 2006 a ‘Separation Plan’ was agreed with
the USA and tabled in the Indian Parliament on the 7th March, 2006. The Separation Plan provides
for assurances by USA on uninterrupted nuclear fuel supplies to reactors that would be placed
under India-specific safeguards in perpetuity, together with India’s right to take corrective measures
in the event of fuel supplies being interrupted. The USA also gave assurance of support to India’s

15
right to build up a strategic reserve of nuclear fuel to meet the lifetime requirements of India’s
rectors. In turn, the USA agreed to have their laws adjusted and also to work with allies to adjust
the international regime such as ‘Nuclear Suppliers Group’ (NSG) to enable full civil nucIear
encrgy cooperation and trade with India.
18.3 The Committee was also informed that on 7th December, 2006 the US Congress adopted
the ‘Henry Hyde – US – lndia Peaceful Atomic Energy Cooperation Act 2006’. India’s concerns
on certain provisions in the Hyde Act were taken up with the USA. A draft Agreement on
Cooperation between the Government of India and the Govcrnment of the Unites States of America
concerning Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy has been negotiated and finalized between India and
USA on 1st August, 2007.
18.4. The Ministry further informed that according to the India-US Agreement finalized in July,
2007, India was required to complete the negotiation of ail India specific agreement with the
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Thereafter adjustment of the guidelines of the NucIear
Suppliers Group (NSG) and the approval of the US Congress for the operationalisation of the
agreement will be sought. The fifth round of discussions with IAEA on an India-specific agreement
has concluded in February, 2008. Considerable progress has been made during these 5 rounds of
negotiations and further consultations are on with the Agency
18.5 The Committee is of the opinion that the agreement with the United States of
America has to be looked at from the larger perspective of national security as well as
national interest. While acknowledging the increasing energy requirements of the country,
the thrust must be on the indigenous ‘Three-stage Programme’ on which our scientists are
working with great confidence and optimism. The Indo–United States Nuclear Agreement has
caused serious concerns with regard to our foreign policy and security related issues on
which our Parliament had to debate several times. The sense of the Parliament needs to be
taken into consideration.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and
Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorized by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred Ninety-second Report on the Functioning of Central
Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
2. The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests in its meeting held on 8th September, 2006, decided to take up for
examination on the aspects relating to Functioning of Central Pollution Control Board and report
thereon. The Central Pollution Control Board is the apex technical body of the Ministry of
Environment and Forests to advise the Government on matters related to protection of
Environment. In this regard the Committee heard the views of the Secretary Ministry of
Environment and Forests and the representatives of certain State Pollution Control Boards viz.
Uttarakhand, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Orissa, Delhi, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. In
addition, the Committee also heard the views of some experts. A list showing the details of the
representatives of various Ministries/Departments who appeared before the Committee for oral
evidence is given in Annexure-I.
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Ministry of Environment and
Forests, CPCB and different State Governments for replying to the clarifications sought by the
Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinize the same.
4. In the meeting held on 13th June, 2008 the Committee considered the draft report and adopted
the same.
DR. V . MAITREYAN
N
EW D ELHI; Chairman,
June 13, 2008 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests.

1
REPORT
CHAPTER-I
I. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Nature has since the hoary past been attached utmost significance in our country so much
so that it has been personified, revered and worshiped. Be it the sun, air, water, rivers, lakes,
ponds, mountains or the earth – all the constituents of environment were regarded in high esteem
and treated as sacrosanct. Whatever the religious or spiritual rationale behind this, one thing was
certain, that all these elements of nature individually as well as collectively were regarded vital for
the existence and survival of mankind, and hence such an august and holy treatment. This theory
still holds good. These elements of nature are still vital for the well being of mankind but with the
gradual change in our socio economic priorities, the reverence and significance accorded to them
has somehow been put on back burner. Basically and primarily an agrarian economy till mid Fiftees
of the last century, it started drifting towards industrialisation which led to urbanisation and now
in the age of globalization, economic development has acquired such a predominance that there can
be no looking back. Economic development and environment came into direct conflict with each
other, the latter often understood as anti-thesis to the former.
1.2 That the overriding economic priority would have its impact on environment was visualised
in the early seventies of the twentieth century. It was around this period that pollution had started
getting manifested or reflected in rivers and other water bodies due to industrial or sewage
discharge. To nip the problem in the bud a Central Board for Prevention and Control of Water
Pollution (CBPCWP) was constituted under the provision of the Water (Prevention and Control of
Pollution) Act, 1974. The mandate of the board as spelt out in the above Act was:
“To promote cleanliness of streams and wells in different areas of the States through
prevention, control and abatement of water pollution”.
1.3 A major step in this direction was taken in the year 1976 with the enactment of the
Constitution (forty second Amendment) Act through which a new article i.e., article 48A under
Directive Principles of State Policy and a fundamental duty i.e., 51A (g) were inserted which
read as follows:
48A: Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life–
The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the
forests and wild life of the country.
51A: It shall be the duty of every citizen of lndia—
(g) To protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild
life, and to have compassion for living creatures.
1.4 The former provides that the State shall endeavor to apply the principle in making laws
while the latter makes it obligatory on the part of every citizen of the country to protect and
improve the natural environment.
1.5 Thereafter with the manifestation of pollution in air came the Air (Prevention and Control
of Pollution) Act in 1981 and the responsibility to improve the quality of air and to prevent control
or abate air pollution in the country was also entrusted to the CBPCWP. Later on under Water
(Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act 1988, CBPCWP was rechristened as “Central
Pollution Control Board”. Thereafter a number of legislative and administrative measures of far
reaching consequences for Pollution Control were introduced some of which are:

2
(i) The Environment (Protection) Act 1986;
(ii) The Hazardous Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1989;
(iii) The Bio-Medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1989;
(iv) The Plastics Manufacture, Sale and Usage Rules, 1999;
(v) Municipal Solid Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000;
(vi) The Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000;
(vii) The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000;
(viii) The Batteries (Management and Handling) Rules, 2001;
(ix) The Plastics Manufacture and Usage Amendment Rules, 2003.
1.6 The present national policies for environmental management are contained in the National
Conservation Strategy and Statement on Environment and Development, 1992, the Policy Statement
on Abatement of Pollution, 1992 and National Environment Policy 2006.

3
CHAPTER-II
2. CENTRAL POLLUTION CONTROL BOARD (CPCB)
2.1 The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) is the apex technical body of the Ministry of
Environment and Forests entrusted with the task of abatement and control of pollution in the
country. Department of Science and Technology has recognized CPCB as a scientific and technical
organization. It is a multi-disciplinary organization where engineers and scientists of various
disciplines are in position. It gets 100 per cent grant-in-aid from the Ministry of Environment and
Forests both for plan and non-plan expenditure.
2.2 Sub-clauses (1) and (2) of clause 3 of ‘The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution)
Act, 1974 provide that to exercise its powers and discharge its functions, there shall be a Central
Board consisting of the following members:
• a full-time Chairman, being a person having special knowledge or practical experience
in respect of matters relating to environmental protection or a person having knowledge and
experience in administering institutions dealing with the matters aforesaid, to be nominated
by the Central Government;
• such number of officials, not exceeding five, to be nominated by the Central
Government to represent Government;
• such number of persons, not exceeding five, to be nominated by the Central
Government, from amongst the members of the State Boards, of whom not exceeding two
shall be from amongst the members of the local authorities;
• such number of non-officials, not exceeding three to be nominated by the Central
Government, to represent the interest of agriculture, fishery or industry or trade or any
other interest which, in the  opinion of the  Central Government, ought to be represented;
• two persons to represent the companies or corporations owned, controlled or managed
by the Central Government, to be nominated by the Government; and
• a full-time Member Secretary, possessing qualifications, knowledge and experience of
scientific, engineering or management aspects of pollution control, to be appointed by the
Central Government.
2.3 The total number of Members of the Board comes to 15 excluding the Chairman and
the Member Secretary. Out of fifteen, twelve Members are such officials who hold additional
charge of the  Membership of CPCB. Out of the twelve, five officials represent the Government and
five persons are nominated from amongst the members of State Boards. All the appointments are
made by Government. Further sub section 3 of section 5 of the Act provides that the  Central
Government may remove any Member of a Board before the expiry of his term of office which
is three years.
2.4 The Act does not prescribe any time limit within which the vacancy of Chairman or other
Members has to be filled up. As a result the post of regular Chairman of CPCB, lying vacant for
almost two years, has not been since filled up and an officer of the rank of Joint Secretary in the
Ministry of Environment and Forests is holding the charge of Chairman, CPCB ever since.
3

4
2.5 The Committee is of the view that with such a composition dominated by
Government representatives and constituted by Central Government, CPCB can not be
expected to act as a watchdog of environmental protection. The Committee also expresses
its displeasure over the fact that no qualifications or criteria have been fixed for Members
of such an important technical and scientific body. The eligibility criteria for Chairman
prescribing a person having special knowledge or practical experience in respect of matters
relating to environmental protection or a person having knowledge and experience in
administering institution dealing with the matters aforesaid are too general and vague as
to accommodate anyone who is even distantly related with environment.
2.6 The Committee has been informed that key posts in CPCB and SPCBs are being
manned by officers of Indian Administrative Service or bureaucrats who neither possess the
necessary capabilities and expertise in properly managing and planning pollution control
activities nor have enough time to pay attention to these activities for obvious reasons. This
trend has led to virtual relegation and replacement of technically capable persons to the
place of exile from the keyposts. The Committee has been informed that this point has
been highlighted by Prof. Menon Committee set up by the Supreme Court with regard to
management of hazardous waste. According to the report of the Supreme Court Monitoring
Committee on Hazardous Waste, 77 per cent of Chairpersons and 55 per cent of Member
Secretaries in different state pollution control boards are not qualified enough to hold the
post. The Committee observes that this is a very disturbing trend and that this practice
needs to be stopped forthwith.
2.7 The Committee feels that Chairman and Members of the Board should be persons
who have rendered remarkable and distinguished service to the cause of Environment. They
should be persons of repute and widely acclaimed. They should be appointed for a fixed
tenure and the sword of removal or termination should not be hanging on their heads.
Members like Chairman should be full time. The Committee also feels that the present
large composition is hampering its effective functioning. The size of the Board may be
reduced, so as to ensure that decisions are taken and translated into action in the right
earnest.
2.8 If the creation of CPCB is seen in the present day context, when pollution has started
posing numerous challenges it appears that the very foundation on which it has been established
is shaky and weak. It has been established under a subject which is primarily the concern of State
Governments. Water supplies, irrigation and canals, drainage and embankments, water storage and
water power is a state subject as per Entry 17 of the State List of the seventh schedule to the
constitution. But prevention and control of water pollution overtly or covertly does not seem to fall
under the ambit of this item as it has nothing to do with drawing or sharing of water that could
affect rights of the states. It involved the larger issue of cleaning up and maintaining the
wholesomeness of water.
2.9 The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 has been enacted under Article
252 of the Constitution and not under Article 248 or 249. Article 248 gives exclusive powers to
Parliament to make law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the concurrent or state list
while as per Article 249 Parliament shall have power to legislate with respect to a matter in the
state list in the national interest. Article 252 provides that it shall be lawful for Parliament to pass
an act if it appears to the Legislatures of two or more states to be desirable that any matter on
which Parliament has no power to make laws for the states except as provided in article 249 and
250 should be regulated in such states by Parliament by law, and if resolutions to that effect are
passed by all the legislatures of those states. Accordingly, resolutions to the effect that prevention
and control of water pollution would be regulated in the states of Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana,

5
Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tripura and
West Bengal, were passed by all the Houses of the legislatures of those States. In pursuance of
the above Act, the Central Government constituted a central Board called the Central Pollution
Control Board (CPCB) and the respective State Governments constituted State Pollution Control
Boards to exercise power conferred on and perform function assigned to them under this Act. Thus
two parallel Boards- one at the centre and the other at State level came into existence with the
latter being entrusted with important and critical functions and the former being given the advisory
and coordination role. This resulted in the Central Pollution Control Board turning into a weak and
lame duck organization.
2.10 The Committee feels that our experiment with the existing framework/model i.e.
simultaneous existence of two parallel boards one at the Central and the other at States level each
one working as independent and autonomous entity in its own capacity with no Central authority
to command and control, has led us to no where over the last 33 years. Environmental degradation
and pollution is growing at an alarming pace and has acquired alarming proportions. Rivers, lakes
and other water bodies are getting polluted unabatedly and recklessly and air is getting dirtier day
by day. To ensure compliance by way of inspection, vigilance and sampling falls under the domain
of SPCBs with CPCB acting merely as a guiding and coordinating body. The end result is that
SPCBs are masters in their own rights and they do whatever they desire.
2.11 Further, section 61 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, empowers
the Central Government to supersede the Central Pollution Control Board if at any time the Central
Government is of the opinion that the Central Pollution Control Board has persistently made default
in performance of the functions imposed on it by or under this Act or that circumstances exist
which render it necessary in the public interest so to do for a period of one year. Such a provision
renders Central Pollution Control Board to act as mere puppet in the hands of Central Government
and does not allow it any space for independent and autonomous functioning.
2.12 For creation and appointment to certain posts, Central Pollution Control Board is also
required to obtain prior sanction of the Government (Rule 8 of Water (Prevention & Control of
Pollution) Rules; 1975).
2.13 Sections 3 and 5 of the Environment (Protection Act) 1986 read as:—
‘‘Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Central Goverrment, shall have the power to take
all such measures as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and
improving the quality of the environment and preventing controlling and abating
environmental pollution’’;
“Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law but subject to the provisions of this
Act the Central Government may, in the exercise of its powers and performance of its
functions under this Act issue directions in writing to any person, officer or any authority
and such person, officer or authority shall be bound to comply with such directions”.
Explanation—For the avoidance of doubts, it is hereby declared that the power to issue
directions under this section includes the power to direct—
(a) the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process; or
(b) stoppage or regulation of the supply of electricity or water or any other service.
2.14 Ministry of Environment and Forests vide its notification dated the 10th July, 2002 delegated
its powers conferred upon it under section 5 of the Act  to the Chairman, CPCB to issue directions
to any industry or any local or other authority for the violation of the standard and rules relating
to hazardous waste, bio-medical waste, hazardous chemicals, industrial solid waste, municipal solid

6
waste including plastic. But delegation of this power is subject to the condition that it may be
revoked if in the opinion of the Central Government such a course of action is necessary in public
interest.
2.15 These are some of the highlights which corroborate the fact that it is the Central
Government/Ministry of Environment and Forests and not the Central Pollution Control Board
which de-facto is the chief custodian of Environment preservation and protection. Central Pollution
Control Board devoid of any effective legal authority is a mere body or board without teeth.
2.16 The Committee’ expresses its anguish over the fact that the Central Board created
for the purpose of control and abatement of pollution is being given such a raw deal so
much so that it has virtually been reduced as a near defunct body. If all the powers and
functions were to be concentrated into the hands of the Central Government/Ministry of
Environment & Forests the very need to have such an apex body is untenable. The
Committee feels that the country can ill afford to let this sorry state of affairs prolong any
further as it has already started bearing the brunt of pollution and climate change and
hence drastic measures are required to be taken. Central Pollution Control Board needs to
be given adequate statutory and legal support to make it effective and functional and for
this purpose its constitution under Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
needs to be urgently reviewed. The Committee recommends that environment protection
should be included as an item in the seventh schedule to the constitution in the concurrent
list and CPCB be brought under its ambit with all necessary powers and functions to meet
the challenges that pollution and its after-effects pose before us without disturbing the
federal character of our constitution. This new body should be given functional as well as
financial autonomy so that it can discharge its duties without fear or favour.
