The telemedicine programme has been specially beneficial for the work up and treatment
planning for patients of BKW Hospital Dervan TMCROP for pre visit work up by the TMH
consultants. The patients taking advice at Hospitals in the North East have been spared a costly
and time consuming trip to Mumbai. Only 7 patients seen at remote sites were asked to come to
TMH for further or initial treatment. It is noticed that the patient satisfaction and comfort level is
very high. Satisfaction with consultation is very high and most would repeat a follow up
consultation. Physician satisfaction is also high overall. There was no limitation on their ability to
treat/diagnose. They rated most consults same as face-to-face.
Plans are in hand to expanding the reach of telemedicine through the Government of India
ONCONET Programme for Teleconsultations, medical education and also for connecting with
additional nodes on the ISRO network. It is also envisaged to increase patient education and

6
awareness for follow up from remote nodes. Further, it is indented to enhance the Value addition
through Regular CME by broadcasting weekly clinical meetings to the remote nodes and
Broadcasting lectures and demonstrations in Preventive Oncology and Early Detection, Nursing
Techniques, ICU care, Catheter Care, Infection Control etc.
All out effects are taken by the Department to spread the telemedicine network by
connecting more and more hospitals in the country.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply with satisfaction and urges that the work of
spreading the network is continued.
Recommendation (Para 10.4 and 10.5)
The Committee notes that, while allocations under some of the heads of the ‘Assistance to
Universities’ have been decreased, they have remained constant for most of the programmes like
public awareness and neighbourhood programme, exhibitions, symposia, etc. In some programmes
viz. fellowships, prospective research in funding, etc. insignificant increases have been effected.
The Committee is of the opinion that budgetary allocations under these heads are relatively meager,
keeping in view the fact that there is an urgent need to develop interest and awareness amongst
the masses and especially the younger generation towards the subject of Atomic Energy and to
dispel the negative impression of the public towards nuclear power. The Committee is of the
opinion that more funds should be allocated towards mass awareness programmes in the field of
nuclear science.
The Committee feels that the Department should concentrate on increasing its investments
significantly, in the field of research in nuclear science at University level, which would help in
inculcating interest towards nuclear science and attracting more students to this field. In this
direction the Committee recommends that a proactive system of funding should be initiated by the
department, which would focus towards bringing more and more universities across the country
under its coverage of grants.
Action Taken by the Government
The budget allocation towards Public Awareness and Neighbourhood Development
programmes referred to are pertaining to the allocation of expenditure towards this head only from
the DAE Secretariat (through its Public Awareness Division). In addition to this, its Public Sector
Undertakings (like Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, Uranium Corporation of India
Limited etc.), Industrial Organisations (like Board of Radiation and Isotopes Technology, Heavy
Water Board, Nuclear Fuel Complex etc.) and R&D organizations (like Atomic Minerals Directorate
for Exploration and Research, Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic
Research, Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology, Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre etc.)
are also carrying out such programmes in their respective neighbourhood. Both Nuclear Power
Corporation of India Limited and Uranium Corporation of India Limited conduct their own Public
Awareness and Neighbourhood development programmes in the villages surroundings their operating
facilities and also in the areas where they intend to set up new facilities. Thus, the overall
expenditure on Public Awareness and Neighbourhood Development is to the extent of requirement.
The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) recognizes the need for funding the Indian
Universities and programmes are already in place to provide funding for carrying out R&D projects
on topics of interest to the mandate of the Department to leading universities, academic institutions
and recognized R&D labs in the country through the Board of Research in Nuclear Sciences

7
(BRNS). A typical distribution of BRNS funding for the past 10 years is shown in (Annexure-B).
The BRNS has not only helped several universities to establish excellent state-of-the-art labs/
facilities/centres enabling them to carry out high end research in the areas of nuclear science and
technology, but has also played a significant role in training human resources (both faculty and
students) in these areas.
In the past 2-3 years, there has been substantial increase in the efforts to enhance these
links further by proactive measures under BRNS by inviting senior faculty from local university /
colleges and NITs in the regional Theme Meetings for their larger participation in the DAE
programmes. A series of such meetings have already been conducted in the southern, Central and
northern region of the country which have yielded good return in terms of R&D projects,
registration of students for carrying out project work leading to post-graduate/doctoral degrees and
signing of several MoUs for tie-up with the DAE activities. Similar meetings are scheduled in other
parts of the country.
The DAE has also signed a MoU with Mumbai university for establishing a DAE-Mumbai
University-Centre of Excellence in Basic Sciences (CBS) in 2007 with a provision of total funding,
from BRNS, of Rs.52.00 crore during a period of five years. The Centre aims to offer integrated
MSc courses in physics, chemistry, life science, mathematics and computer sciences with major
emphasis on experimental science to the bright students in the country after (10+2) stage. While
the first batch in the Physics was started in 2007, batches in Chemistry and life sciences will be
commencing from Aug., 2008.
Department of Atomic Energy and University Institute of Chemical Technology, Mumbai
have entered into MoU for setting up the DAE-UICT Centre for Chemical Engineering Education
and Research in 2008 with an outlay of Rs.75.00 crore with the objectives such as: (1) to provide
Doctoral degrees to promising candidates with talent and aptitude for carrying out advanced
research and development activities in science and technology (2) to furnish a multidisciplinary,
flexible and innovative Ph.D research programme in Chemical Engineering with special emphasis
on, (a) Acquisition of proficiency in research, knowledge, data generation and analysis,
mathematical modeling, and management with sharpening skills in innovative experimental methods
and problem solving capabilities; (b) Creation of pool of young talented, dedicated and committed
individuals with passion and involvement in pursuing research and development as a career;
(c) inculcation of attitude, temper and outlook for developing social commitment as well as high
level of scientific ethics and integrity.
R&D units of Department of Atomic Energy such as Bhabha Atomic Research Centre,
Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology, Atomic
Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research etc. actively collaborate with local Universities
to motivate them to carry out research on topics of relevance to the Department of Atomic Energy.
Comments
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department towards funding of
scientific institutions and various universities in carrying out research and development in
the field of Atomic Energy. The Committee also feels that the Department should initiate
such programmes at under graduate level to inculcate interest among the young science
students.
Recommendation (Para 11.5)
The Committee is of the opinion that the contribution to this sector is quite significant for
a developing economy like ours. There is a need to augment the existing programmes as it has a

8
direct bearing on the societal needs. Activities related to fuel fabrication, spent fuel recycling,
recovery of fissile and fertile materials, recovery of Uranium from secondary sources, etc. would
help the country to be less dependant on the external sources for pursuing our nuclear programme.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the allocation of funds to this sector be augmented
adequately to meet the needs of activities being pursued by the Department.
Action Taken by the Government
The activities related to fuel fabrication, spent fuel recycling, recovery of fissile and fertile
materials, recovery of Uranium from secondary sources etc., have been augmented in Eleventh Plan
period. Towards this end Bhabha Atomic Research Centre has envisaged three major projects which
would help the country to be less dependant on the external sources for pursuing nuclear
programmes. (1) “Spent Fuel Recycle Project” with an outlay of Rs.970.00 crore; (2) “PUSHP AK”,
Tarapur, with an outlay of Rs.990.00 crore; (3) “Integrated Reprocessing and Waste Immobilisation
Plant”, Vizag, with an outlay of Rs.900.00 crore.
The main objective is to set up facilities to reprocess spent fuel discharged trom Pressurized
Heavy water Reactors (PHWR) and manage radioactive waste arising from the reprocessing
operations. As per the Indian nuclear power programme based on a closed fuel cycle, spent fuel
received from PHWRs is to be reprocessed to recover fissile and fertile materials and recycle the
same in the nuclear power plants.
Plutonium and Uranium will be separated from spent-fuel and purified to the specifications
for further handling and reuse. Plutonium is required as a fuel for the Fast Breeder Reactors
(FBRs) for producing power as well as for converting Thorium into fissile Uranium. The Plants
will reprocess spent fuels from PHWRs at the rated capacity of 300 tons/year and the separated
Plutonium will be made available for reuse in FBRs.
The PUSHPAK, at Tarapur will reprocess spent fuel from PHWRs of 220/500 MWe to
generate the input material for the second (Fast Breeder Reactors) of three stage power programme.
The liquid and waste generated during reprocessing operations will be treated and conditioned in WIP-
3B project to ensure safety to environment and general public on a long term basis.
The Integrated plant for fuel reprocessing and waste management with a capacity of 300
Te/yr of HM and a reprocessing plant with a capacity of 400 tonnes/year of heavy metals will be
set up for achieving recovery of fissile material, which in turn helps to meet the part demand of
fresh fuel for the nuclear reactors. It also includes treatment and conditioning of liquid, solid and
gaseous waste generated during the process operations. The interim storage of Vitrified Waste
Product canisters and solid alpha waste packages before disposal to underground geological
repository.
Similarly, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research is currently involved with technology
development of fuel fabrication and spent fuel reprocessing of Fast Reactors Fuels, besides
development of metanic fuels for future FBRs.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and reiterates that all such indigenous activities
which result in reducing dependence on external sources must be accorded top priority.
Recommendation (Para 12.2 and 12.3)
The Committee feels that both these technologies can prove to be boon for conservation
of nature and environment and for the society at large which is grappling with the problem of

9
disposal of sewage as well as solid waste generated in metropolitan cities and small towns. What
is required is the propagation and popularization of these technologies because their efficacy lies
in their use on a large scale. In view of the fact that environment protection is the need of the
hour as hazards of global warming and climate change are looming large, the urgency of such a
step becomes more prominent.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take effective steps for
marketing these technologies, if possible by creating a special cell for the purpose, within Radiation
Technology Development Section of Bhabha Atomic Research Centre. The cell should interact with
the municipalities/corporations/State Governments/Ministry of Urban Development, Ministry of
Environment and Forests, etc. to demonstrate the merits of the technology.
Action Taken by the Government
Sludge Hygienization Research Irradiator (SHRI), in V adodara has provided valuable
experience regarding the design, operational parameters and irradiated sludge has been shown to be
useful as a fertilizer in agricultural practice. Efforts are on to popularize this technology by
constant interactions with large municipal bodies and Ministry of Urban Development.
The NISARGRUNA technology developed by Bhabha Atomic Research Centre offers a
comprehensive decentralized solution for handling the biodegradable waste materials. The process
combines aerobic and anaerobic degradation of the biodegradable waste materials and converts the
waste into biogas and organic manure. Department of Atomic Energy is interacting with the
Municipalities/State Governments, Ministry of Urban Development, Ministry of Non-conventional
Energy Sources and various other end-users in the public and private sectors. About 50
entrepreneurs have bought the technology document.
It is expected that units of 1,2, 5 and 10 ton per day capacities would be ideal for rural
areas and urban local bodies in the country. Thirty such NISARGRUNA plants are already operating
in various States and many more are in the process of being installed.
The Technology Transfer and Coordination Division of BARC is strongly promoting these
two technologies in rural as well as urban areas as applicable. For this purpose continuous
interactions are on with municipal bodies, industries, private entrepreneurs, local self Government
departments of State Governments, and NGOs active in rural areas. This activity is a part of
specially conceptualized initiatives such as AKRUTI (Advance Knowledge and Rural Technology
Implementation), KRUTIK (Knowledge and Rural Technology Implementation Kendra) and FORCE
(Farmers Organization for Rural Creative Entrepreneurship). Radiation Technology Development
Section and Nuclear Agriculture and Biotechnology Division of BARC shall be providing the
scientific and technological inputs for this propagation of these technologies.
Comments
The Committee commends the efforts of the Department in developing technologies
for societal benefit besides its main activities in the field of atomic energy research and hopes
that such urban waste disposal technologies would be popularized throughout the country.
Recommendation (Para 13.4)
The Committee is of the view that the need for exploring and extracting uranium from
reserves available in the country assumes utmost importance in the context of attaining greater self-
reliance for the country’s nuclear programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that priority
be given towards this.

10
Action Taken by the Government
During the Tenth plan period, Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research
(AMD) had implemented seven plan projects with the approved Tenth plan outlay of Rs.107.00 crore.
The project “Augmentation of Uranium Resources” has successfully been implemented and
2433 tonnes (te) of additional uranium resources in Wahkyn (1681 te) and Lostoin (752 te),
Meghalaya was established. Heliborne Frequency Domain surveys were carried out over parts of
Gwalior basin, Madhya Pradesh and North Delhi Fold belt, Rajasthan and Haryana. Many potential
areas were identified in parts of Bhima, Gwalior, Vindhyan, Chhattisgarh and other Proterozoic and
Phanerrozoic basins of India for further investigations. The procurement of the heliborne Time
Domain Electromagnetic (TDEM) Geophysical survey system and exploratory mining at Gogi,
Karnataka are in progress. Technology Demonstration Pilot Plant (TDPP) has been commissioned
at Uranium Corporation of India Limited, Jaduguda and flow sheet for processing of Tummallapalle
ore using industrial oxygen as an oxidant has been developed under the project “Technology
Demonstration and Infrastructure Development”.
The projects (i) Evaluation and Augmentation of Rare Metal and Rare Earth and Beach Sand
Heavy Mineral Resources with the identification of many potential rare metal bearing pegmatities
and recovery of 19.185 te of columbite-tantalite concentrate and establishment of India’s biggest
beach sand heavy mineral deposit containing 120 million te of heavy mineral resources out of
which 60 million te is that of ilmenite at Brahmagiri, Puri district, Orissa. The envisaged target of
another project “Contract drilling for Uranium Exploration” has also been successfully achieved
with the establishment of 13,811 te of additional uranium resources at Rohil, Rajasthan: 2953 te;
Gogi, Karnataka: 3818 te; Koppunuru: 1240 te and Chitrial, Andhra Pradesh: 5800 te against the
target of 10,000 te. A total of 68,241 m of drilling was completed against a target of 1,36,000 m.
The target of contract drilling could not be achieved due to socio-economic/naxalite problem in
Andhra Pradesh, poor infrastructure facilities and logistics problem in Meghalaya and technical
problem (borehole deviation and drift) in Rajasthan. The project is being continued in Eleventh plan
to achieve the physical targets.
The Eleventh Plan programme of AMD envisages several projects aiming to identify 75,000
tonnes of uranium resources. During Eleventh plan, AMD would be implementing 18 plan projects
with the Eleventh plan outlay of Rs. 549.19 Crore. The main emphasis is being given to extensive
survey and exploration for locating high grade large tonnage unconformity related, hematite breccia
complex, quartz pebble conglomerate (QPC), sandstone and calcrete types of uranium deposits.
High tech technique like heliborne Time Domain Electromagnetic (TDEM) survey is being adopted,
for locating deep seated concealed unconformity related deposits in the Proterozoic Basins of India.
This technique is useful in locating deep seated electromagnetic conductor which is suitable
location for high grade large tonnage unconformity related uranium deposits as in Canada and
Australia and many Proterozoic Basins in India have similar geological setup.
The detailed project proposals have since been formulated accordingly and targets for
various activities have been set up, which are about 4 to 5 times higher as compared to Tenth Plan
programme. In order to achieve the desired objectives, thrust areas like Proterozoic Basins are
selected to identify concealed large tonnage; high grade unconformity related uranium deposits apart
from other areas like Mahadek Basin for sandstone type, North Delhi Fold Belt for vein/albitite type.
The R&D sector projects includes a comprehensive set of uranium exploration activities
including airborne geophysical survey (4.0 lakh line km), ground geological and radiometric (30,000
sq. km), geochemical (8,000 sq. km) and geophysical surveys (as per requirement) and
departmental reconnoitory and stratigraphic drilling (3.0 lakh m) with the expected outcomes of
discoveries of promising uranium occurrences and evaluation and prioritization of potential target

11
areas for detailed subsurface exploration. The I&M Sector project includes detailed subsurface
exploration through contracts for evaluation drilling of 4.3 lakh m which is expected to have a
outcome of augmenting the uranium resources of the country by 75,000 tonnes.
All the activities proposed, especially with regard to uranium exploration are interdependent
and synergistically welded together so as to realize the overall Eleventh plan objectives of AMD,
the most important of which is identification of 75,000 tonnes of uranium deposits.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that sustained efforts would be made
towards exploration/mining of uranium deposits within the country, to reduce dependence on
external sources.
Recommendation (Para 14.3)
The Committee is of the opinion that awareness regarding health hazards should be created
in the affected population before the mining activity starts and therefore recommends that mass
awareness campaigns should be conducted at regular intervals for the population residing near the
mining area. The issue of displacement of the local population and sufficient compensation for the
displaced, should also be dealt with sympathetically to avoid public discontentment at a later stage.
Action Taken by the Government
An intensive Public Awareness Programme is already being carried out by the Department
of Atomic Energy (through its Public Awareness Division) in collaboration with Uranium
Corporation of India Limited and Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research in the
areas where uranium mining is proposed. These activities are being given further impetus. Specially
in Meghalaya, a mass contact programme in Khasi language is being launched which will consist
of distribution of pamphlets, providing scientific information through games made available on CDs,
seminars in Khasi language, quiz, essay and elocution competitions. Since last more than one year,
a primary Health Centre is being run by the Uranium Corporation of India Limited at Wahkaji in
the West Khasi Hills where we propose to set up uranium mine and processing plant. An integrated
rural development programme for the six villages in the immediate neighbourhood of Jaduguda,
Jharkhand is being carried out by Uranium Corporation of India Limited and the Department. The
Department ensures that the recommendations of the Committee is implemented in letter and spirit.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and reiterates that a greater sensitivity towards the
issue of displacement of local population due to mining activities be adopted by the
Department.
Recommendation (Para 15.6)
The Committee is of the opinion that Nuclear Energy is a very clean source of energy
devoid of any environmental pollution that the production of Thermal or Hydel energy causes.
Therefore, conscious efforts should be made to produce the maximum amount of energy from
Nuclear sources.
Action Taken by the Government
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) is involved in the first stage

12
programme of setting up a total Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR) capacity of 10,000
MWe. Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited has been making all efforts towards this end
and has achieved several milestones in this endeavor. At present, a PHWR capacity of 3800 MWe
is in operation and 660 MWe under construction. The operation of nuclear power plants at high
capacity factors of about 90% and construction of nuclear power projects in about five years have
been achieved. The operational and safety performance of NPCIL’s plants have been excellent.
Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited’s current plans include setting up of eight
indigenous PHWRs of 700 MWe each. The design of indigenous 700 MWe PHWRs has been
completed. Pre-project activities for four of the reactors, KAPP 3&4 and RAPP 7&8 are nearing
competion and the projects are poised for launch. Commencement of work on these projects is
linked to establishment of fuel linkages.
The second stage of Indian nuclear power programme consists of Fast Breeder Reactors
(FBRs). FBR programme can sustain a generation capacity of about 42231 GWe – year and expected
to provide energy security to our country in the long run. Bhartiya Nabhikiya Vidhyut Nigam Limited
is constructing 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam. PFBR is the
forerunner of the second stage of India’s nuclear power programme and represents the
commencement of the commercial phase of the second stage. By constructing and operating the 500
MWe PFBR, India will be demonstrating techno-commercial viability of the second stage nuclear
power programme. It is planned to construct four more 500 MWe FBRs by year 2020. Indira Gandhi
Centre for Atomic Research will also initiate R&D design activities for 1000 MWe FBRs.
Comments
The Committee is of the opinion that the department should be able to achieve the
targets/schedules set, as regards the nuclear power projects and maximize nuclear power
generation in the near future.
Recommendation (Para 16.3)
The Committee is of the opinion that to gain self-sufficiency in the country’s requirement
of nuclear fuel, the Department has to make concerted efforts towards development of technology
which uses Thorium as Nuclear fuel instead of Uranium, keeping in view the vast reserves of
Thorium. The use of Uranium makes the country dependent on other countries and also results in
outgo of foreign exchange.
Action Taken by the Government
The three stages of the Indian Nuclear Power Programme are to be taken up sequentially.
The first stage is based on uranium and is already in commercial domain. The spent fuel from the
first stage reactors is reprocessed to recover plutonium and depleted uranium. The recovered
plutonium – depleted uranium is the fuel for the Fast Breeder Reactors for the second stage. Fast
Breeder Reactors produce more fissile material than they consume and thereby enable growth in
nuclear reactor installed capacity based on fast reactors. Physics characteristics of thorium can
enable sustaining a given installed capacity, but not its growth. Early deployment of thorium would
slow down growth of installed nuclear capacity based on fast reactors and is not desirable. While
it is proposed to set up an Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) which would get 2/3rd of its
power from thorium, to acquire industrial scale experience in thorium, large scale introduction of
thorium has to wait till a large enough fast reactor installed capacity has been set up.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply of the Department.

13
Recommendation (Para 17.2)
The Committee expresses its serious concern at the fact that the present remuneration being
paid to the scientists is not attractive enough to attract the best of scientific talent available in the
country. Further, to make matters worse, there is a high level of attrition of scientists from the
department, who move towards the private sector for better salaries and promotion prospects. The
Committee recommends that the case for grant of special allowance over and above the normal
salaries may be taken up emphatically with the Government, keeping in view the special
requirements of the department, and the scientific community at large, specially in view of the
tremendous contributions of the scientists in the field of Atomic Energy.
Action taken by the Government
The concerns expressed by the Committee have already been taken up at appropriate levels
in the Government.
Comments
The Committee strongly reiterates its recommendation and urges that the issue of
proper remuneration for the scientist be given top priority and taken up forcefully with the
Government.
Recommendation (Para 18.5)
The Committee is of the opinion that the agreement with the United States of America has
to be looked at from the larger perspective of national security as well as national interest. While
acknowledging the increasing energy requirements of the country, the thrust must be on the
indigenous ‘Three-stage Programme’ on which our scientists are working with great confidence
and optimism. The Indo-United States Nuclear Agreement has caused serious concerns with regard
to our foreign policy and security related issues on which our Parliament had to debate several
times. The sense of the Parliament needs to be taken into consideration.
Action Taken By The Government
Indigenous three stage programme is being pursued on priority. Autonomous pursuit of our
domestic nuclear programme as well as our foreign policy would remain independent of any
international civil nuclear cooperation which would be an additionality to strengthen our energy
security.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the domestic nuclear programme will
not be compromised in pursuit of international civil nuclear co-operation.

ANNEXURE - A
ADDITIONAL INFORMATION ON FOOD IRRADIATION
No other method of food processing has been subjected to such a thorough assessment of
safety as the radiation processing. The various aspects of wholesomeness and safety of radiation-
processed foods have been studied in great detail. These include:
• Possibility of induced radioactivity
• Microbiological safety
• Safety of chemical changes
• Nutritional adequacy
• Animal feeding
• Human trials
At the energies of the gamma rays from cobalt-60 (1.3 MeV) and those recommended for
X-rays (7.5 MeV) and accelerated electrons (10 MeV), no induced radioactivity has been observed
in food. The microbiological aspects of radiation-processed foods have been studied in detail. None
of these studies have indicated that foods preserved by radiation pose any special problems in
relation to micro flora. It has been found that unique radiolytic products are not formed and most
of the free radicals in the system disappear depending on the nature of the commodity either
immediately after irradiation or during its post-irradiation storage and processing. Though the
composition of food remains largely unchanged, some minor losses in vitamins, comparable to
those from any other food processing method, may be encountered. Short-term or long-term animal
feeding studies have not shown any adverse effect.
International Approval
In 1980, a joint FAO/IAEA/WHO Expert Committee on Food Irradiation (JECFI) reviewed
the extensive data on wholesomeness of irradiated foods collected up to that time and concluded
that irradiation of any commodity up to an over all dose of 10 kGy presents no toxicological
hazards and introduces no special nutritional or microbiological problems. An Expert Group
constituted by WHO in 1994 once again reviewed the wholesomeness data available till then and
validated the earlier conclusion of JECFI (WHO, 1994). In 1997 another Expert Group constituted
by WHO af firmed the safety of food irradiated to doses above 10 kGy. In 2003 Codex Alimentarius
Commission revised its Codex General Standard for Irradiated Foods to include application of doses
higher than 10 kGy. The Agreements on Sanitary and Phytosnitary (SPS) Practices and Technical
Barriers to Trade (TBT) under the World Trade Organization (WTO) have provided for adoption
of irradiation as an SPS measure in international trade under the principle of equivalence. Thus,
irradiation can be applied to overcome quarantine barriers, and to hygienize products for
international trade. These agreements are administered under the standards, guidelines, and
recommendations of the international organizations such as Codex Alimentarius Commission,
International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC), and The International Office of Epizootics. In
2003 IPPC included irradiation as a plant quarantine measure. This was subsequently followed by
the final rule irradiation phytosanitary treatment of imported fruits and vegetables under USDA-
17

18
APHIS. Australia and New Zealand have also amended their food standard, FSANZ, allowing import
of radiation treated tropical fruits and vegetables. USFDA has further gone ahead with providing
key approvals that would benefit radiation-processing industry. These include increase in the energy
levels permitted for X-ray applications to 7.5 MeV and the approval for use of radiation for
microbial decontamination of molluscan shellfish at a dose of 5.5 kGy.
Today, some 40 countries worldwide including India have approved the use of food
irradiation for over 100 food items and about 30 of them are applying the technology on a limited
commercial scale.
Approval of radiation processing of food in India
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre has been engaged in R&D work on the technology of
radiation processing of foods for the past more than 50 years. The safety and wholesomeness of
the technology was endorsed in 1981 by world bodies like World Health Organization, Food &
Agricultural Organization, and International Atomic Energy Agency, and by the Codex Alimentarius
Commission that sets global standards for food, in 1983. Government of India constituted a
National Monitoring Agency in 1987, to oversee commercial application of food irradiation in India.
Subsequently, in 1991, Atomic Energy (Control of Irradiation of Food) Rules (amended in 1996)
were framed and in 1994, amendment of PFA Act rules was carried out to approve radiation
processing of onion, potato and spices. The PFA Act rules were further amended in 1998 and 2001
to approve additional items of food. Ministry of Health has been approached for approval of the
food and agricultural commodities on wider generic/class-wise basis for radiation processing, so
that the radiation processing plants could be operated around the year for better economic gains.
The draft notification for generic approval on class basis was published in May, 2007.
The Department of Atomic Energy has the necessary expertise and know-how for setting
up radiation processing plants. It has set up two technology demonstration units, one commissioned
in 2000 for high dose irradiation at Vashi, Navi Mumbai, primarily for hygienization of spices, and
another in 2002, a low dose irradiation facility, KRUSHAK at Lasalgaon, near Nashik, for sprout
control during storage in potato and onion and insect disinfestation of agricultural commodities.
In 2004 as a result of persistent efforts of FTD, the Ministry of Agriculture and Co-
operation, Government of India, amended the plant quarantine regulations, Plant Quarantine
(Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003, to include irradiation as a phytosanitary treatment.
In 2006, the United States Department of Agriculture and Department of Agriculture and Co-
operation, Government of India, signed a Framework Equivalency Work-plan, to use irradiation as
phytosanitary measure for the export of mango to the US, and the USDA-APHIS final rule
‘Importation of Mangoes From India’ was published on March 12, 2007. More than 157 tons of
mangoes of different varieties were processed at KRUSHAK and exported to US after a gap of 18
years. This year the exports to US are likely to be higher. A landmark breakthrough was thus
achieved in demonstrating commercial feasibility of radiation technology in overcoming quarantine
barrier to international trade and obtaining market access, that would ultimately bring economic
benefits to mango farmers of the country.
Department of AYUSH, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, have
also given permission for use of radiation for microbial decontamination of medicinal herbs and
formulations.

the recommendations contained in the One Hundred and Eighty-ninth Report of the Department-
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Space on
the recommendations contained in the One Hundred Eighty-ninth Report of the Department-Related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on the
Demands for Grants (2008-2009) of the Department of Space, which was presented to both the
Houses of Parliament on 29th April, 2008. The One Hundred Eighty-ninth Report of the Committee
contained fifteen recommendations. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of the Committee
were received from the Department on 29th September, 2008.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee
on the Action Taken by the Department of Space are set out in the succeeding paragraphs:—
ELEVENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN (2007-12) OUTLAYS AND PROPOSALS
1. Recommendation (Para - 4.3)
The Committee hopes that the major thrust of the Indian Space Programme during the
Eleventh Five Year Plan 2007-12 would not only be towards continuing and reinforcing the space
technologies already developed but also to venture into newer and greater space challenges by
further enhancing our capabilities in the advanced areas of space technology. Efforts should also
be made towards exploring the commercial prospects in the field of space science specially in the
area of Launch Vehicle Development, so that additional funds could be generated. The Committee
also hopes that the Department would achieve the goals set for itself during the 11th plan period
in the field of space applications for communication, broadcasting, remote sensing, launch vehicle
technology etc. which will ultimately benefit the society at large.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. The Eleventh Five Year Plan, besides strengthening the already established operational
space capabilities, also envisage development of advanced communication technologies, Microwave
Remote Sensing, advanced propulsion systems, Human Space Flight and planetary exploration
which are intended to enhance India’s space technology capabilities in advanced areas Expansion
of Space Commerce in the areas of launch services, Transponder capacity leasing Remote Sensing
Data Services, spacecraft hardware and other value added services are also planned. The
Department will thrive to achieve the targets set for Eleventh Five Year Plan.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and appreciates the efforts undertaken by the
Department to enhance Indian Space technology capabilities. It also hopes that the
Department would make every effort to achieve the targets set for the Eleventh Five Year
Plan as per schedule.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2. Recommendation (Para - 5.3)
The Committee notes that the Plan allocation (2008-09), which was sought by the
Department has seen a drastic reduction of Rs.862.18 crores and the same has been effected at

2
the cost of some of the new but important schemes. A similar cut had to be made at the RE stage
in 2007-08 due to resource constraints. The Committee expresses its deep anguish over the fact
that even scientific departments are not spared of the routine reduction on the ground of resource
constraint and feels that this is not a healthy trend. This also shows the degree of seriousness and
significance that Government attaches to the scientific bodies and institutions which are being put
at par with other Ministries/Departments of the Government of India. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the formula of routine cut should not be applied to scientific departments.
3. Recommendation (Para - 5.4)
The Committee also expresses its concern over the cuts in Plan allocations to the
Department and recommends that the Planning Commission should thoroughly examine the
proposals, before imposing cuts, as the Indian Space Programme is vital to meet the developmental
needs of the country in a self reliant manner.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. The recommendations of the Committee will be conveyed to the Planning
Commission during Performance review Meeting.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and urges the Department to ensure that due
cognizance of the recommendations made by the Committee in this regard is taken at R.E.
stage for releasing required budgetary support.
MONITORING MECHANISMS FOR ONGOING SCHEMES
4. Recommendation (Para - 6.4)
The Committee recommends the strengthening of the existing mechanism developed by the
Department to monitor the progress of the ongoing schemes before finalizing proposals for
budgetary support, so that a clear picture regarding fund requirements can be presented to the
Planning Commission and the possibility of shortage or surrender of funds at a later stage could
be avoided.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted for compliance.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and reiterates that the Department must strengthen
its monitoring mechanism and should monitor its ongoing programmes/projects for its
implementation in a time bound manner.
VILLAGE RESOURCE CENTRES
5. Recommendation (Para - 7.4)
The Committee is of the opinion that VRC is a tool which can be used for strengthening
and uniting the country in addition to its main objectives of providing information regarding various
rural services. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made to establish

3
VRCs in the far-flung, inaccessible, remote border areas of the country, to help confidence-building
among the population and remove the feeling of alienation from the country.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. As on date 417 Village Resource Centres (VRCs) are set up in different States and
Union Territories of the country, in association with selected partner agencies viz., NGOs, Trusts,
Academic institutions and Government. These include 13 VRCs in Assam, 1 in Meghalaya, 8 in
Nagaland, 17 in Sikkim and 4 in Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Further expansion of VRCs is in
progress.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that sustained efforts would continue to
be made by the Department to set up more Village Resource Centres in different States and
Union Territories.
6. Recommendation (Para - 7.5)
The Committee is of the opinion that to make VRC programme a success, there should be
proper co-ordination among all the agencies connected with the programme. In this direction the
Committee recommends that local bodies across the country, district offices and other agencies
involved in planning of the VRC programmes at the rural areas should be inter-connected resulting
into dissemination of vital information.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. The VRCs set up by Department of Space are primarily managed and operated by
NGOs, Trusts, V oluntary Agencies and Government Agencies who organize necessary linkages
among various players including local bodies connected with the programme and services.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
7. Recommendation (Para - 7.6)
The Committee also recommends that special focus should be given to issues related to
self-employment and forming self-help groups through them. The Committee further recommends
that the information should be disseminated in local language so that the local youths and people
could attach themselves fully with the programme.
Action Taken by the Government
The variety of activities carried out by the VRCs encompass management of land and water
resources; agriculture development; supplementary education, training and skill development for
livelihood support; healthcare and social empowerment, including forming self-help groups. The
interactive programmes carried out by VRCs and dissemination of information by them are
necessarily in local languages.
Comments
The Committee while taking note of the reply is of the view that while establishing
Village Resource Centres, more representation should be given to the remote areas.

4
DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPPORT SYSTEM
8. Recommendation (Para - 8.3)
The Committee is aware that a lot of economic devastation and human loss is caused
regularly by the floods, cyclones, storms, etc., across the country. In this direction the Committee
recommends that there should be proper co-ordination among the various agencies involved in the
DMS programme so that there is quick dissemination of information to the District Headquarters
after the data is obtained from the satellites, in order that human and material losses can be
minimized.
Action Taken by the Government
The Disaster Management Support (DMS) Programme of the Department is conceived and
developed in close coordination with the concerned Central and State Ministries/Departments and
District Authorities, such as, Ministry of Home Affairs; National Disaster Management Authority;
National Institute of Disaster Management; Department of Agriculture and Cooperation; India
Meteorological Department; Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services of Ministry of
Earth Sciences; Central Water Commission; and District Authorities. All the disaster management
support related data and information generated using satellite and aerial survey data by the
Department are disseminated to these agencies on near real-time basis, through an exclusive
Decision Support Centre set up for the purpose at NRSC, Hyderabad.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
TELEMEDICINE
9. Recommendation (Para - 9.3)
The Committee is of the opinion that investment in a highly capital intensive area like Public
Health may not be always possible, particularly in the backward areas of the country. Telemedicine
provides an excellent alternative. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the telemedicine
network should be expanded further to include the disease-prone areas which have been left out
so far, specially in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The Department should make concerted efforts
towards solving the procedural, problem through consistent persuasion and liaisoning with the State
administration.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. Expansion of Tele-medicine program is progressing well and Telemedicine facilities
have been established in 310 hospitals as on August, 2008. Telemedicine facilities in North East
(28) and Orissa (9) cover the disease-prone areas also. Discussions have been initiated with the
State Governments of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar for introduction of Telemedicine systems.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and would like the Department to continue its efforts
towards establishing telemedicine network in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar as both these States
are disease prone and require better and suitable healthcare facilities. The Committee would
also like to be informed about the progress of discussion in the matter.

5
CHANDRAYAAN-I
10. Recommendation (Para - l0.4)
The Committee hopes that the Chandrayaan-I mission progress as per schedule and the
spacecraft would be ready for launch in the second quarter of 2008. The Committee is of the
opinion that the Chandrayaan-I mission would upgrade India’s space technological capabilities and
in future help in launching manned missions to moon.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. The integration and checkout activities of Chandrayaan-I spacecraft have been
completed. The spacecraft is undergoing environmental testing and then onwards, it will be
transported to launch site at Sriharikota for launch onboard PSLV-C11. The launch campaign
activities for PSLV-C11 is also in advanced stages.
Comments
The Committee expresses its satisfaction that Chandrayaan-I mission is progressing
as per schedule and hopes that it would improve Indian space technological abilities once
it has been launched successfully.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
11. Recommendation (Para - 11.3)
The Committee expresses its serious concern at the fact that the present remuneration being
paid to the scientists are not attractive enough to attract the best of scientific talent available in
the country. Further, to make matters worse, there is a high level of attrition of scientists from
the Department, who move towards the private sector for better salaries and promotion prospects.
The Committee recommends that the case for grant of special allowance over and above the normal
salaries may be taken up emphatically with the Government, keeping in view the special
requirements of the Department, and the scientific community at large, specially in view of the
tremendous contributions of the scientists in the field of Space. The Committee also recommends
that in order to retain the scientists in the Department enhanced increment at the rate of 25 to 30%
may also be seriously considered for the scientists who perform and deliver.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. The matter has been referred to the Government.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
12. Recommendation (Para - 11.4)
The Committee is of the opinion that to contain the mass exodus of scientists from our
premier institutions, formulation of a wage policy has become imperative, keeping in view the huge
difference that exists between the Public and Private sectors. The Committee recommends that
efforts must be made to work out an understanding on wages on the lines of the one already
existing in the advanced countries.
Action Taken by the Government
Extract sent to Ministry of Labour.

6
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
13. Recommendation (Para - 11.8)
The Committee is of the opinion that the Department has delayed the creation of a
specialised manpower base for its growing space programme as the only specialised Institute
catering specifically for space technology has been set up just a year ago, though the Department
was set up in the year 1972. However, though delayed, it is a welcome step. The Committee feels
that the Department should be pro-active in initiating such projects.
14. Recommendation (Para - 11.9)
The Committee is also of the opinion that the possibility of introduction of Space Science
as a subject at the graduate/higher secondary level may be explored to generate the interest of the
younger generation in this field and more such institutes should be set up by the Department across
the country to train scientists/engineers, to create a manpower base of dedicated scientists.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. At the higher secondary level, the subject related to Astronomy , Astrophysics and
Space Science have already been introduced in 10th, 11th and 12th standards in CBSE. Some of
the Universities are also running MSc. Programme with specialization in Atmospheric and Space
Science. Further, as a part of space science promotion, the National Advisory Committee on Space
Science (ADCOS) has taken steps to strengthen space science education in ten selected universities
as Phase-l across the country by initiating space science research activities, offering Fellowships
to MSc. and M. Tech. programs in Atmosphere and Space Sciences and setting up experimental
facilities in space science research such as Automatic Weather Stations, Microwave radiometer,
GPS systems, spectral radiometers etc.
Comments
The Committee expresses its satisfaction on the initiatives taken by the Department
to strengthen space science education under the supervision of the National Advisory
Committee on Space Science (ADCOS). The Committee desires that Department should
further enhance its potential in the field of space science education and expand its activities
in various other universities apart from selected ones.

 ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS ON THE NATIONAL ENVIRONMENT TRIBUNAL BILL, 
1992 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Scien ce and Technology, Envir onment and Forests to
which the Bill to provide for strict liability for damages arising out of a ny accident occurring while
handling any hazardous substance and for the establ ishment of a National Environment Tribunal fo r
effective and expeditious disposal of cases arising from such accident , with a view to giving relief an d
compensation for damages to persons, property a nd .the environment and for matters connected
therewith or incidental thereto, wa s referred, having been authorised to submit the Repor t on its behalf,
present its Report, with the Bill, as amended by the Committee, annexed thereto. 
2.         The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha  on the 18th August, 1992. The Bill was referred to the
Committee by the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consulta tion with the Speaker, Lok Sabha for examination
and report.** 
3.         The Committee held 5 meetings in all. 
4.         In the first meeting held on the 17t h August, 1993, the Committee he ard the representatives o f
the Ministry of Environment and Forests on the provisions of the Bill. 
5.         In its second meeting held on the 18th August, 1993, the Committe e sough~ clarifications on
certain provisions of the Bill from the Secretary, Ministry of Environment and Forests and the Secretary,
Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs. 
6.         In its meeting held on the 25th A ugust, 1993 general discussion took place on the amendments
suggested by Members. 
7.         The Committee held clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill on the basis of amendments 
suggested by Members at its meeting held on the 26th August, 1993. 
8.         The Committee considered and adopted  the report at its meeting held on the 13th September,
1993. 
9.         The observations of the Committee with regard to the principal chan ges proposed in the Bill are
detailed in the succeeding paragraphs. 
10.       Clause 4. -- This clause confers power on  the Central Government to  exempt from the operation 
of the Act, the Central Government , any State Government, any corporation owned or controlled by the
Central Government or a State Government or any local author ity. While handli ng any hazardous
substance a mishap or an accident can take place in  an organisation or corpor ation owned or controlled
by the Central Government  or any State Government or lo cal authority. In order to provide
compensation in such cases, the Committee strongl y feels that there should be no exemption. The
Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that the pr ovisions relating to exempt ion from liability may be
dropped from the Bill. Accordingly, Clause 4 of the Bill has been deleted. 
11.       Clause 5. -- In sub-clau se (1) it has been provided as to who can make applic ation for claim fo r
compensation. The Committee is of  the opinion that the National Environment Tribunal may also be
empowered to take up cases of claim for compensation sue motu. The Committee has, therefore, added a 
new sub-clause (2) after sub-clause  (1) in Clause 5. Existing sub-clau ses (2), (3), .(4) & (5) have 
accordingly been renumbered as (3), (4), (5) and (6).

the Bill should be substituted by the words 'Chairpe rson' and 'Vice-Chairper son'. Accordingly, these 
changes have been incorporated in the Bill.

13.       All other modifications not enumerated in the foregoing paragraphs are either of consequential or
of drafting nature. 
14.       The Committee  recommends that the Bill as amended, be passed. 
General Recommendation 
15.       The Committee was informed that the decisions which were taken at the United Nations
Conference on Environment and De velopment held at Rio de' Jane rio in 1992, in which India also
participated, called upon the participat ing countries to devel op national laws rela ting to liability and
compensation for the victims of pol lution and other environmental dama ges. Pursuant to  this decision,
arrived at the United Nations Conference on E nvironment and Development, the Ministry o f
Environment & Forests informed th e Committee that the Government of  India has brought forward the
National Environment Tribunal Bill. The Committee, however observed that though the ti tle of the Bill
conveys an impression that the Bill is very comp rehensive and covers within its ambit all cases o f
liability and compensation arising due to environmental damage or pol lution whatever be its cause, its
scope is actually restricted to cases concerni ng the protection of envi ronment and payment o f
compensation for damage to persons; property a nd the environment whil e handling the hazardous
substances. The representati ve of the ministry clarified that the Na tional Tribunal Bill  is an altogethe r
new piece of legislation and: its scope has been presently restricted to the environmental damage caused
due to handling of hazardous substances  but the scope of the Bill can be  enlarged later on in the light o f
the experience gained. 
The Committee strongly feels that the Government may seriously think of enlarging the scope of the
Bill by including under the ambit of the Bill, cases of compensation for damages which are caused even
by such substances as have not been identified as hazardous by the Ministry of Environment and Forests
because environmental pollution can be caused by s ubstances which may not be  hazardous as per the
specifications of the Ministry but the scale of damage which they can cause may be quite extensive.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf present this Twentieth Report of the
 Committee, This Report deals with three specific areas of activity of the Department of Ocean Development, namely--0)
 Marine Satellite Information Service (MARSIS); (ii) Pollution Monitoring Programme-Coastal Ocean Monitoring and
 Prediction System (COM-PAS) and (iii) National Programme for Identification of Marine Bioactive Substances for use as
 Drugs; on the basis of its Annual Report (1993-94).
 
2. The committee held in all three meetings 6n January 23, 24 and April 27, 1995 to consider the aforementioned
 programmes of the Department. In the meeting held on January 23, 1995 the Secretary of the Department made a presentation
 about the overall activities of the Department, highlighting in particular the thrust being imparted to its programmes in the
 above three areas. On January 24, 1995 the committee further discussed these subjects and the Secretary and other officials of
 the Department of Ocean Development gave clarifications on some of the points raised by the Members.
 
3. The committee thanks the officials of the Department of Ocean Development for giving it-necessary information and
 placing before it relevant papers/background note which facilitated examination of its Annual Report for the year 1993-94.
 
4. The Committee considered and adopted this report at its meeting held on the 27th April, 19.95.
 
New Delhi;
April 27, 1995
SYED SIBTEY RAZI
Chairman,
Committee on Science and
Technology, Environment and Forests
 
 
REPORT
 
The oceans constitute a repository of living and non-living resources, which are

 particularly of value to a nation like India which has a long coastline and therefore access to these, in the Indian Ocean as a
 whole, and more specifically the Bay of Bengal and the  Arabian Sea. A substantial segment of our population depends upon
 these for their    livelihood. An increasing faction of our population, through a process f migration will move:        to the coastal
 areas, and to urban centres located in these which are likely to become mega cities, sucha vast coastline, however, is of little use
 if he country is not ableto optimallyexploit this sea wealth. The development of oceans related programmes and a cogent
 strategy for tapping the marine resource potential has therefore, to be a key element of   country's planning. Apart from the
 direct living and non-living resources, the Ocean has a   profound impact on natural life. Climate and weather, the monsoons,
 disasters such as           cyclones and tidal waves, marine transportation, direct water resources in coastal areas and
 much more, relate directly to the ocean. To understand the ocean around us and to ensure         their health is a matter of
 paramount importance. The Ocean Policy of the Government enunciated way back in 1982 lays down some well defined
 parameters of the thrust which  ocean related activities would have to take over a span of time. This effort has of necessity to be
 a multi-disciplinary and multi-agency effort, since a number of Ministries/agencies of Government are concerned and have to
 be involved; but Department of Ocean Development has been given a nodal role to co-ordinate these activities and has to
 perform this as its highest priority. The mandate of the Department includes:--
                 (i)    Promotion of Research and Development in the marine: sector.
                 (ii)    Surveys to locate and map the resources potential, living and non-living, in the Exclusive, Economic Zone.
                 (iii) Development, conservation and protection of coastal ocean.
(iv)  Marine environment on high seas.         
(v)
     Development of skills and manpower.
(vi)   Exploration and development of seabed mining.
(vii)
    Promotion and co-ordination of Antarctic Research.
(viii)   Collaboration with other agencies/countries.
(ix)  Legal regime for the oceans and Antarctica.
(x)  Matters relating to oceans not specifically allotted to any other    
       Department.
 
2. The Department of Ocean Development has, in furtherance of its mandated objectives, been carrying out various
 programmes/projectThe Committee decided to examine the following three programmes which are economically and socially
 relevant, on the basis of the Annual Report (1993-94) of the Department.
(i) Marine Satellite Information Service (MARSIS)
(ii)  Pollution Monitoring Programme Coastal Ocean Monitoring & Prediction System (COMAPS)
                  (iii) Identification of Marine Bio-active Substances for use as Drugs.
The Committee heard the "Secretary and other officials of the Department on programmes of the Department in general with
 specific focus on various aspects of the implementation of the above three Programmes.
               
I. Marine Satellite Information Service (MARSIS)
 
3. This is a National Programme of the Department of Ocean 13evelopment, in which satellite remote sensing techniques are
 employed, to generate user--friendly oceans data products, and to disseminate them on an operational basis. A three-year Phase-
I of MARSIS was launched by the Department in 1990. The Programme is structured around four major projects viz.
(i) Ocean related remote sensing application,
            (ii) Sea truth collection,
            (iii) MARSIS-Centres, and
            (iv) Ocean Modelling Studies.
 
4. The National Remote Sensing Agency Hyderabad is the nodel agency to carry this programme forward, with participation
 by Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad, National Institute of Oceanography, Goa, Centre for Mathematical Modelling and
 Computer Simulation-NAL, Bangalore and other associated organisation. In Phase-I of the programme (1990--93) the
 following data products were made operationally available:--
 
a. Sea Surface Temperature (SST) maps.
b. Potential Fishing Zone (PFZ) maps.
   c. Coral Reef maps in respect of Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Manner, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar
 group of Islands.
d. Shoreline changes maps for Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
e. Wetland maps for Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
 
SST is an important parameter that has wide ranging significance in the field of climatology, weather forecast, fisheries,
 predictions of cyclones, etc. PFZ advisory is an SST by-product which was made operational in 1991. SST Maps and PFZ
 advisory maps are the data products being disseminated to the user agencies through a variety of modes such as facsimiles,
 radio bulletins and local newspapers on a. regular basis, and are stated to have been well received by them. The PFZ maps are

 reported Catch Per Unit Effort (CPUE) being significantly higher than those obtained from non-PFZ areas. The Department
 proposes to continue dissemination of PFZ mapsto coastal fishermen till the end of the 8th Plan, after further refinement of data

 are dealt with later in this Report.

II. Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS)
 
19. The Department of Ocean Development has been entrusted with the responsibility of protecting the marine environment
 of the country, and for preservation of the health of the sea waters, which is vital not only for the abundant living resources but
 also for all activities in the Coastal Zone. In furtherance of this objective, the Department has been carrying out scientific
 monitoring of marine pollution, and conducting studies on the level a~ source of pollutants in the coastal and offshore areas of
 the country, under a programme of Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System (COMAPS) since 1.990. Under this
 programme, health of Indian marine environment is constantly assessed to indicate areas that need immediate and long term
 remedial action. 13 DOD centres/units have been assigned specific areas of coastal waters for monitoring, as per the details
 given in Annexure-I. A Centre for Marine Analytical Standards has been set up at Regional Research Laboratory, Trivandrum
 to conduct inter calibration exercises, and to analyses the quality of data generated under the programme.

III. Identification of marine bio-active substances for use as drugs--National Project on Development of Potential Drllgs from
 the Ocean
 
28. Over recent years the study of marine organisms has evoked considerable interest as an area of research to find bioactive
 substances for use as drugs; and quite a few countries have focused their biomedical research in this area. A large number of
 organisms have been Screened for anti-viral, anti-cancer, anti-hehninthic, anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor activities; one
 success hasbeen that of prostaglandins from organisms in the Caribbean Sea which has been transformed into a drug for the
 medical termination of pregnancy. Marine fauna and flora still continues to be a relatively unexplored field for new drug leads.
 Research efforts of the countries so far involved in the exercise of looking for drugs from marine organisms, however, have
 centered around organisms collected from different oceanic regions in the world, but the fauna and flora from the Indian coast
 has not attracted much attention. The Department of Ocean Development, therefore, launched a national programme of
 systematic evaluation of marine organisms of the Indian Coast and nearby islands in the year 1990-91 to isolate bioactive
 substances for use as potential drugs (This is a programme that was mooted and intensively discussed over a decade and a half
 ago for Indo-US collaboration). The present project involves 10 R & D centres including 2 universities, 3 medical colleges and
 5 CSIR laboratories spread all over the country, with the Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow being the apex institution
 for co-ordination. Samples of marine organisms are collected by each of the participating institutions from specified zones, and
 a vouche specimen is maintained at the national repository at NIO, Goa. so far 936 samples have been screened-402 in Phase-1
 and 534 in Phase-II-out of which, as per the information given to the Committee, 121 have shown different types of promising
 biological activities ranging from anti-viral, anti-bacterial and anti-implantation; etc. In addition to the extracts and fractions,
 about 40 pure compounds isolated from different organisms have also been screened for specific biological activities including
 anti-viral, HbsAg binding, hypotensive and other pharmacological activities.   The potential bioactive organism identified for
 follow up are given in Annexure-IV and the new compounds isolated under the programme are shown in Annexure-V.  In
 Phase-II of the progrmme priority has been accorded to developing leads/drugs for family planning, viral infections (anti-viral),
 diabetes (hypoglycemic),  liver disorders (hepatoprotective) and cardiovascular diseases.. The Department is laying special
 emphasis on follow up studies but fresh collections are also being continued to identify new leads/activities.
 
29.The Committee was informed that this is one area where thee is some scope for India to be globally competitive, but as at
 present only one drug (prostaglandin) has been developed, which is being marketed; one more device (Iaminaria tent-cervical
 dilator) has been found off the Japanese cost.  Though the Department’s coverage in this field is fairly large, with as many as 10
 institutions being associated with the programme, yet having regard to the investments made by other leading nations, it will
 need a Herculean effort to be internationally competitive.  The Department would, to begin with, like to develop an anti-viral or
 anti-malarial drug.  Responding to a suggestion from the Committee as to whether it would not be more desirable to explore
 and exploit the anti-amoebic area, an official replied that only one organism has shown anti-amoebic activity, and in so far as
 anti-malarial and anti-filarial activity is concerned, not a single organism has yet been found.

30.The attention of the Secretary of the Department of Ocean Development was drawn to the fact that even though the
 development of drugs from the sea was a national programme, no specific allocations for this programme had been made during
 the Budget for 1994-95.  The Committee wanted to know as to what was the position and how much expenditure had been
 incurred on it thus far.  The Secretary explained that the expenditure incurred on this programme during the last 3 to 4 years
 was to the tune of a little over Rs. 3.68 crores.  Responding to a pointed query from the Committee as to whether there has been
 any breakthrough in any area, he stated that there have been some positive leads.
 
31.The Secretary of the Department was asked as to whether any time-frame had been set to realize the objectives of the
 “Drugs from the Sea Programme” and whether the organism which give promising leads for bioactive substances will be
 naturally available on a sufficient scale for large scale drug extraction needed for societal use; or it would be possible to
 multiply their production through cultivation.  The information given to the Committee was that the new drug development
 involves a time and cost intensive process and that the leads which have been identified so far were anticipated to lead up multi
 centric clinical trials.  It may be possible to transform any one of these into a dug by the year 2000.  This would entail long term
 investments as well.  Regarding availability position of marine organism, the Committee was informed that they might not be
 sufficiently  available in nature to meet drug demands and even if the organisms were available, the collection would be
 restricted so as not to disturb the eco-system.  Extensive cultivation/culture will, therefore, have to be initiated to meet
 developmental demands once positive potential significance has been established.
           
            32. The Committee has noted that the National Programme on the “Development of Potential Drugs from the Sea’ is
 merely four years old.  It is a matter of satisfaction that with a modest investment the institutes involved in the programme have
 done a creditable job in screening quite a large number of marine organisms and have been successful in obtaining positive
 leads in some areas.  The programme being still in an experimental stage, it would be too early to draw any conclusion about
 drugs likely to be developed from marine sources and then potential market.  The country has strong infrastructural base in the
 area of drug development, which could be fully utilised in this effort. The Committee, however, feels that the allocations for a
 national programme of this nature are rather meagre. They do not reflect in real terms its potential, and the direction it is taking.
 The Committee recommends that a clear assessment of the priority that needs to be given to this programme must be carried
 out, and an estimate of the funds needed has to be worked out to obtain meaning results in a reasonable time frame. It is
 important to ensure that the efforts is a viable one and above the critical level of support.

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Earth Sciences
on the recommendations contained in the One Hundred Eighty-seventh Report of the Department
Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on
the Demands for Grants (2008-09) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, which was presented to both
the Houses of Parliament on 29th April, 2008. There were twenty recommendations in the One
Hundred Eighty-seventh Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of
the Committee were received from the Ministry on 7th August, 2008.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee
on the Action Taken by the Ministry of Earth Sciences are set out in the succeeding paragraphs:—
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FOR 2008-09
1. Recommendation (Para - 3.5)
The Committee is constrained to note that the projected demand of Rs.1566 crore made by
the Ministry was drastically reduced to virtually half to the tune of Rs.750 crore only. This will
adversely affect the major programmes that are to be undertaken during the current year. The
Committee is of the view that unless there is a raise in the allocation, the Ministry will not be able
to translate their dream into reality. The Committee, at the same time is of the opinion, that
Ministry should also plan its projects/schemes meticulously so as to avoid any drastic cut in their
projections because of poor performance in utilization of previous fund.
Action Taken by Government
The Ministry appreciates the concerns expressed by the Committee towards allocation of
funds for the year 2008-09. The Ministry had undertaken a detailed exercise by conducting a series
of review meetings at different forums such as Research Advisory Council, Earth Commission,
Council of Earth Science Organisation (ESO) etc. to assess the realistic Budget requirement for
various programmes. Further, upon approach of the Ministry, the Planning Commission had assured
the necessary additional required budgetary support to meet the shortfall in the allocation at R.E.
Stage. Although, a great deal of planning had taken place, the Ministry could not achieve the target
in the previous year due to lack of financial delegation to the Earth Commission, which was
discovered only in November, 2007. Currently, the Ministry is working out a strategy for utilization
of funds judiciously.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and opines that the Ministry should monitor its
programmes/projects in a time bound manner and strive for implementation of its projects.
It also opines that Ministry must ensure that Planning Commission release necessary
additional budgetary support to meet the shortfall at R.E. stage as per its assurance.
MECHANISM DEVELOPED TO MONITOR AND REVIEW THE ONGOING SCHEMES
2. Recommendation (Para - 4.2)
The Committee notes with concern that despite the existing mechanism to monitor and
review the ongoing schemes, most of the major programmes, which were undertaken during the
last year saw a large scale under utilization of funds. The Committee hopes that the Department
will further strengthen this mechanism for effective implementation of its programmes so as to
avoid delay in the implementation of various projects and also in avoiding underutilization of the

2
funds allotted to it. The Committee is of the view that procedural and administrative delays could
have been avoided through well focused planning and management. Therefore, the Committee
recommends the Ministry to review its mechanism and make sure that fund allocations are made
as per requirements and are utilized to the maximum possible.
Action Taken by Government
A strong mechanism has already been embedded for review and monitoring of the schemes.
However, due to lack of financial delegation and full-fledged Financial Adviser to the Ministry for
obtaining the approvals for implementation of this programme, there was some under utilization of
funds in the previous years. The Ministry has now initiated corrective measures to avoid
administrative delays and focus on proper planning and management, by quickly adopting
conventional mode of approval viz., EFC/SFC. A significant number of programmes have been
appraised so far. Also the Ministry is in the process of setting up of a review mechanism for
utilization of funds as per the requirement. During the last Earth Science Organisation (ESO)
Council meeting, all the centres of the Ministry have been advised to gear up with implementation
of the programme including the financial targets set for the current financial year.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that the Ministry will stick to its objective
of strict monitoring of schemes. It further desires that administrative shortcomings must
be overcome through proper planning and management, and urges the Ministry to uphold
its commitment to avoid any delays in future.
POLAR SCIENCE/ANTARCTIC RESEARCH
3. Recommendation (Para - 6.5)
The Committee commends the research work carried out by the Ministry in the Antarctica
as initiating scientific research and exploration in extreme cold conditions is not an easy task.
In addition, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry may also conduct a prospective
study on heart rate variabilities under extreme cold climate and prolonged isolation on expedition’s
team members to reveal the physiological changes in the heart due to exposure to cold climate.
At the same time study may also be carried out to examine the effect of such cold climate on
vital body parameters like blood pressure, pulse rate, hemoglobin levels, sleep duration of the
members.
Action Taken by Government
A specialist from All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, namely Dr. S.K.
Khandelwal was deputed with the team of 27th Indian Antarctic Expeditions for undertaking
the studies on the stress on human health and performances, associated with isolation in
extreme climatic conditions at Antarctica. Health assessment at different phases was completed by
Dr. Khandelwal and the same will be followed by the current wintering team medical officer,
namely Dr. A. Bhatia. The studies will include the examination of vital body parameters like blood
pressure, heart rate, hemoglobin level, sleep duration and other points recommended by Hon’ble
Committee.
Comments
The Committee expresses its satisfaction over the efforts made by the Ministry in
conducting health assessment studies on the members of its expedition team. The
Committee hopes that the Ministry would also undertake studies on the psychological
changes on the members of the expedition’s team as extreme cold climate could also affect
the human psychology.

3
4. Recommendation (Para - 6.6)
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should study the icy continent’s atmospherics

5. Recommendation (Para - 6.7)

always been significant to the Indian subcontinent due to the probable tele-connection between the
northern polar region and Indian monsoon intensity, which is critical for an agrarian economy like
