th Five Year Plan. The Department 
has made some special allocations under Human Resource Development (item1) for 
meeting the ongoing commitments and Grand Challenge Programmes (item 6) for taking 
up a special programme on Molecular breeding  of crops as a follow up of mid-term 
evaluation of 11
th Five Year Plan by the Planning Commission. Partnership with Indian 
Council of Medical Research for sharing costs and activities has also been considered to 
make up the gap in the areas of agriculture biotechnology.  
5.5 When the Committee enquired from the Depa rtment as to why the total budgetary 
allocation of Rs. 1024.00 crores at the B.E. le vel was reduced to Rs. 925.90 crores at the 
R.E. stage last year and also that why a similar trends of reduction at R.E. stage are found 
under some other programmes, such as S upport to Autonomous R&D Institutions, 
Research and Development, Grand Challenge  Programme for Promotion of Excellence 
and Innovation, etc.  and whether such a reducti on is due to underutilization of budgetary 
allocations provided for those programmes or  it is due to some other reasons.  The 
Department replied that even when it was ab le to incur an expenditure of more than 54 
per cent of B.E. allocations as against the ta rget of 50 per cent, th e Ministry of Finance 

exercised a mandatory cut of 10 per cent of B. E. outlay resulting in reduced allocation at 
R.E. stage.   The same reason holds good for the reduction of funds at R.E. stage for other 
programmes.  Hence the reduction at the R.E.  level is due to a policy decision taken by 
the Ministry of Finance and not  because of under utilization of funds by the Department.  
The Committee expresses its dismay over the fact that despite the track record of 
utilization being as high as 98.55 per cent, 90.15 per cent and 99.82 per cent during 
the last three years respectivel y, the Department has to face mandatory cut off       
10 per cent of B.E. under most of the pr ogrammes.  The Committee is of the view 
that such routine cuts should not be effected in scientific Departments as it 
adversely affects not only research and development, but also scientific and 
technical advancement of the nation.  Th e Committee, therefore,  recommends that 
the Department of Biotechnology should be exempted from such routine cuts and 
the entire allocation as requested by  the Departme nt for the year 2010-11 at B.E. 
stage should be released at the R.E. level also.  The Committee also recommends 
that the Department should vigorously take up this matter with the Planning 
Commission so as to ensure that no routine reduction is resorted to at the R.E. level. 
5.6 The Committee expresses its serious con cern over the drastic cut in the Plan 
allocation for the Department.  Even in ca se of allocation for priority areas where 
realistic projections were made by the De partment, there has been a cut which has 
forced the Department to reprioritize and reassess the expenditure on new 
initiatives.  The Committee is of the view th at unless there is substantial increase  in 
the allocation, the Department will not be able to translate their dream of making 
India to take a giant leap in innovation and research because growth is closely 
linked with investments made.   
5.7 As regards the minimum requirem ent of Rs.200.00 crores more for the 
research & development, public-private partn ership and infrastructure sectors; the 
Committee suggests that the department shou ld take up the issue emphatically with 
the Planning Commission and  give a compre hensive note  providing cogent reasons 
and details of the funds required under each sector. 
6. The Committee fails to understand the ra tionale behind not fulfilling the projected 
demand of the Department, especially, when the Committee takes note of the 
achievements made by the Department in the 10 th Five Year Plan.  During the 10th Five 
Year Plan period, biotechnology industry has been growing @ 40 per cent and in 2006-07 
exceeded $2.0 billion annual turnover.  The social impact of biotechnology has also been 
substantial as is evident from performance in vaccines, diagnostics, insect resistant 
cotton, medical devices and a number of bi o therapeutics in the Indian market and 
exported to many countries.  Th e 10th Plan period investme nt has been very productive 
and as informed by the Department the cost Vs. total pooled output is about 1:7 and 
productivity per scientist funded Vs . total pooled output is about 1:6.   The Committee 
feels that as against the backdrop of such a brilliant performance by the 
Department of Biotechnology it is sheer injustice with the Department if  Finance 
Ministry fails to provide total budgetary support at le ast for strategic programmes 
being undertaken by the Department. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends that brilliantly performing  Department should be rewarded and 
encouraged by providing total budgetar y support as per their demand.  The 

Committee, therefore, also recommends that  the financial requirements of the 
Department must be met by the Ministry of Finance at the R.E. level.   
7. SUPPORT  TO  AUTONOMOUS  R& D  INSTITUTIONS 
7.1 The Autonomous Institutions have b een established by the Department to 
demonstrate the increasing emphasis on research and process-product development. 
These institutions generate a new syner gy towards capturing research leads and 
converting them into products. Presently there are 14 existing Autonomous institutions 
and 6 new institutions have been proposed. 
7.2 When the Committee enquired about th e increase  in allocation made 
under the programme of 'Support to Autonomous R&D Institutions' from 
Rs.281.10 crores at B.E. stage in th e year 2009-2010 to Rs.330.10 crores this 
year; the Department informed that  this is due to implementation of action plan of 
six new institutions recently approved by the Government in terms of construction, 
procurement of equipments, appointment of manpower, establishment of interim 
facilities etc.  
7.3 The Committee in its 190
th report on the Demand for Grants (2008-2009) 
had strongly recommended that the Department should draw a reasonable time 
frame for establishing new autonomous in stitutions and devise a mechanism to 
monitor their progress periodically so as to avoid time and cost overruns.  However 
the Committee is constrained to note that th e six new institutions are yet be to set 
up.  The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction at the undue delay in the obtaining 
of the necessary Government approvals and reiterates its recommendation for 
expediting the setting up of the proposed si x institutions, so that they could  be 
completed as per schedule and the new institutions could start functioning at the 
earliest and become centres of excellence.  
7.4. The Committee also recommends that  the Department should focus on 
research and development in bio energy a nd bio fuels, partic ularly, the green 
sources of energy which is badly required today in view of the climate change & 
global warming.  The network programme on biobutanol and green diesel should, 
therefore, be launched at the earliest, so as  to expedite the early breakthrough in 
this regard. 
8. HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
8.1 The programme has been designed to generate skilled human resource in multi-
discliplinary area of Biotechnology and popularization of the various aspects of this field. 
While apprising the Committee of  the upto date actual achievements, the Department 
stated that 15 short term training courses ha ve been organized, number of fellowships for 
Ph.Ds has been increased from 100 to 250 per year, 35 colleges have been  supported 
under Star College scheme which has been  started to strengthen life science  
and biotechnology education and training at undergraduate le vel, 6 months industrial 
training have been  provided to B.Tech./ M.Sc./M.Tech biotechnology students, teaching 
programmes in 8 new universities have been  supported, support to ongoing programmes 
at 62 universities have been continue d and 72 national and international 
seminars/symposia/conferences have been  supported under bi otech popularization 
programmes. 
8.2  The Committee was informed that t
he Allocation for 'Human Resource 
Development' had been marginally increased from Rs.36.00 crores from               

RE 2009-2010 to Rs.54.00 cr ores this year as there are ongoing commitments in 
programmes such as starting of 72 PG cour ses all over the countr y, enrolling of 1500 
students with fellowship, 400 Junior Research  Fellowships (JRFs), 400 Post Doctoral 
Fellowships (PDFs) and support to 35 colleges. Besides, in 2010-2011, the annual 
activities include support to 30 short term courses, 100 i ndustry attachment of Post 
Graduate students for skills development, 100 JRFs and PDFs each, support to 15 more 
colleges. These are all ongoing activities comm itted in the 11 th Plan on annual basis. 
Further, due to increases in the fello wships by 50-60% across categories, the 
requirements have doubled and therefore, allocation has been increased in 2010-2011.  
8.3 The Committee feels that quality human resource forms the backbone of 
research activities in a country and as such the Department need to accord greater 
priority to lapping, nurturing and involving ta lented students in scientific pursuits.  
The Committee is of the opinion that the De partment must play a pro-active role in 
this regard. The Committee appreciates th e efforts being made by the Department 
in creating capable human resource in th e biotechnology sector and extending 
support to students at the college level through fellowships, short term training 
courses, providing industrial training to B.Tech./M.Sc./M.Tech biotechnology 
students and hopes that such schemes would be encouraged and expanded to 
universities/colleges in all the states, howe ver, it recommends that this programme 
should be further intensified and st rengthened and more funds should be 
earmarked for this prgramme. 
 8.4 The Committee also recommends that the Star College scheme which aims 
towards strengthening of life science, biotechnology education and training and 
provides experience to biotechnology st udents in the cutting                       edge-
technologies needed for modern biologica l studies at undergradua te level in life 
sciences should be supported to the maxi mum extent through funds allocation and 
hopes that as a result of such experiences, more students will take up life science as a 
career. 
 9. RESEARCH AND  DEVELOPMENT  
9.1 In reply to a query as to what are the new Research and Development 
programmes that are proposed to be initia ted by the Department with the enhanced 
allocation, the Department informed that  the allocation made for 'Research and 
Development' has been increas ed from  Rs.308.40 crores  in R.E. in  2009-2010 to 
Rs.394.40 crores in B.E. 2010 -2011 due to the fact that  about 300 more new R&D 
projects are expected to be sanctioned acr oss disciplines and also for taking up new 
initiatives within approved schemes such ha s ‘Welcome Trust’ - DBT affordable health 
care projects funds for cancer genomics, wh eat and chickpea genomics and establish one 
more unit of bio-energy centre.  
9.2 On being enquired about the role of  ‘The International Crops Research Institute 
for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), in the development of agricultural bio-technology, 
the Department informed that it is a nonprofit, non-political or ganization that does 
innovative agricultural research and capacity building for sustainable development with a 
wide array of partners across the globe with a mission to help millions of  poor people to 
overcome hunger, poverty and a degraded environment in the dry tropics through better 
agriculture. The Department also informed th at a ‘Clinical Resear ch Organisation’ has 
been established in Hyderabad for Agri-biotech  translation and field trials of genetically 

modified (GM) crops to meet the needs of agricultural bio-technology. This project will 
help the scientists working with the Government institutions to gain technical and 
managerial knowledge from the scientists wo rking with the private sector and develop 
new varieties of crops and hybrids to increase agricultural produce. 
9.3 When the Committee enquired the Depart ment about the progress  made over 
the last 10 years in the field of research and publications of quality research papers in the 
country, the Secretary, replied th at significant progress have been  registered in this field 
ever since 2001 with the rise in investment in this field.  The Secretary further replied 
that in an article published in ' New Global Science Report' it has been remarked in 
respect of India that a sleeping giant finally awakens.  In this  article, it has been stated 
that India is finally turning a corner in publication in science and by their projections, 
India will takeover the entire Europe in another 10 years of time. 
9.4 The Committee appreciates the Departme nt in taking initiatives towards 
promotion of new R&D projects across var ious streams of Bio-technology. The 
Committee is also of the opinion that the eco nomy of our  country is basically based 
on agriculture and for the development of  the country and for providing food 
security to the masses, agricultural yields  have to be increased many folds. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the  Department should concentrate its R&D 
activities on Agriculture Bio-technology to  develop new variety of higher yielding, 
pest and disease resistant crops. Th e Committee also recommends that the 
Department should engage itself in explor ing the possibilities for the use of barren 
and desert land for agricultural or hort icultural purposes with the help of bio-
technology, as this would help bring vast unutilised tracts of land under productive 
cultivation in the country and also prevent desertification of the productive land in 
the country. 
9.5 The Committee also appreciates the init iative of the department to start a 
public-private partnership with the ICRISA T for development of new varieties of 
crops and feels that better and faster results in the field of research in agricultural 
biotechnology can be obtained only if th e expertise gained by the government and 
private sector are pooled together. The Committee therefore recommends that such 
pubic-private partnership projects should  be encouraged and sufficient funds 
should be allocated to initiate the projects across the country. 
10.    BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT  
10.1 The programme aims at demonstration of proven biotechnological techniques for 
application to be benefit of SC/ST population, women and rural areas for training to skill 
development, self employment and income generation. The projects are implemented by 
the self help group, NGOs in partnership with  local universities/in stitutions and Krishi 
Vigyan Kendras. About 200 projects are ongoing annually benefitting about 10000 
people. The areas in which activities are undertaken currently  include mushroom 
cultivation, production of fruit and vegetable,  use of biofertilisers and biopesticides, 
utilization of local biores ources for example lantana as  a substitute for bamboo, 
enhancement of agricultural productiv ity, aquaculture, integrated farming, 
vermicomposting, goat farming, quails farming, health care, organic farming, sustainable 
animal husbandry practices, off-season ve getables cultivation, pulse cultivation, 
cultivation of medicinal & aromatic plants etc.  
 

10.2 The Committee was informed that "Biotechnology for Societal Development" has 
been allocated Rs.10.00 crores at B.E. and Rs.9.40 crores at R.E. in the year 2009-2010. 
This year the allocation has b een raised to Rs.13.00 crores. The Department clarified that 
allocation has been increased during 2010- 2011 due to commitments in the ongoing 
projects and for setting up a public communi cation system for biotechnology involving 
State Agricultural Universities focusing on agriculture biotechnologies.  
10.3 The Committee is of the opinion that the benefits of science and technology 
should percolate to the lowest strata of  society and help in upliftment of rural 
masses and women. The Committee is also of the view that popularization of Proven 
and field tested technologies will help the target rural population in their skill 
development, employment and income ge neration in the field of agriculture, 
sericulture, production and manufacture of biopesticides and biofertilisers. In 
health sector too, such projects result in creating awareness on nutrition including 
traditional food and healthcare. The Committee therefore recommends that such 
programmes which involve local people through self help groups and result in 
overall societal benefit should be encourage d by the Department  and efforts should 
be made to ensure that bene fits of such programmes reach the various parts of the 
country. 
11. GRAND CHALLENGE PROGRAMMES 
11.1 The objective of the Grand Challenge Programme is to support biotechnology 
interventions which can bring about significant value addition, cost effectiveness and 
competitiveness in products and processes. Seven such programmes have been launched 
in the areas of Microbial pr ospecting for genes and molecu les, Vaccine Grand Challenge 
Programme, Food Science and Nutrition, A ccelerated Molecular Breeding, Biodesign, 
Gemomics and Bioenergy and Biofuels. The overall objective of Vaccine Grand 
Challenge is to accelerate development of candi date vaccine such as Rotavirus, Cholera, 
Typhoid, Rabies, Anthrax, Malaria, dengue, T uberculosis and Japanese Encephalitis. 
Microbial prospecting involves discovery of genes and molecules in drug development for 
anti-cancer, diabetics, inflammation and infection with participation of 12 institutions and 
screening at private sector facility.  
11.2 While apprising the Committee of th e upto date actual achievements the 
department stated that Micobial prospecti ng programme for genes and molecules in drug 
discovery & development and Bio-fortifi cation programmes of wheat, rice and maize 
using molecular breeding has already been started, while 4 Universiy/IIT departments 
have been supported for starting integrated food science and nutrition research.  
11.3 The department also informed the Co mmittee that the allocation for "Grand 
Challenge Programme" was substa ntially increased from Rs.38.00 crores at R.E. stage in 
the year 2009-2010 to Rs.54.00 crores in B.E 2010-2011. The Department also informed 
that the enhancement in 2010-2011 is due to ongoing commitments in 5 grand challenge 
programme on microbial prospecting, vaccines, biodesign, food science and nutrition and 
genomics. Further, as a follow-up of the midterm evaluation by the Planning 
Commission, a major challenge programme na mely crop breeding by design shall be 
implemented as mega project through settin g up of molecular breeding platform in 
collaboration with Indian Council of Ag ricultural Research/S tate Agricultural 
Universities. Under the biodesi gn program, it is also proposed to establish a Centre for 
Biodesign addressing diagnostics and medical devices in healthcare.  

11.4 When the Committee enquired as regards the development of new medicines, the 
department explained that presently eleven drug s are being developed by the department    
and funds to the tune of Rs.1000.00 crores  are required for this purpose. The                     
public-private partnership pattern is being followed for the drug development. One of the 
outstanding drugs which have been developed is the ‘oral insulin’ for persons suffering 
from diabetes, which will eliminate the requirement for injections. 
11.5 The Committee is aware that global research towards discovery of vaccines 
and medicines for diseases afflicting the western countries find precedence over the 
diseases which are commonly found in the developing countries  such as Cholera, 
Typhoid, Rabies, Malaria, dengue, Tuberculosis.  It is therefore the responsibility of 
the scientific departments to concentrate on drug discovery & development for the 
aforesaid diseases which afflict millions of  people across the country and also make 
them available to the poor pe ople at affordable prices.  The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Department should accelerate the development of vaccines 
and medicines through its Vaccine Gr and Challenge Programme and ensure 
participation of both premier government sc ientific and the private sector research 
institutions in this regard. 
12. PUBLIC- PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP  
 The Committee desired to know about the efforts made by the Department to 
encourage and involve industrie s in the field of biotechnolo gy.  The Department replied 
that it is running a programme, named, Pu blic Private Partnership which has two 
components, i.e., Small Business Innovative Research Initiative (SBIRI) and 
Biotechnology Industry Partners hip Programme.  The Secretary further informed that 
Department have now 300 companies while it had only 50 companies 6 years ago.  He 
further informed the Committee that actually concentration is being made on building a 
lot of young companies in the country and DBT had moved into the field.  The 
Committee while appreciating the efforts ma de by the Department so far in this 
fields, however, recommends that the Depar tment should make concerted efforts to 
involve more and more Indian  industries and encourage young entrepreneurs to 
give a boost to the area of biotechnology which as already emerged as promising and 
fast growing sector for feeding the economic development of the country. 
13. PROJECTS /SCHEMES FOR THE BENEFIT OF THE NORTH-EASTERN 
AREAS AND SIKKIM 
13.1    The main objectives of the progra mme has been human resource development 
at all levels in healthcar e, agriculture and bioresour ce biotechnology; upgradation of 
research facilities in universities, colleges of agriculture and medicine; implementation of 
North Eastern relevant product oriented R&D projects such as swine fever network for 
vaccine and diagnostic development and de monstration of proven technology for the 
benefit of society to promote skill development, entrepreneurship and self-employment.  
13.2 The department informed that the total allocation made for provision for 
projects/schemes for the benefit of "North Eastern Areas and Sikkim" has been increased 
from Rs.90.20 crores at R.E stage in the year 2009-2010 to Rs.120.00 crores in                 
2010-2011. Therefore, out of the total alloca tion of RS.1200.00 crores of plan budgets, it 
is mandatory to allocate Rs.120.00 crores for North Eastern Region.  
 

13.3 The Department informed the Committ ee that considerable efforts through 
various interactive meetings with Vice-Chancellor of universities, Director of institutions, 
colleges and non-profit organizations in the North-eastern region to  implement various 
projects so far with variable success rates.  
 The main challenges faced by the Depart ment for utilization of this mandatory 
budget of 10% of Gross Budgetary Support(GBS) have been following:  
(i) The fund absorption capacity in biotechnology in North Eastern Region 
and Sikkim is highly limited due to severa l factors such as lack of skilled human 
resource, no biotech industri al activity and other social factors. Year after year 
spending 10% GBS is practically not feasible and even if it is spent somehow, it is 
at the cost of certain high quality projects and initiatives in  biotechnology which 
have far ranging benefits irrespective of region. 
  (ii) The Department has no adequate human and institutional resources to 
mobilise expenditure in North East in biotechnology under such challenging 
conditions described above. Therefore, DBT has drawn up to collaborate and 
partner with other agencies such as ICAR, CSIR and ICMR to strengthen the 
programme implementation.  
  (iii) The Department would like to take  up the matter with the Department of 
North Eastern Region (DONER) to limit annual allocation at RS.80.00 crores 
instead of 10% of GBS for expenditure with high success rates.  
13.4 The Committee is of the opinion that mandatory 10% allo cation of total 
budget to Northern-Eastern Region would be more beneficial for the Region. The 
Committee therefore recommends that instea d of thinking of limiting the annual 
allocation to Rs.80.00 crores, the Department should make efforts towards creation 
of skilled human resource  and setting up institutional resources of the Department 
to ensure that the funds a llocated are fully utilized, specially when the region is in 
dire need of  the funds for its development. The Department should also plan 
towards cooperation with other scientific departments to ensure the much needed 
growth in this region.   
14. The Committee is of the view that th e Department of Biotechnology through 
its various research and development progra mmes is striving to uplift the standard 
of living in the country.  Keeping in view the excellent work that the Department has 
undertaken, the kind of competence it has exhibited and the kind of core and critical 
programmes it has envisaged for the future, the Committee strongly recommends 
that the Department of Biotechnology shou ld be properly and adequately funded 
and any kind of reduction in outlay at R.E. stage should be strictly avoided.

Despite being a developing economy, I ndia has effectivel y developed space 
technology and has applied it su ccessfully for its rapid de velopment and today it is 
offering a variety of sp ace services globally. India has come a long  way in mastering 
the complex space tec hnology in a self-reliant manner . The ever challenging task 
of space technology devel opment and its utilis ation, has gradua lly graduated from 
experimental and demonstrat ion phases to an operation al era, commendable and 
notable progress has been ma de in the design, development and operation of space 
systems, as well as, using them for vital services like telecommunications, 
television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster management support and natural 
resources survey and management, which are of direct relevance for national 
development. The space programme has become largely self-reliant with capability 

to design and build satellites for providing space services and to launch them using 
indigenously designed and deve loped launch vehicles. Th e diverse roles of space 
technology and services in various fro nts - social, economic, commercial and 
strategic - have made the space systems an important component of our national 
infrastructure.  
 
2.  OBJECTIVES OF INDIAN SPACE PROGRAMME 
2.1. The primary objective of the Indian Space Programme is to promote the 
development and application of space technology and space science for the                        
socio-economic benefit of the nation thr ough establishment of operational space 
services in a self-reliant manner. The main thrust areas of the programme are: 
 Satellite-based communication for various applications. 
 Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring. 
 Meteorological applications 
 Development and operationali sation of indigenous satell ites, launch vehicles and 
associated ground segment for providing space-based services. 
3. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP 
3.1. The Space Commission and the Department of Space (DOS) were set up in 1972.  
DOS implements the policies framed by th e Space Commission.  These are carried out 
through the Indian Space Resear ch Organisation (ISRO) and th e Grant-in-aid institutions 
viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research Laboratory 
(NARL), North-Eastern Space Applicati ons Centre (NE-SAC), Semi-conductor 
Laboratory (SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST).  
3.2 The major Centres, Units and establishments of DOS/ ISRO, responsible for 
carrying out research and development activities as well as for undertaking various 
projects and programmes, are :- 
(a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, which provides 
the technology base for the country’ s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) 
development. 
(b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC),  with its facilities at Bangalore, 
Thiruvananthapuram and Mahendragiri, which is responsible for development 
of liquid propulsion and cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite and launch 
vehicles. 
(c) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota (Andhra Pradesh), 
is the launch base.  It also provides th e facilities for processing of solid rocket 
motors. 

(d) ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bangalor e, which is entrusted with the prime 
responsibility for satellite development.      
(e) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Syst ems (LEOS), Bangalore which has the 
responsibility for development and produc tion of electro-optical sensors for 
satellites. 
(f) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ah medabad, which carries out research 
and development in space applications as well as development of application 
payloads. 
(g) Development and Educational Comm unication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad, 
which is involved in the conception, definition, planning and socio/techno-
economic evaluation of development communication programmes. 
(h) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRS C), Hyderabad is responsible for 
satellite data acquisition and processi ng, data dissemination, aerial remote 
sensing and decision support for disaster  management. (The erstwhile NRSA, 
an autonomous society, was converted into NRSC as a Government entity 
w.e.f. 1st September 2008);  
(i) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC), with its ground 
stations at Bangalore, Sriharikota,  Lucknow, Bearslake(U.K.), Biak 
(Indonesia), Brunei and Mauritius, whic h provides the telemetry, tracking and 
command support and spacecraft mission ma nagement for the Indian remote 
sensing satellite missions, space scien ce missions and satellite launch vehicle 
programmes. 
(j) Master Control Facility (MCF) with its main facility at Hassan, Karnataka and 
backup facility at Bhopal, Madhya Prad esh which has the responsibility for 
control and operation of INSAT/GSAT/METSAT satellites. 
(k) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, which carries out 
research and development in the area of  inertial systems for satellites and 
launch vehicles. 
3.3 A National Natural Resources Manage ment System (NNRMS), with the 
Department of Space (DOS) as the nodal agency, has been established to ensure optimal 
utilisation of natural reso urces using remote sensing data in conj unction with 
conventional techniques. Under NNRMS, five Regional Remote Sensing Service Centres 
(RRSSCs) at Bangalore, Dehradun, Jodhpur, Khar agpur and Nagpur have been set up for 
execution of remote sensing application pr ogrammes in the respective regions.  With 
effect from December 2009, the RRSSCs have  been redesignated as Regional Remote 
Sensing Centres (RRSCs) and amalgamated with NRSC).      
3.4 The organisations receiving Grants-in- aid under the Department of Space are: 

(a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous 
institution supported mainly by the Department of Space, carries out 
research in space sciences. 
(b) The National Atmospheric Research La boratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki 
near Tirupati, conducts atmospheric research. 
(c) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) established as an 
autonomous body under the Department of Space provides space technology 
inputs for developmental activities in the North-Eastern Region.  
(d) The Semi-conductor Laboratory located at  Chandigarh is a research and 
development society and is entrusted with the design and development of 
Very Large Scale Integrated Circu it (VLSI) devices and development of 
micro-electronic systems to meet the strategic needs of the country.  
(e) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an 
autonomous body under the Department w ith the objective of creating 
quality human resources tune d to suit the requirements of state-of-art space   
research programme.  The Institute offers graduate, post-graduate and 
doctoral programmes in the area of space science, technology and 
applications.  IIST has started the c ourses from the academic year 2007-08 
around the existing infrastructure at Thiruvananthapuram.  
3.5 Apart from this, the RESPOND programme of ISRO supports sponsored research 
activity in space science, space applications and space technology in various national 
academic/research institutions and Space Technology Cells in premier technological 
institutes of the country through grants-in-aid.  
3.6 The Secretariat of Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located 
in Bangalore. Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall 
programmes like satellite communication, Satellite Navigation, earth observation, launch 
vehicle, space science, atmospheric science, space industry development, disaster 
management support, international co-operation, publications and public relations, budget 
and economic analysis and human resource development.  
3.7 The Antrix Corporation Limited, Banga lore, established in 1992, is a wholly 
owned Government Company for marketing space products and services.  
3.8 The detailed budget allocation of the De partment of Space for the year 2010-11 
was considered by the Department-rela ted Committee on Science & Technology, 
Environment and Forests on the 23
rd March, 2010 and the Demands for Grants of the 
Department has the following provisions: 
4. MONITORING  MECHANISMS FOR ONGOING SCHEMES 
4.1 The Department informed the Committee that in order to monitor and review the 
progress of all the ongoing projects / scheme s and to provide overall directions, the 
Department has evolved a two- tier project management stru cture consisting of Project / 

Programme Management Council and Projec t Management Board / Project Executive 
Committee (PMC/PMB/PEX) for all the major projects / schemes in the area of Satellites, 
Launch Vehicles and Space applications.  Before formulating the budget proposals, 
detailed and critical analysis  and reviews are carried out by the ISRO Headquarters with 
the Centres/Units/Projects. The budgeted items  are reviewed in totality including Plan 
and Non-plan components. The ISRO Council undertakes a rigorous review of all the 
budget proposals, addressing the managerial/ programmatic / financ ial aspects preceded 
by detailed technical review of  the programs/ projects / activities.  The essentiality of 
each item, the schedule-budget linkages and cash flow requirements are addressed during 
these reviews.  The overall budget proposal s thus formulated ar e reviewed by Space 
Commission, a high level body constituted by Gove rnment of India, before submitting 
the proposals to the Government. 
5. ELEVENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN OUTLAYS AND PROPOSALS 
5.1 The Committee has been informed that the total Plan outla y allocation for the 
Department of Space for the 11
th Five Year Plan (2007- 2012) is Rs. 30,883 crores 
excluding, the Non-plan budgetary support of around Rs. 4,000 crores.  Thus, the total 
budgetary allocation for the 11th Five Year Plan is expected to be Rs. 34,883 crores.  
5.2       As informed by the Department the major thrust of the Indian Space programme 
during the 11 th Five Year Plan 2007-12 will be to continue and strengthen the already 
established space services and to develop cap ability in the advanced areas of space 
technology.  The programmes envisaged for the 11th Five Year Plan include:

and development of critical technol ogies required for Reusable Launch 
Vehicle.  
 Augmentation of INSAT/GSAT system to meet the projected demand for 
satellite communication services in the country. 
 Establishment of Indian Regional Navigational Satellite System. (IRNSS)  
 Maintaining leadership in Earth Observation system with three series of 
thematic satellites viz., Resourcesat series, Cartosat series and Ocean / 
atmospheric series.  
 Front-ranking research in space science and planetary exploration.  
 Manned Mission Initiatives.   
 Thrust areas of applications – expans ion of Tele-education, Tele-medicine, 
Village Resource Centres, Satellite Navigational services, Disaster 
Management Support and developmental ap plications in the area of natural 
resource management.  
 Human Resource Development including se tting up of Indian Institute of 
space science and technology, Industry Interface, academic interface and 
International co-operation.   
5.3 The Committee observed that the overal l thrust of the Space programme during 
the 11
th Five Year Plan (2007-12) is to sustain and strengthe n the already established 
space based services towards socio-ec onomic development of the country.  The 

Committee recommends that in addition to continuing and strengthening its already 
developed space technologies, the Depar tment should also quest for mastering 
critical technologies and attaining furth er progress in its launc h vehicle programme 
for successful launching of its spacecraft indigenously. It also recommends that the 
services of Antrix, the commercial arm of  the Department, which markets India’s 
space services globally must be fully utilised.  The Committee hopes that the 
Department would achieve the goals set for itself during the 11 th Five Year Plan 
period in the field of space applicatio ns for communication, broadcasting, remote 
sensing, launch vehicle technology etc. for the benefit of the society at large.   
6.       BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
6.1 From the information furnished by the Department of Space on the budget 
approved and actually utilized during the last three years, i.e., 2007-08, 2008-09 and 
2009-10,  the Committee finds that there has been a consistent reduction in the outlay at 
the revised estimates level.  The total budgetary allocation of Rs. 3858.80 crores, 4074.07 
crores and 4959.04 crores at Budget Estimates (B.E.) level during the financial years 
2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10 respectively have  been reduced to Rs. 3290.09, Rs. 
3499.04 and Rs.4167.04 in the respective years at the R.E. Stage.  When the Committee 
enquired from the Department as to whether the reduction at the R. E. Stage  has been 
made due to underutilization of funds allocated at B.E. level or because of some other 
reasons, the Department stated that the allocat ion have been reduced to comply with the 
ceilings fixed by the Ministry of Finance during Revised Estimates.  The Department 
further stated that in fact  it projected budgetary requirements of Rs. 5119.98 crores for 
revised Budgets 2009-10 taking into account th e programmatic aspects and spendability.  
The Committee is surprised to note that desp ite the actual expenditure  being as high as 
99.63 per cent, 99.84 per cent during th e financial years 2007-08 and 2008-09 
respectively and the R.E. allocation expected to  be fully utilized in the Financial Year 
2009-10.  The compulsory reduction by fixing ceilings by Ministry of Finance is not at all 
justified.  The Committee expresses its concern over such a pr actice adopted by the 
Ministry of Finance, especially for the scie ntific departments like Department of Space 
which has done our country proud by landmark achievements.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department of Space should be exempted from such 
ceilings in future and there must not be any reduction at R.E. stage for this 
Financial Year.  The Committee also recommends that incase the Department 
requires more resources at Revised Estimates stage, it should be positively 
considered and desired allocation should the granted by the Ministry of Finance. 
6.2  The Committee has been informed that  the Department of Space has projected a 
budgetary demand of Rs. 7485.56 crores for the year 2010-11 at the Budgetary Estimates 
stage.  However, the total financial outlay allocated fina lly is Rs. 5778.00 crores which 
includes Rs.5000.00 crores for plan and Rs. 778.00 crores for non-plan expenditure.  The 
Committee finds that in net term s, there is an increase of Rs. 819 crores this year as 
against the last year allocation of Rs. 4959.00 cr ores at the B.E. stage.  The Committee 
notes with concern that this increase is quite  negligible if inflationary trends are taken 
into consideration. The Committee, therefore, expresses its serious concern over non-
adequate allocation of budgetary provisi ons for the Department of Space and 
recommends that sufficient budgetary provisions  should be made for the Department in 
order to enable it to carve a niche in space technology and space applications.   

6.3  When the Committee enquired from the Department as to whether the budgetary 
allocations made for 2010-11 are sufficient to  carry out the planned activities of the 
department,   it was informed that funding for some of the new projects/schemes, such as, 
Cartosat-3, TES-Hyp, GISAT, GSAT-13 a nd follow on Missions and Human Space 
Flight Programme have been phased out to subsequent years in order to contain the 
funding within the allocated funds.  Th e Committee understands that these new 
projects/schemes which are basically meant for the purpose of earth observation are 
going to suffer due to lack of funds which is  not at all a healthy scenario if such a 
dynamic and performance oriented department  like Space is made to suffer from the 
shortage of funds.  In such a situation th e possibility of desp eration and lack of 
motivation among scientists due to resource crunch cannot be ruled out.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that th e Department of Space should not be 
made to starve of funds in future and expects that Government will extend all 
budgetary supports required by the Department in future. 
7. MANNED MISSION INITIATIVE  
7.1 The Committee finds that in 2009-10, the Manned Mission Initiative/ Human 
Space Flight Programme was allocated Rs. 238 crores at B.E. stage which came down to 
Rs. 30 crores at R.E. stage.  When the Committee desired to know the reasons for the 
drastic reduction of allocation at R.E. stag e, it was informed that the Department 
submitted the Budget Report for the Human Space Flight Programme which had been 
reviewed and cleared by Space Commission, as well as, by a high level committee 
chaired by the Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission.  However, it was indicated 
through the subsequent discussions that th e Human Space Flight Programme could be 
taken up in phases and the first phase shoul d focus on developing critical technologies, 
such as, crew module, service module, crew escape system, environment control and life 
support systems.  The R.E. provision, therefor e, has been reduced in view of the pre-
project activities.  When the Committee enquired about the im portance of this 
programme from the Secretary, Department of  Space it was informed that it is a very 
crucial and important programme because ma ny countries, like U.S.A., Russia, China, 
Japan, etc., are looking at the ha bitat in Mars which is consid ered a better place for life, 
with full of water, land bearing clouds, atmosphere, pressure, etc. by 2030-2035.  Moon 
becomes an inter-mediary point where they should put a habitat and have the propulsion 
system made and go up.  The Committee fails to understand that when the Space 
Commission, the highest policy making body of the Department of Space has given ‘a go 
ahead’ to this programme, why stumbling blocks were created at the Government level?  
Planning Commission should not come in the way of conception an d realization of a 
programme only because it is instrumental in providing allocations for the Department.   
7.2  The Committee is of the view that Human Space Flight Programme is a very 
important one which should not only be take n up in right earnest,  but also be made 
successful at the earliest, so that India is not left far behind in the race of making a habitat 
in mars.  The Committee strongly recommends that the right to take final decision in 
scientific and technical matters should be vested with the Department of Space only 
and financial constraints should not be allowed to come in its way towards progress 
of these crucial and critical programmes. 
7.3 It has been observed that higher allocations are made on certain 
schemes/programmes at Budgetary Estimates level 2009-10, but they remain unutilized at 

the R.E. stage owing to some reasons or th e other. Provision of Rs . 155.00 crores for the 
Semi-Cryogenic Engine Development and its re duction to 36.00 crores, allocation of Rs. 
90 crores for Indian Lunar Mission Chandr ayan I & II and its re duction to Rs. 19.50 
crores at R.E. stage are some of the gl aring instances. When the Committee enquired 
about the reasons for such a gross underutilization of funds under the above programmes, 
the Department replied that in  case of semi cryogine engi ne Development the provision 
has been reduced at R.E. stage because the project was approve d in January, 2009.  
Secondly, due to complexities of the technolo gies and iterative process involved in 
evolving the engine design, th e specification details of th e engine and engine test 
facilities took more time than anticipated.  For Indian Lunar Mission, the Department 
stated that more than 30 experimental pr oposals received for conducting scientific 
investigations on moon onboard are being currently evaluated by an Expert Committee to 
finalise the scientific payloads to be flow n up Chandrayan-2. Pendi ng the finalization of 
the payloads and their specifications/in terface details, the activities related to 
procurement of components/materials and sub-sy stem fabrications has been re-scheduled 
to next year.  Hence, the budget during the current year has been reduced at R.E. Stage. 
7.4  The Committee feels that demand for these schemes/programmes had been made 
without doing proper homework and extensive and critical assessment of the actual 
requirements.  The Committee feels that budgetary demands should be sought by the 
Department only after comprehensive analys is of the actual requirements for the 
programme.  Scarce resources should not be ma de to be blocked by asking for ambitious 
allocations and not utilizing them subsequently.  The Committee recommends that 
such instances, though, only a few should be avoided in future by the Department.   
8. INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 
8.1 The Committee is pleased and proud to no te that India is be ing recognized today 
as one of the fast growing and a leading country in the field of space programmes.  A 
number of developed countries  like, U.S.A., U.K., Russia,  France, Germany, etc., are 
seeking cooperation and actively participati ng in our space programmes.  India’s maiden 
mission to Moon, the Chandrayan-I is a classic example of international cooperation with 
its international payloads  – including Moon Mineralogy, Mapper of NASA  which 
identified presence of water molecules on the Moon.  While the Committee extends its 
compliment to the Indian scientists for su ch a path breaking and landmark achievements, 
it expresses its displeasure over the way cred it for this has been taken by others.  An 
impression has been given through the mass media that it is basically a finding conducted 
by foreign scientists and not by the Indian scientists.  When the Committee enquired from 
the Department, the circumstances under which such an impression has been created, the 
Secretary, Department of Space explained that  NASA put two instruments, i.e., (i) Moon 
Mineralogy Mapping, (ii) Microw ave Payload, onboard Chandray an.  In fact, they were 
the primary instruments which found water on the Moon.  He further explained that based 
on an arrangement of the instruments that were carried by other countries on Chandrayan, 
we had investigated from our side.  It was a joint paper which was written by the 
American and Indian scientists.  The Secretary further added that the first press statement 
was issued in the U.S. and then it was done  here.  This was done standing between the 
two because the prime instruments were from  the U.S.  The Committee, however, is not 
convinced by the argument given by the Secretary.  The Co
 mmittee recommends that 
in future, in case of joint collaboration, it must be ensured that there is a clear 

understanding between the participatin g countries that credit for landmark 
achievements should be shared equally and the announcement is made jointly.   
  PARTICIPATION OF SPACE INDUSTRY PARTNERSHIP 
8.2 The Committee enquired from the Depart ment whether it has evolved any policy 
for involvement and participation of Indian i ndustry in manufacturing and 
development of space technology.   The Secretary, Department of Space informed the 
Committee that it has been the stated policy, ri ght from 1970s that the services Indian 
industry will be used to the maximum possible extent.  It was further informed that as on 
today the Department has association with mo re than 500 small, medium and large-scale 
industries and about 60-65 per cent of our budge t allocation goes to th e Indian industry 
both in public and private sectors.   
8.3  The Committee appreciates the efforts ma de by the Department in this direction, 
however, it feels that in this buoyant space market, there are great opportunities for space 
technology and Department of Space should invol ve and nurture Indian  industry to play 
leading role as establis hed manufacturer and supplie r in the global market.  The 
Committee is of the opinion that involvement and participation of more and more 
Indian industries will lead to self-reliance and would bring down our dependence on 
foreign industries for equipm ents and technologies.  Ex pansion of Indian industry 
would also lead to large-scale employmen t generation.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department of Space sh ould make concerted efforts in this 
direction.  The Committee also desires th at Department of Space should look 
forward to transfer more and more technolo gies which may be us eful for civilian 
applications to Indian Industries.   
  INVOLVEMENT OF YOUT H IN SPACE PROGRAMMES  
8.4 The Committee enquired from the Department about the status of interests 
enthusiasm and zeal among youth towards joining space programme and take up space 
science as a career.  The Secretary inform ed the Committee that a few years ago the 
position was that about 5 to 15 percent youngsters  used to leave after training.  But now 
on the one hand Chandrayaan Mission has given a lot of encouragement to the youngsters 
to get into this programme and on the ot her hand Sixth Pay Commission has given 20 
percent extra payment based on organizationa l performance and about 10 percent on the 
individual performance. This marks a pay packet  which is 30 percent more than the other 
agencies.  As such there has been no attrition in the last two years.  The Secretary further 
informed the Committee that we are seeing large number of applicants for our induction 
programme now.  
8.5 While the Committee expresses its sati sfaction over the current indicators of 
involvement of youth in space programmes, it desires that the Department of space 
should make all out efforts to encourage  more and more youngsters to join its 
programme.  The Committee, therefore, r ecommends that the Department should 
accord priority to this init iative.  A long term goal shou ld be fixed for involvement  
of youth in space programmes. 
R&D PROGRAMMING  
8.6 The Committee finds that ISRO Sponsored Research Programme (RESPOND) is 
a very useful and important programme which extends support to research and 
developmental projects, scientific activities at the academic institutions, R&D labs in the 
areas of relevance to the space program me. RESPOND also suppo rts basic research 

which have futuristic linkages with the Indian Space Programme.  Thus, the main 
objectives of this programme are to strength en space academia interaction for generation 
of wider research infrastructure a nd research bag and developing quality 
scientific/technical manpower in the niche areas of space technology, space science and 
space applications. 
8.7 But the Committee finds that for such an important programme the allocation this 
year has been reduced to Rs. 15.00 crores as  against Rs. 16.50 crores  last year at the 
Revised Estimates level.  The Committee feels that the budget allocated for this 
programme is not sufficient as the Development should further intensify and strengthen it 
so that adequate quality human resources are created to meet the future requirements.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that  the Department should seek more 
resource at R.E. level under this programme, if need be.   
8.8 It has been informed to the Committee th at the Department of Space envisages to 
setup an institute to carry out focused research in climate change and environment. When 
the Committee desired to know about the progr ess made in this regard the Department 
stated that this idea has b een mooted jointly with the Ministries of Environment & 
Forests, Science and Technology and Department of Space.  It was further informed that 
this proposal has to be got cleared in the inter Ministerial Comm ittee.  The Committee 
observed that no allocation whatsoever had be en made under this programme during the 
year 2009-2010.  This year also only a token provision of Rs. 1 crore has been made.  
The Committee fails to understand as to w hy such an important programme on climate 
change is not being taken seriously.  The Committee feels that when the adverse effects 
of global warming and climate change have  started manifesting in many forms, the 
Department must accord greater priority to this programme.  According to the studies 
conducted by the Department of Space, the Hi malayan Glaciers have shown an over all 
reduction in Glacier area from 5866 sq. km. to 4921 sq. km. since 1962 showing an 
overall deglaciation of 16 percent.  The Committee recommends that in view of the 
rapid climate change taking place, it has become absolutely necessary and urgent to 
study climatic and environmental change s and, therefore, recommends that the 
National Institute of Climate Change and Environment Studies be  made functional 
at the earliest and preferably during this financial year. 
8.9 The Committee while referring to its ea rlier discussion with the Ministry of 
Environment & Forest pointed out that Space Satellite deployed for collecting primary 
data for forest cover in the country takes about 2 years to analyse data  and finally 
handing over the same to forests department .  This is too long a peri od to collect data 
and finally handing over the same to Forest Department for further action.  In reply to 
this, Secretary, Department of Space appris ed the Committee that this undue delay in 
final handing over of the data to forest department of Ministry of Environment and Forest 
could be avoided if the Ministry of Envi ronment & Forest and Department of Space 
could have a mutual discussion among themselves and can form a working group on how 
to operationalize data in a short time period which could be worked out in a strategic 
manner. 
8.10 The Committee agrees that essentially two years time as pointed out  is too long a 
time and welcomes the idea of Secretary of Space that a working group to operationlize 
data in a shorter period of time could be  formed by mutually discussing  the matter 
between the Ministry of Environment & Forests and Department of Space.   

  SPACE APPLICATIONS 
9. TELEMEDICINE   
9.1 Telemedicine is one of the unique app lications of Space T echnology for societal 
benefit.  DOS Telemedicine programme, which started in 2001 has been connecting 
remote/rural/medical college hospitals a nd Mobile Units thr ough INSAT and EDUSAT 
to major specialty hospitals in cities and towns. The Committee has been informed that 
the telemedicine network has been further e xpanded to cover the areas of Mobile Tele-
health and Continuing Medical Education. Th e network covers the areas of Jammu & 
Kashmir, Ladakh, Andaman and Lakshdweep Islands, North Easter n States, mainland 
states including tribal districts of mainla nd states like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu 
Chhatisgarh, Punjab, West Bengal, Orissa, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Jaharkhand and 
Rajastan.   
9.2 Presently, the ISRO telemedicine ne twork covers, about 382 hospitals. 306 
remote/rural/district/medical college hospitals connected to 60 specialty hospitals. 
Sixteen Mobile Telemedicine units have also  been established. The Mobile Telemedicine 
units cover diverse areas of Opthalmo logy, Cardiology, Radiology, Diabetology, 
Mammography, general medicine, women and child health. 
9.3 Under the programme, the Department of Space provides Telemedicine systems 
software, hardware and communication equipment as well as give satellite bandwidth. 
State governments and the speciality hospitals give funds for the infrastructure, 
manpower and maintenance. The Committee is of the opinion that this is a very useful 
and workable proposition as far as providing quality health care facilities in remote and 
far flung areas of the country is concerned. The Committee recommends that the 
telemedicine network should be expanded further by covering the most backward 
states, extreme remote and inaccessible and disease-prone areas which have been 
left out so far.  
  TELE-EDUCATION 
9.4  EDUSAT launched in 2004 is India’s firs t thematic satellite dedicated exclusive 
to education services, which is already providing a wide range of educa tional delivery 
modes including one way TV broadcast, in teractive TV, Video conferencing, Computer 
conferencing and Web based instructions at present there are more than 5617 interactive 
classrooms and 46541 receive only classr ooms thus making it a total of around 52158 
classrooms.  About 15 to 18 lack stude nts are being benefitted through EDUSAT 
annually and its networks have been setup in 24 states.  The Committee feels that this is a 
very path breaking educationa l programme which has the pote ntial to go a long way in 
raising the literacy rate of the country.  The Committee therefo re recommends that 
EDUSAT programme should be  expeditiously implemented in remaining states of 
the country.  
 DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPORT SYSTEM 
9.5 The Committee has been informed th at the main objective of Disaster 
Management Support (DMS) Programme run by th e Department is to provide timely and 
reliable space inputs and servi ces to the DMS in th e country and is a vital area of space 
applications.  The major initiatives planned during 11
th five year Plan period includes 
realization of a National Data Base for Emergency Management, Impact mapping and 
monitoring support for Disaster events, Satellite based communication support for 

Disaster Management, strengthening of early warning systems and development of tools 
and techniques for decision support systems for Disaster Management.  
9.6 The work on realisation of a National Data Base for Emergency Management has 
been initiated.  Besides creation of data laye rs, several application tools like river-watch 
tool, flood hazard information system, flood disa ster decision support system, etc., have 
been developed. An Airborne Synthetic Aper ture Radar (ASAR) has been developed for 
aircraft based surveys as a part of disaster management support system and demonstration 
flights have been completed. Towards emergency communication for disaster 
management activities, a Virtual Private Ne twork (VPN) has been set up with 29 Nodes 
networking the State and District level emerge ncy control centres with Ministry of Home 
Affairs for near real time management of natura l disasters.   As a part of impact mapping 
and monitoring support, over 160 Flood Inundati on maps were generated covering the 
flood disaster events in Andhr a Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Ori ssa, Uttar Pradesh and West 
Bengal States.   The Government have also approved setting up of dedicated aerial survey 
facilities consisting of exclus ive aircraft, sensor instruments and onboard real time data 
processing facilities to support Disaster Management System in the country.  
9.7     The Committee is of the view that India has been traditionally vulnerable to 
natural disasters on account of its unique geo-climatic conditions. Floods, droughts, 
cyclones, earthquakes and landslides have been a recurrent phenomena and a lot of 
economic devastation and human loss is caused on account of these natural 
calamities. The Committee feels that the s ervices of Virtual Private Network (VPN) 
which has been set up for networking the St ate and district leve l emergency control 
centres for near real time natural disaster s management must be optimally utilized 
for rapid dissemination of information to minimize the human and material loss. 
  Keeping in view the excellent and ou tstanding work that the Department of 
Space has undertaken, the kind of competen ce that the Department has exhibited 
and the kind of core and critical programme s that they have en visaged for future, 
the Committee strongly recommends that the Department of Space should be 
properly and adequately funded and any kind of reduction in outlay at R.E. Stage 
should be strictly avoided.

REPORT 
         The acquisition of knowledge of th e controlled release of atomic energy and its use 
has been recognized as path-breaking event in the human history. India has a long history 
of development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes and has developed its own 
nuclear power programme, which has b een recognized around the world. For the 
development and industrialization of the count ry, atomic energy has become not merely 
an aid but an absolute necessity, keeping in vi ew the fast depleting reserves of coal and 
oil in the country. On the more, atomic energy is a clear and green  energy which is the 
need of the day in view of global warming and climate change.  The Department of 
Atomic Energy has therefore been engaged in the development of nuclear power 
technology, besides promoting other applications of radiation technologies in the field of 
agriculture, medicine, industry and basic research. The Atomic Energy Commission 
(AEC), which is the apex body for formulatio n of policies and dire ction of the Atomic 
Energy programmes in the country, implemen ts its policies and programmes through the 
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE).  
2.  The Programmes of DAE have b een divided into four sectors viz.  Research and 
Development, Industrial, Minerals and Power Sector. Some of the significant 
programmes covering all the four above sectors can be briefly summarized as-  increasing 
the share of nuclear power through de ployment of indigenous and other proven 
technologies developing fast breeder reactors and thorium reac tors with associated fuel 
cycle facilities; building and operation of  research reactors for production of 
radioisotopes and carrying out radiation technology applications  in the field of medicine, 
agriculture and industry;  developing advanced technologies  such as accelerators, lasers, 

 
supercomputers, advanced materials and inst rumentation and encouraging transfer of 
technology to industry; support to basic resear ch in nuclear energy and related frontier 
areas of science; interaction with unive rsities and academic institutions; support to 
research and development projects havi ng a bearing on DAE’s programmes, and 
International cooperation in related advan ced areas of research, and contribution to 
national security. 
3.   The programmes   of the DAE are   mu ltidisciplinary   in  nature and for their 
execution, the Department has evolved a broa d based organization comprising research 
centres, industrial units, public sector undertakings and fully aided autonomous 
institutions, along with servic e organizations. The details of these organisations are as 
follows: 
Five Research Centres: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) – Mumbai,  which 
pursues comprehensive research and devel opment (R&D) programmes in the fields of 
nuclear sciences, engineeri ng & technology, basic sciences  and allied fields for 
harnessing nuclear energy and also its utility for the benefit of the society.  
Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic  Research (IGCAR) – Kalpakkam is the second 
largest R&D centre of the Department engaged in basic research in nuclear sciences and 
allied areas, technology development in th e field of nanomaterials and nanotechnology 
and has designed the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR). 
Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) – Indore  is engaged in 
development of particle accelerators and lase rs along with their applications, besides 
carrying out substantial activities in cryogenics and materials research. 
Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) – Kolkata is operating the nation’s largest 
and the first indigenously built  Cyclotron and has been produced for the first time in 
India, the energetic Neon 20 and Argon 40 beams required for conducting research in 
Nuclear Physics.and         
Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and  Research (AMD)– Hyderabad  
Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration & Research carries out  survey, prospecting 
and exploration of atomic minerals require d for the nuclear power programme of the 
country.   
Three Industrial Organisations :  Heavy Water Board (HWB) – Mumbai, Nuclear Fuel 
Complex (NFC) – Hyderabad  and Board of Radiation  and  Isotope Technology (BRIT) 
– Mumbai. 
Three Service Organisations :  Directorate of Purchase  & Stores (DPS) – Mumbai, 
Directorate of Construction, Services and  Estate Management  (DCSEM) – Mumbai, and 
General Services Organisation (GSO) – Kalpakkam.  
Five Public Sector Undertakings :   Nuclear Power Corporation of  India Limited 
(NPCIL) – Mumbai, Bharatiya Nabhikiya  Vidyut Nigam Limited, (BHAVINI)  
Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL) – Jaduguda, 
Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) – Mumbai and Electronics Corpor ation of India Ltd. 
(ECIL) – Hyderabad. 
Nine  Aided Institutions  : Tata Institute of Fundament al Research (TIFR) – Mumbai, 
Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) – Mumbai, Saha  Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP) – 
Kolkata , Institute of Physics (IOP) – Bhubaneswar, National Institute of Science 
Education and Research (NISER) – Bhubane swar, Harish-Chandra Research Institute 
(HRI) – Allahabad, Institute of Mathematical Sciences (IMSc) – Chennai,  Institute for  
Plasma Research (IPR) – Ahmedabad, and Atomic  Energy  E ducation  Society   (AEES) 
– Mumbai.  

 
4. MONITORING MECHANISMS FOR ONGOING PROJECTS 
4.1 As regards the structure of monitoring a nd reviewing mechanisms of projects in 
the Department of Atomic Energy, the Committee was informed of the process of 
monitoring starts with the Pr oject Coordinator and his gro up of assistant reviewing and 
monitoring the progress of ongoing projects on da y to day basis.  Thereafter, the Unit 
Head reviews and monitors the projects on  month-to-month basis and tries to remove 
constraints/lacuna if any and monitors the financial and p hysical progress of projects. 
Finally, at the Department level, Secretar y, DAE takes monitoring and review meeting 
periodically to review the physical and fina ncial progress of the pr ojects and tries to 
remove any procedural bottleneck amongst th e Units/Divisions for smooth progress of 
projects so that there is no time/cost overrun of any projects. After the above review 
process, the Department assesses the requirement of fund in each project and formulates 
the proposal for budgetary support in the form of Revised Estimates for the current year 
and Budget Estimates for the next financial year. 
4.2 The Department also informed that in or der to ensure the Plan targets made, the 
Department has taken concrete steps.  The mechanism of form ulation of projects is now 
based on the concept of Major Programmes. Further, Steering Committee, Internal 
Working Groups and Specialist Groups have been constituted to review the project report 
prior to their sanction and also to review th e progress of each project.  Thereafter their 
recommendations provide the re alistic input to the budget pl anning process. In the R&D 
Sector, the overall programme of the Department has been divided into twenty themes 
and a Specialists Groups have been formed for each one of them for overseeing the 
activities during XI Plan.  Thus monitoring of projects under R&D Sector would be done 
at three levels.  The first level monitoring is at Section or Group level in the Unit, the 
second level monitoring is by the higher leve l of management in the Unit and the third 
level is the monitoring by Specialist Group at DAE level.  
 4.3 The Committee while examining  the details of reasons provided by DAE for 
non fulfillment  of targets in  X Plan under R&D sector observ es that   as against    
the revised outlay of Rs. 3501.35 crore,  utilization of only Rs. 3199.45 crore could be 
done which works out to 91.37 per cent of th e revised outlay and there is a short fall 
of about 8.63 per cent in terms of  utilization.  Similarly under Industries Sector, 
against the Budgetary support of Rs. 1539 crores, the utilization is Rs. 1241.23 
crores which means there is a short fall of Rs. 297.77 crores in terms of utilisation.  
Under power sector against the budget ary support of Rs. 13441.41 crores the 
utilization is only Rs. 10016.83 crores which is about 74.52 per cent of total of the 
budgetary provision.  The Committee therefore, finds that despite the elaborate and 
comprehensive monitoring mechanism adop ted by the DAE underutilization of 
funds under different sectors presents alto gether a different picture because in 
certain cases the underutilization of budgetary support  runs to almost 25.5 per cent 
which is not a healthy indication. 
4.4 The Committee, therefore, recomme nds that the Department needs to 
further strengthen the mechanism of monitoring ongoing schemes for their effective 
implementation and eliminating any scope of  surrender of funds at a later date due 
to under utilization.

7.1 While responding to a query of the Committee for a brief on the research & 
development being handled by DAE, the Secretary replied that R&D is divided into two 
sectors, one is nuclear pow er generation, which provides research support to Nuclear 
Power Corporation, nuclear fuel complex, mineral and also for fast reactor technology. 
7.2 The other research sectors under R&D is in  the area of biological research which 
includes influence of radiation on living being, plants and animals. 
7.3 So far as, R&D in power generation is concerned, Secretary emphasized that at 
present extensive research is going on to extend the lifespan of nuclear reactor for 
electricity generation from initial 40 years to about 60 years, which could further be 
extended for another 20 years, i.e., upto 80 y ears.  In order to extend the life of the 
nuclear reactor, a lot of R&D is necessary like more advance pressure tube, more advance 
degradation mechanism by which minerals coul d be used for effici ent breeding of power 
and also to design nuclear reactor in such a fashion that more effective fuel technology 
could be developed to generate power faster.

been further informed that the Department of  Atomic Energy is vigorously pursuing the 
roadmap of well laid down nuclear power pr ogramme in stages.  After successfully 
putting the first stage in commercial domain  and launching the second stage programme 
by ongoing construction of 500 Mwe prototype fast breeder reac tor, the Department is 
actively engaged in devel oping technologies for th e third stage programme.

sub-critical reactor system, high temperature reactor systems and fusion technologies, etc.

9. Nuclear Irradiation in Agri culture and Food Processing 
  The Committee has been informed that the Deptt. of Atomic Energy has 
developed several applications of radiati on and isotope technologies for improving the 
quality of life and is making concerted efforts on this front.   
9.1 The use of Nuclear irradiation helps in  reducing the inciden ce of diseases in 
seeds. Food-borne diseases can also be reduced by food irradiation techniques.  It can 
also inhibit post-harvest sprouting in pot atoes and onions – disinfect fruits and 
vegetables, delay in ripening of fruits, can eliminate out rightly the food-borne pathogens 
which can be kept for a long time without refrigeration before substantial consumption.  
In addition, the irradiation technology can be used for eliminating pests nuisance, etc. 
9.2 The Committee was informed by the Department that it is taking initiatives in the 
field of Nuclear irradiation in agriculture and food proces sing, to increase agricultural 
yield and for protection of the crops from di seases and pests. The department giving the 
specific details alongwith the successes achieved in this regard stated that eleven 
irradiated varieties of crops, called the ‘Trombay crop’ varie ties have been developed in 
oilseeds and pulses in the last three y ears by Nuclear Agricultu re and Biotechnology 
Division, Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Mumbai and released for cultivation in 
Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Chattisgarh, West Bengal, 
Orissa, Gujarat and Karnataka. The crops include oilseeds such as Groundnut, Soybean, 
Mustard, Sunflower and pulses such as Green Gram, Pigeonpea & Cowpea. 
 

 
9.3   The department also informed that as regards Food Proce ssing the radiation 
Processing Plant, Vashi provides gamma ra diation processing services for spices, 
ayurvedic raw material and pet feed etc. to  more than 130 customers from all over the 
country.  During the current fi nancial year, about 1600 Metric Tonnes(MT) of spices and 
other products were processed till November 2009.  During the financial year, the plant is 
expected to process around 2400 MT spices a nd allied product yielding revenue of about 
Rs.1.50 crore. The Board of Radiation & Isotope Technology(BRIT) signed a tripartite 
agreement with the Maharashtra State Ag ricultural Marketing Board (MSAMB) and 
BARC for service operation of  KRUSHAK Irradiation Facility, Lasalgaon, Nashik from 
this year by MSAMB, for 3 years. Using this facility, about 130 tonnes mangoes were 
processed and exported to Unite d States by various exporters.   The facility is under 
upgradation for multi-tasking i.e. to convert  it into a multi-product processing unit 
covering wide range of food products requiring low dose to medium dose exposure.  
9.4 The department also informed that the in terest of entrepreneurs in using radiation 
technology for hygienising a nd preserving food and allied products is increasing.  
Construction of a radiation processing plan t at Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, was completed and 
trial run was started with support from BRIT.  It is the ei ghth such plant in private sector 
in the country. Radiation technology has also helped India in increasing its exports of 
food items including the most developed markets in the world. 
9.5 The Committee is of the opinion that  the economy of the country being 
primarily based on agriculture with a substantial workforce of the country engaged 
in farming, the economic development of the country largely depends on 
agricultural development. The Committee is al so aware that most of the farmers in 
the country do not have any access to the latest techniques to increase agricultural 
produce and also techniques to prevent the lo ss in produce due to diseases and pests 
and also due to lack of proper storage facilities. Therefore, increase in agricultural 
produce and processing of agricultural prod ucts in the country through scientific 
support, assumes prime importance and the Department of Atomic Energy through 
its reputed  institutions has a pivotal role to play in this regard. 
9.6  The Committee is of the opinion that in troduction of new varieties of disease 
and pest resistant crops in various parts of  the country will help in increasing crop 
yields and give a boost to agriculture and al so help in tiding over shortage of food. 
The Committee is also of the opinion that irradiated food products which have a 
higher shelf life will increase the export of  farm products and thereby help in 
increasing the agricultural incomes. While the Committee appreciates the initiatives 
taken by the Department in this regard, it feels that much more needs to be done 
further.  The Committee, therefore, rec ommends that the department should 
intensify its research in the field of agric ulture and   populariz e its technologies 
among farmers across the country, so that  the benefit of research could percolates 
down to the poor and marginal farmers as well.

12.1 The Committee observes that during the Eleventh Five Plan, so far, AMD has

enhance indigenous exploration and exploitati on of Uranium ore which is critical not

able to establish only 34,080 tonnes of uranium resource as against the target of                   
75,000 tonnes for the Eleventh Five Year Plan period.  The Committee expresses its 
concern over the fact that ev en after three years of the Eleventh Five Year Plan 
have lapsed, the Department has not been ab le to harness even half of the uranium 
resources targeted during the Eleventh Fi ve Year Plan.  The Committee expresses 
its apprehension over the successful achievement of the set target.  The Committee 
therefore, recommends that the obstacles co ming in the way of achievements of the 
target set for the 11
th Plan period need to be overcome  in right earnest so that our
