12.3      The Committee notes with serious concern that a crucial programme such as 
the ‘Drugs and Pharmaceutical Research’ pr ogramme which was started in  1994-95 is 
still in search of a promoting Department/ Ministry. The Committee fails to understand 
as to why the programme is being shifted from Department of the Science & 
Technology to Departments of Biotechnology (DBT), or AYUSH, Minist ry of Health or 
CSIR. The Committee expresses its serious concern  at the fact that even after so many 
years of being in existence, no focused approach has been adopted towards the 
programme. Instead of shifting from one De partment to another, the Committee is of 
the firm opinion that to achieve better resul ts, better coordination should be evolved 
between the Ministries/Departments participating in the programme.  
12.4 The Committee is of the view that in  a country where poverty is rampant and 
substantial part of population suffers from cr itical diseases, continued support to drug 
research programmes is the social respons ibility of the government for providing 
affordable drugs/medicines to the poor mass es and this responsibility cannot be diluted 
or absolved at any stage through reduced allocations. Hence instead of decreasing 
allocation for the programme, a focussed a pproach should be adopted within the  
Department of Science  & Technology to ensu re that the programme is able to deliver 
its intended results. The Committee, the refore, recommends that drug research 
programmes should be focussed on the neglected diseases which are afflicting the large 
populace of our country with renewed vigour.  
12.5 The Committee in its 162
nd report on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research 
Prgramme including the herbal  medicines have comprehens ively examined the various 
aspects of this programme and have given cogent recommendations. The Committee 
while reiterating its recommendations would like to stress upon the urgent need to forge 
effective partnerships between the various research institutions and the pharmaceutical 
companies engaged in the crucial field of  drugs and pharmaceutical research and 
development, keeping in view the profo und influence of R&D on the prospects and 
opportunities for the growth of the Indian  Drug Industry and promotion of Industry-
Institutional Collaboration of R&D in drugs and pharmaceuticals sector is the need of 
the hour.

general  interest towards science subjects wh ich has resulted in a sharp decrease in the 
students who are opting for science as a ca reer and therefore the invaluable creation of

this background the INSPIRE and SHE sche mes which aims towards inculcating an 
interest towards science amongst the school ch ildren at an early age of 10 to 15 years is

students of the country can be nurtured an d retained for research in science streams 
and would eventually enable India to embark on ambitious course of  scientific wealth 
creation.  
13.7 The Committee also appreciates that th e Department will nurture the scheme in 
colleges and post-graduate level too throug h its various fellowships and monetary 
incentives programmes, specially the ‘Ins pire Faculty scheme’ wherein each Post 
Doctoral Fellow will draw a salary equivalent to an Assistant Prof essor of IIT with a 
research grant. The Committee hopes that the scheme, which has been given substantial 
budgetary support, will be initiated as per schedule and the country will be able to reap 
the benefits of the scheme at the earliest. The Committee also appreciates the innovative 
scheme ‘INSPIRE Internship’, which aims  to motivate talented youth to take-up 
research through personal interactions with global icons of science including Nobel 
Prize Winners and recommends that such schemes should be encouraged through 
proper budgetary support.

Rs.2 crores per year to 14 universities base d on objective criteria namely, number of 
publications and H indices, which a global index that attempts to measure both the scientific 
productivity and the apparent scientific impact of a scientist.  
13.9 In reply to a query as regards the lack of funding of  Universi ties in the Northern 
region of the country, under the PURSE progr amme, the Committee was informed that the 
grants are made to the Universities based on the output of publications and Universities 
which have more output, get the grants. 
13.10 The Committee is of the opinion that th e scientific departme nts in the various 
universities across the country suffer from a severe funds crunch and are not able to 
develop their infrastructure which is a serious drawback faced by the students who are 
pursuing a science course. In this direction, schemes such as PURSE have taken a right 
initiative by focusing on the infrastruc ture development of the Universities. The 
Committee recommends that more universities should be provided with grants and that 
such schemes should be extended to the Universities specially in the rural and 
backward areas of the country. The Department  should also explore the possibility of 
expanding the scope of the PURSE funding to st ates, especially the states which have so 
far been left out in the Northern region, through pro-active schemes. 
14. MEGA FACILITIES FOR BASIC RESEARCH  
The Committee was informed that the Basic research in the country has been 
depending upon mega and capital in tensive facilities created by other countries and this 
practice has led to asymmetries in credit sharing.  Further, Indian expertise to build advanced 
scientific instruments and devices does not get fostered outside the strategic areas of research 
where technology denial forces prevents build ing of capacities. The Department along with 
Department of Atomic Energy(DAE) has identifi ed areas where an effective partnership of 
the two departments can bring about an eff ective capacity building in the university and 
academic sector for building mega facili ties for basic resear ch. A Memorandum of 
Understanding has been signed between the Department and DAE. 

14.1 In reply to a query as regards the decrease in allocation to 'Mega facilities for Basic 
Research' from Rs.40.00 crores in B.E. to Rs.20.00 crores in R.E. in the year   2009-2010 and 
also a mere allocation of Rs.30.00 crores made this year, the Department replied that the 
main cause of non-utilisation of the  allocated amount is that one  of the major projects to be 
undertaken under this Scheme viz.  the "Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR)" at 
Darmstadt in Germany, for which India is one of the founding countries and has agreed to 
contribute Rs. 36 million Euros towards its c onstruction, for which the schedule has got 
delayed at the international level itself and, hence, expenditure as regards the Indian 
component could not be made as expected ea rlier and therefore the Department could not 
utilize the allocation under "Mega Facilities for Basic Research". 
14.2 The Department also informed that dur ing 2009-2010, the following activities were 
undertaken under this Scheme – 
 participation in the ALICE (A Large I on Collider Experiment) experiment at 
LHC, CERN, Geneva; 
 participation in the CMS (Compact Muon Solenoid) experiment at LHC, CERN, 
Geneva; 
 participation in the LHC Grid Computing activities at CERN, Geneva. 
During 2009-2010  Rs. 20.00 crores were utilized fo r these activities. It  is expected that 
some of the projects undertak en/to be undertaken in the above schemes would advance 
further or mature for funding during 2010-2011 and, hence, the allocation has been kept at 
Rs. 30.00 crore. 
14.3 The Committee enquired as to why the Ba sic research in the country has been 
depending upon mega and capital in tensive facilities created by other countries and how this 
practice has led to asymmetries in credit sharing.  The Department explained that in the past, 
the resource deployment was meager under the mega-facilities available in the country and 
the scientists had to use the facilities and the t echnologies of the advanced countries and 
those countries used to take cr edit of any invention/innovation in science by Indian scientists 
instead of by our own science intelligentsia. To address this problem the Department has now 
started co-investing and co-generating values an d thereby ensuring that the patent/credits are 
also being equally shared between  the partnering countries and I ndia. This principle is being 
followed as regards the recent agreements of India with the European Union and the United 
States of America. 
14.4 The Committee appreciates the principle of reciprocity and parity adopted by 
the Department as regards the use of mega-faci lities in basic research by our scientists. 
The initiative of the Department will boost th e confidence of our scientists and also lead 
to the acknowledgement of our scientific expertise at an international level. The country 
will also be able to share the credit and the patents on any scientific discovery that 
results from international collaboration.  Although the Committee appreciates the 
partnership between the Department and th e Department of Atomic Energy(DAE) and 
feels that such efforts can develop the much needed capacity building in the university 
and academic sector for building mega facili ties for basic research, it also recommends 
that apart from DAE the partnerships with  other scientific de partments like DBT, 
Earth Sciences, Space and DSIR may also be fostered as the basic research in the 
country is perennially being neglected. The Committee feels that such positive activities 
on the part of the Department needs to be encouraged, and needs to be supported 
through proper budgetary support. 
15. The Committee is of the view that th e Department of Science & Technology 
through its various research and developm ent programmes is striving to uplift the 
standard of living in the country.  Keep ing in view the excellent work that the 

Department has undertaken, the kind of competence it has exhibited and the kind of 
core and critical programmes it has envisage d for the future, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department of Scie nce & Technology should be properly and 
adequately funded and any kind of reduction in  outlay at R.E. stage should be strictly 
avoided.

I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to
 submit the Report on its behalf, present the Twenty first Report, on the Demands for Grants pertaining to the Department of Biotechnology
 (Ministry of Science and Technology) for the year 1995-96 (Demand No. 74).
2. In its meetings held on April 17-18, 1995 the Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology on the
 basis of the documents made available to it and the submission made before it by the Secretary and the other representatives of the
 Department.
3. The Committee thanks the officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Hon'ble Members and placing
 before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology.

REPORT
The Department of Biotechnology (DBT) was set up in 1986. Earlier, the National Biotechnology Board, which was set up by the
 Department of Science and Technology in 1982 coordinated activities in the field of biotechnology. During the last 9 years of its existence
 DBT has been able: to create 16 major infrastructural facilities which serves the large life sciences community in the country; set up 6 centres
 for plant molecular biology-an area of great importance in the future;. initiate and support 32' programmes for teaching and training in
 biotechnology; promote significant research over a broad spectrum of areas in the life sciences; manage two autonomous institutions the
 National Institute of Immunology (NIl), New Delhi and the National Facility for Animal Tissue and Cell Culture (NF A TCC), Pone; setup a
 new institution on DNA Finger Printing; arrange for a network of bioinformatic centres based on computer communications; conduct a
 number of important programmes for demonstration and technology transfer in the areas of oil palm, tissue culture, biofertisers, biopesticides,
 aquaculture, and initiate vaccine research and production. Initially, the Department concentrated on creating several essential infrastructural
 facilities and initiating programmes for Human Resource Development, as well as creating centres of excellence. During the coming two
 years, the last part of the Eighth Plan, the Department plans to focus its attention on supporting large inter ­institutional multi-disciplinary
 projects and those leading to tangible results; rather than creating more new infrastructural facilities which would call for large investments.
2. The Secretary, DBT and the representatives of the Department in their presentation before the Committee gave an account of some of
 the achievements of the Department during the year 1994-95.. The Department has been fulfilling responsibilities towards the National
 Institute of Immunology (NIl), National Facility for Animal Tissue and Cell Culture (NFATCC), International Centre for Genetic Engineering
 and Biotechnology (ICGEB), Bharat Immunologists and Biologicals Corporation Limited (BIBCOL) and Indian Vaccine Corporation Limited
 (IVCOL). The progress of the various programmes of the Department is regularly monitored by experts; in particular the Department has a
 Scientific Advisory Committee and Standing Advisory Committee (Overseas) as also 16 Task Forces. Significant achievements have resulted

 studies. The Department al intends to take up i:e Jnonstrations programmes of proven technologies for reclamation mine dumps and

 Development. T Department also wishes to intensify its work on hatchery development, and feed for prawn, and fish aquaculture. A major
 focus of the Department would be on studies and assess of the environmental impact of aquaculture in different ecological regions.
 Development diagnostic kits and, facilities for diagnosis of shrimp diseases would also be taken up. T Committee was informed about the
 work being done at NII, NF A TCC, and the programm of BIBCOL to product oral polio vaccine. The Centre for DNA Finger Printing to be-
 set at Hyderabad (A.P.) will be jointly implemented by the DBT, Council of Scientific a: Industrial Research (CSIR) and the Ministry of Home
 Affairs (MHA). Regarding ICGE the Committee was informed that the research on diagnostics, plant molecular biology a: vaccine
 development would continue in addition to the training of manpower.
4. After listening to the presentation made by the Secretary DBT and the representation of the Department, the Committee examined the
 budgetary allocation of the Department f the year 1995-96.- While considering the Demands for Grants of the Department, ti Committee also
 got an opportunity to review the work relating to various projects al programmes which fall within the mandate of the Department.
5. The Committee was told that the Department of Biotechnology' had projected demand of Rs, 650 crores for the entire Eighth Five Year Plan
 period. This was lat reduced by the Department itself to Rs. 550 crores. The Planning Commission, during to finalisation of the Eighth Five
 Year Plan, however, indicated an outlay of only Rs. 21 crores for the Department for the period 1992-97. The Department had already spent
 sum of Rs. 244 crores during the first three years of the Eighth Plan thus leaving only Rs. : crores in terms of the initial allocations. Taking
 note of this, a specific question was, askc about the demand projected by DBT for the remaining two years of the Eight Five Ye Plan, during
 the mid-term appraisal of the Eighth Plan. The representative of t) Department informed the Committee that, during the mid-term review, the
 Planning Commission agreed that, based on the progress and the performance of the Department adequate outlays would be provided to the
 Department every year during the Annual Ph discussion. for the year 1995-96 the Department had projected a demand of Rs. 100 crore on the
 Plan side, but a sum of Rs. 90 crores was approved as Plan outlay for to Department. The Committee particularly wanted to know whether this
 reduced plan out would not affect adversely the ongoing programmes of the Department. The Committee w: told that the Department would
 make efforts to use the facilities already created are develop programmes around those facilities. However, for the year 1996-97 the
 Department would be requiring a sum of Rs. 120 crores as it intends to initiate a number of the activities which would culminate ,into large
 projects.
5.1 Analysing the demands of the Department for the entire Eighth Five Year Plan period this Committee had already recommended' in its
 Eighth Report that a sum of Rs. 450 crore may be agreed to for DUT. The Committee, therefore, feels that an outlay of Rs. 450 crore will be
 needed by DUT for the entire Eighth Plan period to implement its ongoing proJec and also generate new projects In important areas. The
 Committee is convened of the need to this after examination the progress made and the importance of the areas concerned.
6. The Committee evinced keen interest in the programmes of the- Department which intend to benefit 'weaker sections.

The Committee was informed that DBT had constituted an expert committee in 1990-91 to generate biotechnology based programmes for the
 benefit of the Scheduled Castes Scheduled Tribes, weaker sections and rural people. Non­governmental organisations, voluntary agencies and
 field level research institutions are actively involved in these programmes. So far 16 projects have been supported, which include programmes
 like fallen carcass utilisation, vermicomposting, mushroom cultivation, biofertilisers, medicinal and aromatic plants, sericulture, etc. As
 regards allocations for various programmes meant to benefit weaker sections, for the year 1995-96, the Committee was told that the allocations
 are adequate. The Department also follows a flexible procedure to adjust and reappropriate if some priority areas emerge.
6.1 The Committee expresses its satisfaction over the fact that the allocation made for the programmes for the weaker sections and rural areas
 in the budget for the year 1995-96 are adequate. It would, however, like to stress that the extension activities which regard to the
 implementation of biotechnology-based programmes for the benefit of SCIST and other weaker sections of society should be strengthened. In
 this regard, DBT has a responsibility to fully demonstrate the potential of biotechnology-based programmes in generating employment and
 income, and also improving the health status of the poor people. DBT will need to coordinate its endeavours with the socio-economic
 ministries and departments in the Central and the State governments in order to increase the acceptance of· its biotechnology-based
 programmes which have a potential of generating income and providing better quality health to the poor.
7. Bharat Immunologicals and Biologicals Corporation Limited (BIBCOL) was incorporated in March 1989 as a Public Sector Company to
 manufacture oral polio vaccine (OPV) and other immunobiologicals. The Committee was told that during the year 1995-96 the target set for

 BIBCOL is production of 100 million doses of oral polio vaccine which would be supplied for use in the national Immunication Programme.

7.1 The Committee expresses., its satisfaction over the fact that BIBCOL has started trial runs for the production of vaccine from bulk. This
 will build up to a 100 million doses during 1995-96. But the real efforts would have to be directed towards manufacture of the vaccine
 preferably by a route not involving monkeys. OPV has an important role to play in the national Immunisation Programme.
8. The Indian Vaccine Corporation Limited (IVCOL) was incorporated as a joint venture company in March 1989 to produce Injectable Polio
 Vaccine (IPV), measles and rabies vaccine using an advanced vero-cell technology, The company has been promoted by DBT, Indian
 Petrochemicals Corporation Limited (IPCL) and Pasteur Merieux Serums and Vaccines (PMSV) , a French Company. The Committee noted
 that the progress of the project relating to IVCOL was rather tardy and wanted to know the reasons for this. The Committee was told that due
 to a basic policy decision taken by Government, IPV would not be introduced into the National Immunisation programme at present; the need
 for large scale production of this through vero-cell technology was not there; hence the project was kept on hold during 1992-93. A negotiating
 committee of the three promoters reviewed the situation and a new product mix was suggested which would still bring in vero-cell technology
 into the country. In January- 1995, the Cabinet had directed that suitable Indian partners bated who will invest in the company and take over
 its management. During the interim period, the French company, (In which the involvement of the French Government was no longer there),
 lost its interest in the project and the transfer of this advanced technology. The progress of the IVCOL project largely depends on the
 finalisation of negotiations which IPCL and PMSV on the vero cell technology transfer and related issues of product mix which can use this
 technology. Already a sum of Rs. 23.47 croreshas been spent on this project which includes the cost of land, site development, indigenous
 equipment and training of personnel, etc.
8.1 The Committee feels that concerted efforts should be made to find suitable Indian partners who are ready to invest in the Company and take
 over its management. Based on the technology transfer from PMSV, the new management should also attempt to· produce OPV with this new
 technology.

 disease burden, particularly among weaker sections of the society of TB, AIDS, filariasis, hepatitis and several other communicable diseases.
 Naturally, this requires low cost, simple, diagnostic methods. This Department has contacted the institutions which have basic expertise in this

 Rota Viral diarrhoeal infection; DNA probe for tuberculosis; Monoclonal antibody based antigen detection test for Kalaazar; lmmunodot
 enzyme staining test for malaria based on detection of parasitic enzyme, studies on Lipoprotein; Immunodiagnostic test for filariasis based on

 Institute (CRI), Bombay, is in fairly advanced stages. By July 1995 the synthetic Peptide test kit based on work at NII would be tested on more

9.1 The Committee appreciates the approach of the Department with regard to the development of immunodiagnostic methods. The Committee
 would, however, like the Department to deal with a variety of communicable and tropical diseases while are common to India and other parts
 of Asia and Africa. If the Department achieve utilize developing low-cost, simple diagnostic methods for detecting various tropical and
 communicable diseases,  one can explore the possibility, of finding a market for these in other countries well there disease burden particularly
 is also very high and of similar nature. One can also explore the possibility of getting these diapostic kits accepted by the World Health
 Organization (WHO) for its various programmes relating to tropical and communicable disease.   In the developing world. This is an area of
 challenge and of opportunity and since the products are mend to be of low cost and large scale use in Public health delivery systems, they are
 unlikely to be of great interest to the multi-national pharmaceutical companies.
10. For the demonstration and transfer of technology, and manufacturing activities, a sum of Rs. 11.5 crores has been provided for the year
 199'5-96 thought D!pu1l11ent had actually demanded a sum of Rs. 13.5 crores. The Committee Wanted to know whether' the shortfall of Rs. 2
 crores between the demand made and demand approved would not affect the activities of the Department in this important area. The
 representative of the Ministry informed the Committee that some major activities like mission-mod projects required a lesser grant during this
 year as most of the non-recurring grants have already been provided for. On a specific query whether the Department could become
 self-.supporting in this area, the Committee was told that this would not be possible. Financial support would certainly be necessary for large
 scale demonstrations. As regards interaction with industry in some specific programmes, where R&D leads have emerged, DBT has been
 collaborating with the industry and involves them at the initial stage itself for validation and field testing. For example, the Department is
 collaborating in regard to programmes for Poultry Development with Godrej; Biofertilizers with SPIC Science Foundation; Diagnostic
 Development with SPAN, cadila, Lupin and Ranbaxy; Vaccine Development for Animals and ,Poultry with BAIF, etc. Industries contribute
 specially for proto-type development and validation of research results.
10.1 The Committee Is of the view that the Department should continue to give higher priority to the area of demonstration and transfer of
 technology; and there should be intense interaction with the industry. In this regard the Committee would like to mention about the projects
 indicated by the Department like desulphurisation of coal, bio-reclamation of mine dumps and biohydrometallurgy for enhanced gold recovery
 from low grade ores, which have a great potential, and industries should be involved in these projects in a more intense manner.

11. In the budget estimates for the year 1994-95, in the area of basic and project-based R&D projects a sum of Rs. 40.60 crores was allocated.
 In the revised estimates the allocation was brought down to Rs. 39.75 crores. Last year the Department had projected a demand of Rs. 50.43
 crores under this head, but this year only a sum of Rs. 43 crores was demanded and the Department could get only Rs. 42 crores. The
 Committee wanted to know whether this area is receding in the priorities of the Department. The Committee was told that, last year, a higher
 allocation was demanded because the Department wanted to set up some major facilities like X-ray crystallography, FTNMR, etc. In the
 projected  demand for this year no such new major facility is included. The outlay earmarked for the year 1995­96 would be used for
 supporting R&D projects in identified areas. DBT has already set up with DST and CSIR certain joint facilities and there are some other
 proposals in the pipeline. The Department is encouraging joint proposals. The Committee was told of the example of the Food Biotechnology
 Programme of the Department which has been supported with 50% contribution from the Ministry of Food Processing Industries.
11.1 The Committee is happy to note that the Department Is making efforts to generate more joint projects with ICMR, ICAR, various other
 Ministries of Government and industry. The NMR faculty has been set up jointly by the Department with SPIC Science Foundation, with 50%
 contribution from SPIC. The Committee rmds that the concept of joint facilities, particularly in areas which involve very large outlays is
 praiseworthy. The Committee also appreciates the efforts made by the Department in generating certain joint projects. The Department should,
 however, see that the joint facilities which are set up in high-tech areas should be optimally utilised by the scientific· institutions.
12. During the course of its examination, the Committee mentioned to the Department that Issue Culture Technology has a great potential. At
 present, tissue culture material that is made available to fanners and entrepreneurs is costly. The Committee, therefore, wanted to know about
 the steps the Department proposes to take to reduce the costs. The Committee was told that the main advantage of using tissue culture
 technology for large scale production of biomass is to have high quality planting materials with desirable traits.
The Department admitted that the cost of Tissue Culture Technology is relatively high. The representatives of the Department, however,
 mentioned that special studies have been initiated at the pilot plants in Tata Energy Research Institute (TERI) and the National Chemical
 Laboratories (NCL) to reduce the cost.
12.1 The Committee appreciates the studies being carried out for reducing the cost of high quality planting material obtained through Tissue
 Culture Technology; it would like the Department to make more vigorous efforts in this direction. Because of the high cost of the material,
 small farmers are not able to use it. If the cost of planting material, obtained through Tissue Culture Technology, is reduced, it would help in a
 big way .in the afforestation programme of the Government also.
13. Aquaculture is becoming very popular in the coastal areas. The Committee evinced keen interest in the aquaculture programme of the
 Department. Under the programme 'Basic and Product-based R&D Projects', the Committee noted that for aquaculture and marine
 biotechnology an outlay of Rs. 1.5 crores has been made in this year's budget. But under the programme Demonstration/transfer of Technology
 and Manufacturing Activities' in this year's budget the allocation for aquaculture has been reduced to Rs. 2 crores from the earlier year's Rs.
 3.15 crores, though this programme is in the mission mode. The Committee wanted to know as to how the Department proposes to promote
 prawn culture in the coastal region with the reduced allocation, particularly when the feed and the seed has to be made available to fish farmers
 at a reasonable price. The Committee also wanted to know the efforts being made by the Department to develop indigenous feed and help in
 installing hatcheries.
13.1 The Committee was informed that under aquaculture and marine biotechnology, two broad categories of programmes are supported,
 namely, R&D as well as the mission­ mode demonstration projects. For 1995-96, for R&D component, Rs. 1.5 crores have been· provided,
 and for the mission-mode project, Rs. 2 crores have been provided, which is as per the EFC provision. Generally, in the first year of the
 project, 60% of the grant for non­recurring purposes is released. Therefore, in the second year, the expenditure becomes less. The mission-
mode project has been formulated in consultation with the Ministries of Agriculture and Commerce. The total cost is Rs. 9.9 crores for 7 sites;
 the sites in the coastal regions are A&N Islands, West Bengal, Gujarat and Pondicherry. The research results from the R&D component would
 be incorporated. into the mission-mode project. For example, the indigenous feed development under R&D world be tried out in the mission-
mode programme. The total provision for aquaculture during 1995-96 is Rs. 3.5 crores.
13.2 The Committee is of the view that. there is an immense possibility for brackish water prawn culture in the coastal areas of India. To
 achieve the goal, feed and seed at reasonable price have to be made available easily to the prospective fish farmers at their door-steps. To do
 the DBT must take necessary measures to develop the indigenous feed arad to help install hatcheries in required areas.
14. Patenting in the area of life sciences is a very complex problem. It is very different from what obtains in the other fields of science and
 technology. The developments calling for patenting are relatively new, involve many ethical issues and are highly uncertain in interpretation.
 The Committee wanted to know the specific steps that are being taken by the Department on Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) related matters
 in its area of mandate.
14.1 The Committee was told that DBT would provide necessary support to strengthen the Patenting Cell in the Council of Scientific and
 Industrial Research (CSIR) which would help Indian scientists in obtaining patents in the area of biotechnology. The Industry Division in DBT
 has been designated to deal with all patent issues. Support would be provided by DBT for filing patents nationally and internationally; and the
 contingency grant for research projects that can lead to patents would be enhanced suitably. Efforts have also been made, and would be further
 strengthened, to build awareness, disseminate information and organise training programmes for patent-related matters as applicable to
 biological research. The Department is also closely working with the Ministry of Industry on patent related issues.
14.2 While the Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department in the area of IPR, it would, however, like to reiterate the
 recommendation made in its Seventeenth Report the DBT should have a group of its own to suggest how India should develop its strength and
 expertise in the area of IPR in biological sciences. The Department should earmark necessary funds to support this activity, including for filing
 of patents and intensive activity relating to awareness building and training on IPR related matters.
15. Biotechnology is a frontier area of science. The work presented by the Department clearly brings out the highly scientific and technical

  REPORT 
 Over the past few decades, a major cause of concern for countries across the 
world has been the rapid deterioration of  the environment caused mainly due to 
massive deforestation, ever increasing po llution resulting in global warming and 
climate changes.  Fast pace of developm ent and industrial growth has offset the 
delicate balance of nature.  To address these concerns, Ministry of Environment & 
Forests was created in 1985 as the nodal agency for planning, promotion and 
coordination of environment and forestry programmes. The Ministry of Environment 
& Forests is engaged in implementation of policies and programmes relating to 
conservation of the country' s natural resources, including lakes and rivers, its 
biodiversity, forests and wild life, ensuring the welfare of animals and prevention and 
abatement of pollution.  These tasks ar e being carried out through environment 
impact assessment, eco-regeneration, as sistance to organizations implementing 
environmental and forestry programmes, en actment of environmental legislation, 
formulation of environmenta l policies, promotion of environmental and forestry 
research, education and training to  augment the requisite manpower, and 
dissemination of environmental awarenes s among all sections of the country’s 
population. 
2. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP 
2.1  The attached/subordinate offices/ Autonomous organizations, etc. of the 
Ministry, for which provision has been made in the Demands for Grants for the year 
2010-11 are as follows:    
 Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata 
 Zoological Survey of India, Kolkata 
 National Museum of Natural History, New Delhi 
 Indira Gandhi National Forestry Academy, Dehradun 
 State Forest Service and Rangers College, Dehradun 

  
 Forest Survey of India, Dehradun 
 Central Pollution Control Board, New Delhi 
 G.B. Pant Himalayan Environment Evam Vikas Sansthan, Almora 
 Indian Council of Forestry Research & Education, Dehradun 
 Indian Institute of Forestry Management, Bhopal 
 Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun 
 Central Zoo Authority, New Delhi  
 Indian Plywood Industries Research Institute, Bangalore. 
 National Tiger Conservation Authority, New Delhi 
 Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, New Delhi 
 National Biodiversity Authority, Chennai 
 Animal Welfare Board of India, Chennai 
 National Institute of Animal Welfare, Faridabad 
3. MONITORING AND REVIEWING THE PROGRESS OF ONGOING 
SCHEMES 
3.1 The Committee was informed that the Ministry has a well developed 
monitoring mechanism.  Its schemes/projects are monitored regularly in Headquarters 
and by on the spot field visits by officials. Senior officers visit the states regularly and 
monitor progress of scheme s/programmes through the mechanism of nodal officers 
under which each state/UT has been assigned  a senior officer as its nodal officer for 
regular interaction with stat e/UT.  Monitoring process, inter alia, include mandatory 
audit of accounts of grantee organizati on, submission of audited utilization 
certificates, expenditure statement and a progress report on the activities conducted 
by the grantee organization besi des field visits by officers of the Ministry. Research 
projects are monitored/ reviewed by th e concerned Expert Review Committees. 
Regional offices of the Ministry also review/monitor and follow up on various 
issues/programmes in the environment, forestry and wildlife sectors.   
3.2 Under forestry, a multi level monitori ng and evaluation system of projects is 
being pursued under National Afforestatio n Programme (NAP). This includes 
intensive review of projects at the state and central levels by the State Level 
Coordination Committee and National Leve l Coordination Committee. Performance 
of the schemes is also reviewed regula rly by the Secretary by convening meetings 
with senior officers of the Ministry.  Pla nning Commission also conducts half yearly 
review meetings with the Ministry, to moni tor progress of vari ous schemes/projects. 
Proposals received in the Ministry are thor oughly examined, both in-house and also 
through external evaluators like independent experts, peer review, expert committees 
etc., before being posed for funding to the Planning Commission.  
3.3 The Committee observes that despit e such a strong looking monitoring 
mechanism, the utilisation trend of the approved outlay for the 10 th Five Year Plan, 
i.e., 2002-2007 of the Ministry has not been very encouraging.  The actual 
expenditure of the Ministry during this Plan  Period remained at Rs. 5114.58 crores as 
against the actually allocated outlay of Rs . 5723.84 crores.  Although, the overall 
utilisation was 90 per cent, it varied from 86 .85 per cent in 2004-05 to 95.76 per cent 
in 2002-03.  The reasons attributed to th e gap between outlays and expenditure are 
more or less procedural and administrativ e in nature, i.e., delays in approval of 
schemes, change in financial pattern of schemes, implementing agencies being State 
Governments/various Departme nts, delays in receipts of proposals, acquisition of 
land, submission of utilisation certificates, etc.

9. NATIONAL AFFORESTATION AND ECO-DEVELOPMENT 
PROGRAMME 
  9.1 The National Afforestation and Ec o-development Board was set up in 1992 
with the principal aim of promoting afforestat ion, tree planting, ecological restoration 
and eco-development in the country.  Sp ecial attention is being given to the 
regeneration of degraded forest areas and la nds adjoining forest areas, national parks, 
sanctuaries and other protected areas as well  as the ecologically fragile areas like the 
Western Himalayas, Aravallis, Western Ghats, etc.  Main schemes under this 
programme are National Afforestation Sche me, Greening India and National Action 
Programme to Combat Desertification. Th e implementation of the United Nations’ 
Convention to Combat Desertification and So cial Forestry are also covered under the 
ongoing schemes. 
9.2 The total-plan and non-plan budgetary allocation for this programme during 
the year 2009-10 was Rs. 330.62 crores at  B.E. stage which was reduced to Rs. 
279.12 crores at R.E. stage. The budgetary allocation for the year 2010-11 has been 
further reduced to Rs. 274.50 crores.  When the Committee enquired about the 
reasons for reduction in outlays, the Ministry  informed that due to less allocation of 
funds to the Ministry the allocation for National Afforestation Programme (NAP) was 
reduced at the R.E. in 2009-10, similarly, for the year 2010-11 the allocation for NAP 
has been curtailed on account of budgetary constraints.  
9.3 When the Committee asked about the current position of the forest and 
tree cover in the country, the Ministry replied that it is 23.84 per cent of the total 
geographical area of the country as per the India State of Forest Report, 2009 
which includes 21.02 per cent forest cover and 2.82 per cent tree cover.  When 
the Committee enquired from the Ministry as to whether the present forest 
cover of 23.84 is inclusive or exclusive of the forest land diverted during the year 

  
2009,  it was informed that the position of forest cover given is as in December, 
2007, so it does not include the area which is lost or going to be lost by way of 
diversion.  The Committee is of the opin ion that two years time lag in working 
out the state of forest report is too long a period.  On a query that whether it is 
possible to reduce this two years period  to one year, the Ministry agreed to 
reduce this period to one year. 
10.  CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY  
10.1 The Committee feels that massive afforestation is very important. Every 
year, the Ministry of Environment and Forests should have a target of increasing 
the forest cover. But for this massive a fforestation, the huge financial resources 
are required and the Ministry cannot afford to undertake afforestation on a 
large scale in the absence of funds/resources. The Committee finds that in our 
country, Banks, Public Sector Undertakings, major industries in public and 
private sectors have the corporate social responsibility as an obligation to spend 
certain resources out of their profits as Corporate Social Responsibility towards 
the welfare of the society. The Committee feels that if the Government makes it 
mandatory that 50 per cent of the mone y being spent towards corporate social 
responsibility for the massive afforestation   under the guidance of the Ministry 
of Environment and Forests, the millions of hectares of land will be covered by 
forests. At the same time, the Government need not worry for any resources and 
the Ministry of Environment and Forest also not to worry about the funds since 
the Corporate world is already spending by way of corporate social 
responsibility towards welfare activities. Therefore, the Committee strongly 
recommends to the Government of India th rough the Parliament that they must 
make it mandatory to spend 50 percent of their profit on the afforestation under 
the control of the Ministry of Environment and Forests.    
11. PANCHAYAT VAN YOJANA 
11.1 As regards peoples’ participation in afforestation, the Committee finds that 
Panchayat Van Yojana (social forestry with communities), which was originally 
conceived in the very first year of the 11
th Five Year Plan and an outlay of Rs. 900 
crores was earmarked for the en tire Five Year Plan period , this programme is yet to 
take off.  The Committee feels that under this programme, a component of the 
National Afforestation and Ec o-Development Programme, it had been envisaged that 
funds would be released directly to the Pa nchayats.  The Committee is of the opinion 
that such a good programme which has enough sc ope to add to the forest cover of the 
country is suffering due to administrative la xity. The Committee finds that even after 
the lapse of three long years, the Minist ry of Environment & Forests has not been 
successful in launching the programme as it is still awaiting the approval of the 
Cabinet Committee on Econo mic Affairs (CCEA). The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that this programme should be made operational at the earliest and 
the obstacles coming in the way must be expeditiously removed.   
12. AFFORESTATION IN CHINA VIS-À-VIS INDIA 
12.1 The Committee enquired the Ministry regarding the China' s massive plan of 
bringing millions of he ctares of land under afforestat ion scheme and its comparative 
study with that of corresponding programme in India.  
12.2 The Committee was informed that China promulgated a Law in 1981 which 
requires that every citizen over the age of 11  plant at least one tree per year. As a 
result, China currently has the highest affore station rate in the world i.e., about 4.55 
million hectare per year.   

  
12.3 The Committee feels that in or der to achieve a task of gigantic 
proportions, i.e., massive afforestatio n some bold and dynamic decisions are 
required.  The Committee is of the view that the Ministry may also workout 
some modalities to ensure voluntary participation of citizens in the afforestation 
programme.  The Ministry may also thin k in terms of making it a fundamental 
duty of every citizen of the country over the age of 18, to plant one tree every 
year.  Massive awareness pr ogramme particularly among the children to make 
them understand the imperatives of planting and protecting trees would also go 
a long way in realizing the national goal of  bringing one third of the area under 
forest and tree cover.   
13. WILDLIFE PRESERVATION 
13.1 Under Wildlife Preservation, the Mi nistry provides fina ncial and technical 
support to the State Governments for the development of National Parks & Wildlife 
Sanctuaries under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme, i.e., ‘Assistance for Development 
of National Parks and Sanctu aries’. Financial assistan ce is also provided for 
management and conservation of habitat of wildlife in protected areas and for wildlife 
research to institutions, universities and NGOs. Grants are also provided to strengthen 
four Regional Offices located at Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata & Chennai and three Sub-
regional Offices located at Ko chi, Guwahati & Amritsar which have been set up to 
check illegal trade in wildlife and wildlif e products and for better enforcement of 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, Convention on Trade in Endangered Species on Wild fauna 
and Flora (CITES), etc. 
13.2 For the year 2010-11, a total budgetary provision both plan and non-plan, 
Rs.301.36 crores has been made for this programme of wildlife preservation. The 
Committee enquired from the Ministry that whether the activities pursued under this 
programme are proving productive in preservi ng the wildlife. In re sponse to this, the 
Committee was informed that the Wildlife scheme, particularly, the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme-'Integrated Wildlife of Development Habitats' was modified 
during 2008-09 by adding more components like Protection of Wildlife Outside 
Protected Areas and Recovery Programmes for saving critically endangered species 
and habitats to strengthen Wildlife Conservation, habitat improvement and 
infrastructure development. During 2008- 09 the Ministry initiated recovery 
programme for endangered species like Ha ngul, Snow leopard and Vulture in Jammu 
& Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh,  Haryana and Punjab. During the year 
2009-10, three endangered species namely Manipur brow, antlered deer, Swiftlet Nest 
and Nilgiri Tahr have been covered under th e scheme. It is proposed to include other 
endangered species in the financial year 2010-11. Financial assi stance was provided 
for Protection of wildlife outside protecte d areas in States namely Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab last year.   However, due to reduction of fund at R.E. 
stage this year no financial assistance could be provided to States for protection of 
wildlife outside protected areas.   
13.3 The Committee observes that the over all budgetary provision under this head 
for this year is less as compared to the last year B.E. allocation of Rs. 340.77 and R.E. 
allocation of Rs. 329.39 crores.  The Committee fails to u nderstand that at a time 
when wildlife related crimes are on the rise, wildlife animals are coming out of the 
protected areas and mercilessly killed, th e number of endangered species is on the 
rise, reduction in budgetary alloca tions does not augur well.  The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that this programme may not be allowed to suffer due to 
shortage of funds and the Ministry of Environment & Forests should vigorously 

  
take up this matter with Ministry of Fi nance to increase allocation under this 
head appropriately at the R.E. stage.   
13.4 The National Tiger Conservation Au thority (NTCA), a statutory body under 
the Ministry of Environment and Forests has been constituted under the Wildlife 
(Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 200 6, for strengthening tiger conservation.  
‘Project Tiger’ is a Centrall y Sponsored Scheme of the Mi nistry of Environment and 
Forests, providing funding support to tiger range States, for in-situ conservation of 
tigers in designated tiger reserves. 
13.5 The Committee has been informed that the National Tiger Conservation 
Authority, constituted in 2006 has been successful in fulf illing its mandate.  Project 
Tiger has put the endangered tiger on an a ssured path of recovery by saving it from 
extinction, as revealed by the recent findi ngs of the All India tiger estimation using 
the refined methodology.  This independent report also highlights the achievement of 
Project Tiger by showing that  viable tiger population exis ts only in Project Tiger 
areas under the jurisdiction of Project Tige r, while outside populations are highly 
depleted.  Many major policy initiatives have been taken on the tiger front for 
improving the infrastructure in tiger reserves, besides strengthening the field delivery.   
13.6 During the year 2009-10, the budgetary allocation for Project Tiger was of Rs. 
184.83 crores at B.E. stage and was reduced  to Rs. 179.53 crores at R.E. stage. For 
the year 2010-2011, it has been reduced fu rther to Rs. 154.20 crores. The Ministry 
was enquired in this regard and it info rmed that the National Tiger Conservation 
Authority (NTCA) receives funding support for performing its functions through the 
ongoing Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Project Tiger.  Reduction in allocation of RE 
2009-10 and BE 2010-11 in respect of the sche me is due to reduction in overall RE 
2009-10 and BE 2010-11 of the Ministry.  It was informed further that Annual Plan 
(2010-11) demand for the scheme was project ed to Rs. 609.30 crores against which 
reduced funds have been allocated.  
13.7 The Committee has been further informed that the Ministry has taken up 
number of steps – legal, administrative a nd financial for protection of tigers.  8 new 
tiger reserves have been declared and for 4 new reserves, namely, Sahyadri in 
Maharashtra, Pilibhit in Uttar Pradesh, Rata pani in Madhya Pradesh and Sunabeda in 
Orissa, in principal approval has been accorded.  The relocation/rehabilitation 
package for people living in core or critical  tiger habitats has been enhanced from Rs. 
1 lakh/family to Rs. 10 lakhs/ family for 13 tiger reserves.  Crea tion of Special Tiger 
Protection Force (STPF) has also been approved and Rs. 93 lakhs each has been 
released to Corbett, Ranthambore and D udhwa Tiger Reserves for creation of STPF 
during 2008-09.  The Ministry further informed the Committee that Central assistance 
will be provided to States for creation of STPF in remaining 10 tiger reserves during 
2009-10.  The Committee was also informed that the guidelines of the STPF have 
also been revised for deploying various pers onnel in place of police with scope for 
involving local people like the Van Gujjars.   However, the actual expenditure 
physical targets and achievements for the year 2008-09 and 2009- 10 does not reflect 
anywhere if the Special Tiger Protection Force for which Rs. 93 lakhs each had been 
released in 2008-09 and the Cen tral assistance proposed to be released in remaining 
10 tiger reserves in 2009-10 has been created  or not.  As such the Committee fails to 
ascertain the actual position as regards the creation of Special Tiger Protection Force.   
13.8 The Committee observes that in the recent past the Similipal Tiger Reserve in 
Orissa was disturbed on acc ount of left wing extremism.  During the interaction with 
the officials of the Ministry, the Commi ttee enquired about the steps taken by the 
Ministry regarding the naxalite problem in the Similipal Tiger Reserve. The 

  
Committee was informed that  a Special Crack Team was sent to the reserve from the 
NTCA for an appraisal, and it was found th at there was considerable damage to 
infrastructure, habitat and occupancy of ti gers has been reduced in the Northern 
Similipal. It has been felt by the Ministry that there is need for initiating scientific 
monitoring of tiger prey and relocation of villages from the core/critical tiger habitat 
is needed to be expedited. The Ministry has written to the Chief Minister in this 
regard with a request for rebuilding th e damaged infrastructure of Similipal, 
strengthening protection, expediting village relocation and filling up the vacant posts 
(out of a total sanctioned staff strength of 281 in Similipal, as many as 101 are 
vacant) and redeployment of some CRPF personnel for the Tiger Reserve. It is also 
requested to expedite the constitution of the Special Tiger Protection Force, prepare a 
special plan for the buffer zone to pr ovide livelihood options to local people, 
expediting the creation of the reserve sp ecific Tiger Conservation Foundation and 
placing the buffer of Simlipal under the administrative control of the Field Director. 
13.9 The Committee is surprise to note  the way the budgetary allocation has 
been made in respect of  Project Tiger for the current financial year. The 
projected demand of Rs. 609.30 crores has been reduced by the Planning 
Commission to just Rs. 154.20 crores.  The Committee recommend that Planning 
Commission should agree to the Ministry's demand for more funds at R.E. stage 
under the scheme as the same is extremely important to deal effectively with the 
depleting number of Asian cats in the country.   
13.10 The Committee further recommends th at since it is centrally sponsored 
programme, it is necessary to have a strong monitoring mechanism to ensure 
proper utilisation of funds.  The Committee also recommends that achievement 
of physical targets must be carefully and clearly reflected by the Ministry in 
future so that the Committee could get an objective picture of Ministry’s 
performance.   
13.11 The Committee notes that around 35 % of sanctioned staff strength is 
vacant in the Similipal Tiger Reserve despite the fact that the Reserve is afflicted 
with naxal extremism.  The Committee ac knowledges the fact that the Ministry 
has taken action in this regard and has requested the Chief Minister of the 
concerned State to take appropriate action, however it feels that the Ministry 
being the nodal agency for the protection and preservation of w ildlife, it should 
vigorously pursue the matter of filling up  of the vacant posts with the State 
Government and ensure that the sufficient CRPF or paramilitary staff is posted 
in the Reserve to tackle the menace of naxalism.  
14. PREVENTION OF POLLUTION OF NATIONAL RIVERS  
14.1 The Committee has been informed that the scope of the erstwhile scheme 
“Prevention and Control of pollution of Ri ver Ganga” has been widened to cover all 
national rivers and lakes and hence this sc heme has been renamed as “Prevention of 
Pollution of National Rivers and Lakes”.  U nder this scheme, an action plan has been 
drawn up for cleaning the polluted stretches of National Rivers and to oversee its 
implementation.  The major work relates to (i) interception a nd diversion of raw 
sewage water from flowing into rivers through  open drains; (ii) treatment of sewage 
water through setting up of sewage treatment plants; (iii) other sanitation measures, 
such as construction of low cost san itation, electric crematorium, river front 
development works, afforestation on rive r works, etc.  The National Ganga River 
Basin Authority (NGRBA) has been set up as an empowered planning, financing, 
monitoring and coordinating authority for the Ganga River.  

  
14.2  The Committee observes that the Budget allocation for the year 2009-10 was 
revised from Rs.562.33 crore at BE stage to  Rs.413.28 crore at RE stage.  When the 
Committee enquired as to why this happened,  it was informed by the Ministry that 
this revision was due to reduction in allocation for Nationa l Ganga River Basin 
Authority (NGRBA) from Rs.250.00 crore at BE stage to Rs.100.00 crore at RE 
stage.  This revision took place mainly because the Budget announcement on 
allocation for this authority was made in  July 2009 and the detailed Budget head was 
created in August 2009. 
14.3 The Committee finds that for the year  2010-11, an increased allocation of Rs. 
729.64 crore has been made.  The increase as  informed by the Ministry is mainly due 
to increase in the allocation for NGRBA from Rs.100 crore (RE) for the year 2009-10 
to Rs.500 crore for the year 2010-11.  Th e Committee was also informed that the 
Budgetary allocation for National Lake C onservation Plan (NLCP) has also been 
marginally increased from Rs.45 crore (RE)  for the year 2009-10 to Rs.50 crore for 
the year 2010-11.  
14.4 When the Committee enquired about th e status of the constitution of the 
National Ganga River Basin Au thority, it was informed that it has already been 
constituted.  It is chaired by the Prime Minister and Members include some Union 
Ministers, as well as, the Chief Ministers of five States.  This is a high level body and 
is a part of National River Conservation Plan.   
 14.5 The Committee further desired to know from the Ministry as to how much 
money has been spent on Ganga Action Pl an and in what manner National Ganga 
River Basin Authority is different from Ganga Action Plan.  The Ministry replied that 
the Ganga Action Plan was very narrow in its focus as it concentrated on point source 
of pollution, i.e., industrial effluent and sewage and sewerage.  The present 
programme will have a river basin approach  based on four principals, i.e., a river 
must flow, a river is not a drain, a river mu st have space and a river is an ecological 
entity.  It was also informed that roughly an amount of Rs. 900 crores have been spent 
on Ganga Action Plan I and Ganga  Action Plan II.  It was also informed that some 
spillover projects under Ganga Action Plan II are still going on. 
14.6 The Committee feels that despite a huge amount of money spent and whatever 
efforts made thus far under Ganga Action Plan I & II to clean the river Ganga, there 
has not been any considerable improvement in  the water quality of the river Ganga.  
The Committee is happy to note that the Government has initiated a new action to 
clean the river Ganga and allocated a substa ntial amount for this purpose.  It is, 
however, of the opinion that only money is not going to matter much unless and until, 
there is a major change in the strategy.  So  far the Ministry’s main focus had been on 
setting up of sewerage treatment plants, common effluent plants, but the Committee 
feels that this strategy has not worked to the desired level.  Flowing of untreated 
sewage and sewerage, open dr ains and industrial effluent  are still continuing on a 
large-scale.  Sewage treatment plants are not working to their optimum capacity due 
to one reason or the other.  With the ev er increasing load of population on urban 
areas, this problem would further aggravate.   The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry must work mainly on the principal that river must flow.  The 
Committee, therefore, further recommends that besides taking remedial 
measures like setting up of sewage trea tment plants, common effluent treatment 
plants, etc., it must also ensure that the flow of the river Ganga is maintained on 
the level of the flow that was there 10 or 20 years back.   

  
15.  YAMUNA ACTION PLAN (YAP) 
15.1 The Yamuna Action Plan (YAP), a b ilateral project between the Government 
of India and Japan to carry out the task of pollution abatement works of the river 
Yamuna is in its second phase.  Its first phase has been completed with the creation of 
a total of 753 mld sewage treatment capacity in  2003.  It is one of the largest river 
restoration projects in India.  The Committee has been informed that YAP II has been 
approved at an estimated cost of Rs. 624 crores for abatement of pollution of river 
Yamuna in Delhi, Uttar Prad esh (eight Towns) and Haryana (six towns). The cost of 
the works is to be shared between Central and the State Governments in the ratio of 
85:15. As per the Ministry a sewage treatme nt capacity of 189 mld is targeted to be 
created besides major rehabilitation/replacement works for sewers and other pollution 
abatement works. So far thirty one pollution abatement schemes have been sanctioned 
at a cost of Rs. 647.86 crore, out of whic h seven schemes have been completed and 
others are in different stages of progress. 
15.2 The Committee observes that the path etic condition of Yamuna River is for 
everybody to see despite all the claims of the Ministry and completion of Yamuna 
Action Plan-I and ongoing Yamuna Action Plan -II and 100 crores of rupees having 
been spent on Yamuna Action Plan.  The Committee feels that the answer to clean the 
Yamuna is not in building more sewage tr eatment capacity or more drains because it 
is expensive to build sewerage drainage a nd even more expensive to maintain them.  
Most of these treatment plants remain gro ssly underutilized because the city does not 
have drainage to convey all sewage to th e treatment plants and hence these plants 
remain grossly underutilized.  The Committee is of the view that despite best of the 
efforts it would not be possible to treat th e entire sewerage flowing into the river and 
hence recommends that the Ministry should look for alternative measures to clean the 
river.  The Committee is of the view that a steady supply of fresh water in the 
river is urgently required.  The Committee in its 188
th Report on Demands for 
Grants, 2008-09 of the Ministry had rec ommended that a proper system should 
be setup for recharging the river by creating manmade water bodies like 
reservoir and catchment areas which can store the monsoon water which usually 
goes into drains and the stored water can be released into the river during the 
lean season.  The Committee also note that most of the catchment area of the 
river Yamuna has been diverted for purposes other than creating reservoirs.  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that a result oriented time bound 
approach should be adopted with regard to the cleaning of river Yamuna.   
16. CLIMATE CHANGE  
16.1 The Committee observes that recen tly Intergovernmental Panel on Climate 
Change (IPCC) Report on projected loss of Himalayan glaciers by 2035 had created a 
lot of confusion and finally it was settle d that the projection made by IPCC in its 
Report cannot be corroborated by scientific evidences.  But the Committee finds that 
the Department of Space has in it s Annual Report 2009-10 mentioned that 
investigations on glacial retreat were es timated for 1317 glaciers in 10 sub-basins 
from 1962 and this has shown an overall reduction in glacial area from 5866 Sq. 
Kms. to 4921 Sq. Kms. showing an overall decrease of 16 per cent.  When the 
Committee enquired in what manner the Ministry would be able to handle the climate 
change project with a paltry allocation of Rs. 7.00 crores, it was informed that this 
project is meant to protect India’s intere sts on climate change issues in various 
international fora and faci litate India’s participation in various international 
negotiations.  Thus, the Committee finds that there is no specific and exclusive 
programme on climate change with the Minist ry which is dealing with environment.  

  
The Committee, therefore, recommends that since the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests is the nodal Ministry, it mu st have a programme on climate change 
with sufficient budgetary allocations.   
17. PREVENTION OF AIR AND WATER POLLUTION 
17.1  The Committee finds that there has been substantial decrease in the allocation 
of funds under the Prevention of Air and Wate r Pollution.  As against the allocation 
of Rs. 140.25 crores at B.E. and Rs. 270.42 crores at R.E. stage in the year 2009-10, 
this year it has been reduced to Rs. 63.90 crores.   When the Committee enquired the 
Ministry in this regard it was informed that the increase in allocation at R.E stage in 
the year 2009-10 is primarily due to provisi on of Rs.128.16 crores for water cess 
reimbursement to State Pollution Cont rol Boards (SPCBs)/Pollution Control 
Committees (PCCs) and Central Pollution  Control Board (CPCB). 
17.2 When the Committee asked whether th e amount allocated would be sufficient 
to support the programme, the Ministry replie d that the funds allocated would not be 
sufficient to carry out the activities of the Ministry. The Ministry further stated that 
they had in fact asked for more allocation which has not been accepted.   
18. HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCE MANAGEMENT  
18.1 Hazardous waste, bulk of which is generated by the industries, can cause 
environmental pollution and adverse hea lth effects if not handled and managed 
properly. Its effective management, with em phasis on minimizati on of its generation 
and recycling/reuse taking in to account economic aspects, is therefore essential. 
Various actions have been taken to manage  hazardous wastes in the country, which 
include establishing a regulatory and institutional framework, preparation of technical 
guidelines, development of indi vidual and common facilities for recycle/ recovery/ 
reuse, treatment and disposal  of hazardous wastes, prepar ation of an inventory of 
hazardous wastes generation, identification and assessment of hazardous waste dump 
sites for the purpose of preparing remedi ation plans and creating awareness amongst 
various stakeholders. 
18.2 The Committee was informed that during 2009-10, under Hazardous 
Substance Management Schemes, the BE was Rs.17.50 crores which was decreased 
to Rs.7.75 crores at RE stage. It was because under this scheme a provision of 
Rs.10.00 crore was kept in the BE for the Externally Aided Project namely Capacity 
Building for Industrial Pollution Manageme nt Project (CBIPMP). This provision was 
predominantly for implementation phase of  the project. However, the process of 
seeking approval of CCEA and negotiati on with the World Bank could not be 
completed as scheduled during 2009-10. In view of this, RE fo r this project was 
reduced to Rs.0.25 crores, to be used for preparation phase only. Hence the total RE 
is Rs.7.75 crores.   
18.3 It was informed further that the budget allocation for 2010-11 has been 
increased to Rs.32.50 crores against Rs.7 .75 crores RE of 2009-10 in respect of 
Hazardous Substance Management Scheme. The reason for increasing the allocation 
during 2010-11 as compared to the year 2009-10 is the provision of Rs.25.00 crores 
for implementation of CBIPM Pr oject. All pending issues re lated to the project have 
now been resolved and a Note for approva l of CCEA has been sent to the Cabinet 
Secretariat. Implementation of the project will start during 2010-11.  
18.4 For maintaining the eco-system and k eeping in view the climate changes 
and protection of environment and also conservation of forests, the Ministry 
must emphasise and make all efforts to collect full informations and 
clarifications by the concerned Departments and Ministries and if necessary, 
hold regular meetings with the stakeholders in the interest of the Indian 

  
economy. In solving the various issues pending with the Ministry, better 
coordination and cooperation is need of the hour and at the same time the 
Ministry must take final decisions as early as possible while giving permissions 
for the proposals/projects or  rejecting the same. While doing so the Ministry 
must take pains to minimise the delays in giving the clearances to other 
Ministries as quickly as possible. 
18.5 The Committee observes that the rapid industrial developments have led 
to the generation of huge quantities of hazardous wastes which have further 
aggravated the environmental problems  in the country by depleting and 
polluting natural resources. Rational an d sustainable utilization of natural 
resources and its protection from toxic releases is vital for sustainable socio-
economic development. Hazardous substance management involves planning 
and overseeing the implementation of  the policies and programmes. The 
Committee recommends that to attain success under this programme Ministry 
should ensure implementation of efficient plans for management of hazardous 
wastes, environmentally sound manageme nt and active promotion of cleaner 
technologies. 
18.6 The Committee is of the view th at increasing population, rapid 
industrialization, growing urbaniza tion, etc. over the years has made 
tremendous impact on environment.  Th e prevention and control of pollution 
measures have not been commensurate with the pace of adverse impact on 
environment.  The responsibility and wo rkload of the Ministry of Environment 
& Forests whose primary concern is the implementation of policies and 
programmes relating to conservation of the country's natural resources, 
biodiversity, forests and wildlife, the welfare of animals and prevention and 
abatement of pollution has also increased accordingly manifold.  Hence, there is 
a need to correspondingly enhance the manpower, scientific capabilities and 
expertise of the Ministry.  The Committee is of the view that these issues need to 
be urgently addressed. Therefore, it is of the view that the Ministry's manpower 
and infrastructure must be strengthened and augmented.  The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that th e Ministry of Environment and Forests 
should be properly and adequately funded.

PREFACE 
           I, the Chairman of the De partment-related Parliament ary Standing Committee on 
Science & Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorized by the Committee to 
present the Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred and Eleventh Report on ‘The 
Protection and Utilisation of Public Funded Intellectual Property Bill, 2008’. 
2.       In the meetings of the Committee held on the 17 th & 24th December, 2009, 5th January, 8th 
February and 2 nd June, 2010; Secretaries of the Depart ments of Bio-technology, Scientific & 
Industrial Research, Science & Technology and expe rts/representatives of the Defence Research 
& Development Organisation, various institut es, industrial federati ons, scientists and Non-
Governmental Organisations; tendered oral ev idence on the various aspects related to ‘The 
Protection and Utilisation of Public Funded Intellectual Property Bill, 2008’. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to  the Officers of the Departments and 
experts/representatives for rendering their valuable views/clarifications sought by the Members of 
the Committee. 
4.      In the meeting held on 7th June, 2010 the Committee considered the draft report and adopted 
the same.  
 
NEW DELHI
;                                                                                         Dr. T. Subbarami Reddy   
7th June, 2010                                                                                    Chairman, 
                     Department-related Pa rliamentary Standing                      
 Committee  on Science & Technology,    Environment & Forests. 
REPORT  
The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of Rule 270 (b) of the Rules relating to 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, referred* ‘The Protection 
and Utilisation of Public Funded Intellectual Property Bill, 2008’(Annexure-I) as 
introduced on 15th December, 2008 in Rajya Sabha and pending therein, to the Standing 
Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests for examination and 
report. 
2. The Committee held its first meeting with  the representatives of Department of 
Bio-technology, for a general discussion on the various provisions of the Bill.   The 
Committee also heard the views of thirteen experts from va rious Institutes, industrial 
federations, scientists and Non-Governmental Organi sations on the subject on              
17th & 24 th December, 2009, 5 th January, 8 th February and 2 nd June, 2010 (Names of 
experts at Annexure-II). The Committee also heard the views of the representatives of the 
Department of Scientific & Industrial Re search, and Defence Research & Development 
Organisation on the 8 th February, 2010 and Department of Science & Technology on the 
2nd June, 2010. Written memoranda containi ng comments/suggestions on the various 
provisions of the Bill were also received fr om some of the experts mentioned above and 
the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalo re. The Committee adopted the Report in its 
meeting held on 7th June, 2010.
